k: symphony no. 1 in g minor “winter daydreams” pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 13 · 1866; revised 1874 orchestra the first two movements bear landscape titles; the finale moves from a slow introduction towards a folk-song-based contrapuntal culmination.

title: Romeo and Juliet
k: romeo and juliet pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky ·  · 1869–80 orchestra three principal versions. the friar’s chorale, the feud and the lovers occupy sharply differentiated harmonic and rhythmic spaces.

title: Piano Concerto No. 1 in B♭ minor
k: piano concerto no. 1 in b♭ minor pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 23 · 1874–75 piano and orchestra its d♭ major introduction stands apart from the first movement’s main theme. hans von bulow gave the premiere in boston in 1875.

title: Swan Lake
k: swan lake pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 20 · 1875–76 ballet in four acts the recurring swan music binds separate scenes together. distinguish the original score from the drigo-altered 1895 performing tradition.

title: Symphony No. 4 in F minor
k: symphony no. 4 in f minor pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 36 · 1877–78 orchestra brass fanfare, troubled 9/8 movement, oboe song, pizzicato scherzo and a finale whose celebration is interrupted by the opening motto.

title: Eugene Onegin
k: eugene onegin pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 24 · 1877–78 opera; soloists, chorus and orchestra “lyrical scenes” after pushkin. tatyana’s letter, lensky’s farewell and the two great party scenes give personal and public time different musical dimensions.

title: Violin Concerto in D major
k: violin concerto in d major pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 35 · 1878 violin and orchestra the first movement’s cadenza is placed before the recapitulation. a g minor canzonetta joins directly to the dance-driven finale.

title: Children’s Album
k: children’s album pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 39 · 1878 piano; twenty-four pieces miniatures in the tradition of schumann’s pedagogical collections; dances, songs, dolls and domestic rituals reduced to playable but characterful textures.

title: Serenade for Strings in C major
k: serenade for strings in c major pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 48 · 1880 string orchestra a broad chordal introduction, a waltz, an elegy and a finale on russian themes; the opening material returns near the end.

title: Piano Trio in A minor
k: piano trio in a minor pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 50 · 1881–82 piano, violin and cello dedicated “to the memory of a great artist”, nikolai rubinstein. a large variation sequence ends by recalling the first movement’s lament.

title: Manfred
k: manfred pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 58 · 1885 orchestra with organ a four-movement programme after byron, worked out through recurrent material; outside the numbering of the six other symphonies.

title: Symphony No. 5 in E minor
k: symphony no. 5 in e minor pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 64 · 1888 orchestra the opening clarinet motto traverses all four movements. the slow movement’s horn solo and the finale’s major-key march test different forms of lyrical expansion.

title: The Sleeping Beauty
k: the sleeping beauty pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 66 · 1888–89 ballet; prologue and three acts petipa’s exact choreographic plan becomes a framework for contrasting dances and recurring character ideas; premiered in 1890.

title: The Queen of Spades
k: the queen of spades pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 68 · 1890 opera after pushkin the three cards acquire a musical identity that competes with the love story; eighteenth-century pastiche makes obsession sound historically out of joint.

title: The Nutcracker
k: the nutcracker pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 71 · 1891–92 ballet in two acts the celesta, children’s chorus and carefully differentiated dances belong to the complete ballet; the familiar op. 71a suite is a separate selection.

title: Symphony No. 6 in B minor “Pathétique”
k: symphony no. 6 in b minor “pathetique” pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · op. 74 · 1893 orchestra a 5/4 dance and a march precede the slow finale. the ending progressively reduces sound instead of converting minor to a victorious major.

title: Antonín Dvořák
k: antonin dvorak 1841–1904 · romanticism a theatre violist who made dance accents, remembered songs and classical development work inside the same movement.

title: Stabat Mater
k: stabat mater antonin dvorak · op. 58 · b 71 · 1876–77 four vocal soloists, chorus and orchestra ten movements connected by thematic and tonal returns; a decisive work in dvorak’s british reception.

title: Slavonic Dances
k: slavonic dances antonin dvorak · opp. 46 and 72 · 1878; 1886 piano four hands; orchestral versions by the composer sixteen newly composed dances using characteristic slavonic dance types.

title: Symphony No. 7 in D minor
k: symphony no. 7 in d minor antonin dvorak · op. 70 · b 141 · 1884–85 orchestra written for london’s philharmonic society. motives are compact, the rhythmic layers frequently conflict, and the final major turn is hard-won within the formal argument.

title: Piano Quintet No. 2 in A major
k: piano quintet no. 2 in a major antonin dvorak · op. 81 · b 155 · 1887 piano, two violins, viola and cello a cello-led opening, an extended dumka and a furiant scherzo; inner parts participate actively in the argument.

title: Symphony No. 8 in G major
k: symphony no. 8 in g major antonin dvorak · op. 88 · b 163 · 1889 orchestra a g minor opening is answered by a g major flute idea. the finale’s variations change orchestral weight as well as the shape of the tune.

title: Symphony No. 9 in E minor “From the New World”
k: symphony no. 9 in e minor “from the new world” antonin dvorak · op. 95 · b 178 · 1893 orchestra, including cor anglais composed in new york and premiered there under anton seidl on 16 december 1893. the finale brings back themes from all three preceding movements.

title: String Quartet No. 12 in F major “American”
k: string quartet no. 12 in f major “american” antonin dvorak · op. 96 · b 179 · 1893 two violins, viola and cello written at spillville. the viola introduces the first theme; pentatonic outlines and clearly differentiated rhythmic figures keep the four parts transparent.

title: Cello Concerto in B minor
k: cello concerto in b minor antonin dvorak · op. 104 · b 191 · 1894–95 cello and orchestra a substantial orchestral exposition precedes the solo entry. the closing recollections include material associated with josefina, the composer’s sister-in-law.

title: The Water Goblin
k: the water goblin antonin dvorak · op. 107 · b 195 · 1896 orchestra erben’s ballad provides a narrative of marriage, captivity and revenge. distinctive rhythmic figures act as recognisable agents in the unfolding story.

title: Rusalka
k: rusalka antonin dvorak · op. 114 · b 203 · 1900 opera in three acts jaroslav kvapil’s libretto makes a water nymph’s loss of speech central to the drama. premiered at prague’s national theatre in 1901.

title: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov
k: nikolai rimsky-korsakov 1844–1908 · romanticism a naval officer turned teacher who made orchestral register and symmetrical scales the machinery of russian fairy-tale opera.

title: Sadko
k: sadko nikolai rimsky-korsakov · op. 5 · 1867; revised 1869, 1892 orchestra an early underwater fantasy and an important laboratory for the symmetrical harmonic language later expanded in the opera.

title: The Snow Maiden
k: the snow maiden nikolai rimsky-korsakov ·  · 1880–81 opera; prologue and four acts after ostrovsky. seasonal ritual, human desire and the heroine’s supernatural origin form one dramatic system; premiered in 1882.

title: Capriccio espagnol
k: capriccio espagnol nikolai rimsky-korsakov · op. 34 · 1887 orchestra five linked movements built around spanish material; solo violin and winds repeatedly emerge from and return to the ensemble.

title: Scheherazade
k: scheherazade nikolai rimsky-korsakov · op. 35 · 1888 orchestra with prominent solo violin four movements after the thousand and one nights. themes change their function and colour as they recur.

title: Russian Easter Festival Overture
k: russian easter festival overture nikolai rimsky-korsakov · op. 36 · 1888 orchestra chant melodies from the orthodox tradition pass from slow, recitative-like presentation to a fast orchestral celebration.

title: Sadko
k: sadko nikolai rimsky-korsakov ·  · 1894–96 opera in seven scenes novgorod merchants, visiting traders and an underwater kingdom; the three visiting guests sing musically differentiated accounts of distant places.

title: The Tsar’s Bride
k: the tsar’s bride nikolai rimsky-korsakov ·  · 1898 opera in four acts a historical tragedy with a more directly lyrical vocal idiom than the fairy-tale operas; poisoning and mistaken identity destroy marfa’s marriage prospects and sanity.

title: The Tale of Tsar Saltan
k: the tale of tsar saltan nikolai rimsky-korsakov ·  · 1899–1900 opera after pushkin the swan princess and the transformed prince gvidon belong to a magic world distinguished by harmony and orchestration. “the flight of the bumblebee” originated as an operatic interlude.

title: The Legend of the Invisible City of Kitezh and the Maiden Fevroniya
k: the legend of the invisible city of kitezh and the maiden fevroniya nikolai rimsky-korsakov ·  · 1903–04; revised 1905 opera in four acts folk legend, invasion and religious transformation; the orchestral interludes are structural links within a much larger vocal drama.

title: The Golden Cockerel
k: the golden cockerel nikolai rimsky-korsakov ·  · 1906–07 opera in three acts with prologue and epilogue pushkin’s tale becomes a satire of autocracy. censorship delayed the premiere until 1909, after the composer’s death.

title: Gabriel Fauré
k: gabriel faure 1845–1924 · the french line a church organist who made the french song and the chamber ensemble laboratories for harmony.

title: Cantique de Jean Racine
k: cantique de jean racine gabriel faure · op. 11 · 1865 mixed chorus and keyboard; later orchestral versions a french paraphrase of the hymn consors paterni luminis. choral entries grow over a continuous accompaniment; written at the ecole niedermeyer.

title: Violin Sonata No. 1 in A major
k: violin sonata no. 1 in a major gabriel faure · op. 13 · 1875–76 violin and piano a four-movement sonata with a full, active piano part. the scherzo’s rapid exchanges require close rhythmic agreement between the players.

title: Piano Quartet No. 1 in C minor
k: piano quartet no. 1 in c minor gabriel faure · op. 15 · 1876–79; finale revised 1883 piano, violin, viola and cello syncopation destabilises the first movement’s firm opening; the slow movement turns the same ensemble towards sustained, closely voiced lament.

title: Pavane in F♯ minor
k: pavane in f♯ minor gabriel faure · op. 50 · 1887 orchestra, with optional mixed chorus flute melody and restrained dance rhythm; the optional montesquiou text introduces the quarrels and poses of a courtly gathering.

title: Requiem in D minor
k: requiem in d minor gabriel faure · op. 48 · 1887–1900 soprano and baritone soloists, chorus, organ and orchestra; several versions from the dark opening to in paradisum. compare the smaller scoring with the expanded 1900 version.

title: La bonne chanson
k: la bonne chanson gabriel faure · op. 61 · 1892–94 voice and piano; later version with piano and string quintet nine verlaine settings joined by recurring themes. piano memories and rapid tonal changes bind the poems into a single work.

title: Nocturne No. 6 in D♭ major
k: nocturne no. 6 in d♭ major gabriel faure · op. 63 · 1894 piano a long-breathed opening gives way to intensified figuration and harmonic movement; that disturbance colours the return.

title: Pelléas et Mélisande
k: pelleas et melisande gabriel faure · op. 80 · 1898 incidental music for orchestra; concert suite written for the london staging with sarah bernhardt. the suite includes the spinning music, the sicilienne and melisande’s death.

title: Piano Quintet No. 2 in C minor
k: piano quintet no. 2 in c minor gabriel faure · op. 115 · 1919–21 piano and string quartet a concentrated late work with a fleet scherzo and an expansive andante moderato. listen below the first violin for the movement of the middle voices.

title: String Quartet in E minor
k: string quartet in e minor gabriel faure · op. 121 · 1923–24 two violins, viola and cello his final work, in three movements. the andante makes sustained lines and changes of harmonic footing carry the expression without keyboard figuration.

title: Leoš Janáček
k: leos janacek 1854–1928 · fin de siecle a moravian composer who studied the inflections of speech and built operas from short cells, repeated figures and abrupt changes of perspective.

title: Jenůfa
k: jenufa leos janacek ·  · 1894–1903; revised later opera in three acts after gabriela preissova; premiered in brno in 1904. the kostelnicka’s crime and confession turn the final act towards forgiveness.

title: On an Overgrown Path
k: on an overgrown path leos janacek ·  · 1900–11 piano short pieces assembled in two series. repeated figures, intimate recollections and sharply different registers anticipate the concentration of the late chamber music.

title: Taras Bulba
k: taras bulba leos janacek ·  · 1915–18 orchestra with organ three movements after gogol, centred on the deaths of andrei, ostap and taras; the last movement turns execution into a defiant orchestral proclamation.

title: Káťa Kabanová
k: kata kabanova leos janacek ·  · 1919–21 opera in three acts after ostrovsky’s the storm. repeating orchestral cells carry the pressure beneath kata’s attempts to speak and act independently.

title: The Cunning Little Vixen
k: the cunning little vixen leos janacek ·  · 1921–23 opera in three acts after tesnohlidek’s newspaper serial and lolek’s drawings; first performed in 1924. the forester’s final scene connects generations without cancelling individual deaths.

title: String Quartet No. 1 “The Kreutzer Sonata”
k: string quartet no. 1 “the kreutzer sonata” leos janacek ·  · 1923 string quartet after tolstoy’s novella. short cells, tremolo and abrupt tempo changes replace any comfortable distinction between lyrical theme and neutral accompaniment.

title: Sinfonietta
k: sinfonietta leos janacek ·  · 1926 orchestra and additional brass ensemble the opening fanfare uses nine trumpets, two bass trumpets, two tenor tubas and timpani; its material returns in the finale on a larger orchestral scale.

title: Glagolitic Mass
k: glagolitic mass leos janacek ·  · 1926; revised 1927 four vocal soloists, mixed chorus, orchestra and organ old church slavonic liturgical text, framed and interrupted by instrumental movements. the original and revised versions differ materially.

title: From the House of the Dead
k: from the house of the dead leos janacek ·  · 1927–28 opera in three acts after dostoevsky; first performed posthumously in 1930 with editorial alterations. prisoners’ narrated lives supply a succession of dramatic centres.

title: String Quartet No. 2 “Intimate Letters”
k: string quartet no. 2 “intimate letters” leos janacek ·  · 1928 string quartet associated in janacek’s letters with kamila stosslova. the viola has particular prominence; an initial plan to use viola d’amore was abandoned.

title: Edward Elgar
k: edward elgar 1857–1934 · fin de siecle a worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.

title: Serenade for Strings in E minor
k: serenade for strings in e minor edward elgar · op. 20 · 1892 string orchestra three movements; the central larghetto gives the lower parts melodic independence.

title: Variations on an Original Theme “Enigma”
k: variations on an original theme “enigma” edward elgar · op. 36 · 1898–99 orchestra; optional organ in the revised finale theme and fourteen variations, dedicated “to my friends pictured within”. the finale recalls alice and jaeger as well as the opening theme.

title: Sea Pictures
k: sea pictures edward elgar · op. 37 · 1899 contralto and orchestra five songs, including a setting of alice elgar’s “in haven”. “the swimmer” requires an unusually wide vocal range and an orchestral conclusion of symphonic weight.

title: The Dream of Gerontius
k: the dream of gerontius edward elgar · op. 38 · 1900 tenor, mezzo-soprano, bass, chorus and orchestra newman’s catholic poem becomes a continuous drama in two parts, with recurring motives connecting earthly death to judgment and purgatory.

title: Introduction and Allegro
k: introduction and allegro edward elgar · op. 47 · 1904–05 solo string quartet and string orchestra a modern concerto grosso: the quartet separates from and rejoins the larger body; a fugue converts string virtuosity into contrapuntal argument.

title: Symphony No. 1 in A♭ major
k: symphony no. 1 in a♭ major edward elgar · op. 55 · 1907–08 orchestra the opening motto frames a four-movement design. the scherzo and adagio are connected without a pause and transform closely related melodic material.

title: Violin Concerto in B minor
k: violin concerto in b minor edward elgar · op. 61 · 1909–10 violin and orchestra dedicated to fritz kreisler. the finale’s accompanied cadenza revisits earlier themes over a delicate orchestral pizzicato.

title: Symphony No. 2 in E♭ major
k: symphony no. 2 in e♭ major edward elgar · op. 63 · 1909–11 orchestra after the energetic opening, c minor funeral procession and hammering scherzo, the finale withdraws into quiet.

title: Piano Quintet in A minor
k: piano quintet in a minor edward elgar · op. 84 · 1918 piano and string quartet an unsettled introduction returns in a large three-movement design; the piano often shares the argument with the strings.

title: Cello Concerto in E minor
k: cello concerto in e minor edward elgar · op. 85 · 1918–19 cello and orchestra four compact movements. solo recitative, a fleet scherzo and a short adagio leave the finale vulnerable to interruption by its own memories.

title: Giacomo Puccini
k: giacomo puccini 1858–1924 · fin de siecle an opera composer who made a remembered tune, a stage noise or a change of orchestral register determine the timing of a scene.

title: Le Villi
k: le villi giacomo puccini ·  · 1883–84; revised later opera; soloists, chorus and orchestra a supernatural revenge story with substantial orchestral narration. its first staging in milan in 1884 brought puccini to ricordi’s attention.

title: Edgar
k: edgar giacomo puccini ·  · 1884–89; revised later opera the four-act first version failed at la scala. puccini repeatedly revised the work, including a reduction to three acts.

title: Manon Lescaut
k: manon lescaut giacomo puccini ·  · 1889–92 opera in four acts premiered in turin in 1893. the orchestral intermezzo between acts ii and iii connects separate locations through thematic recollection.

title: La bohème
k: la boheme giacomo puccini ·  · 1893–95 opera in four tableaux premiered in 1896. the crowded public space of act ii contrasts with the sparsely furnished garret of the outer acts.

title: Tosca
k: tosca giacomo puccini ·  · 1896–99 opera in three acts premiered in rome in 1900. political coercion is audible in the score’s bells, offstage voices, recurring chords and sharply timed interruptions.

title: Madama Butterfly
k: madama butterfly giacomo puccini ·  · 1901–04; revised to 1907 opera; two-act original, subsequently divided and revised the long vigil turns the passage of a night into orchestral drama. consult the version when comparing recordings or productions.

title: La fanciulla del West
k: la fanciulla del west giacomo puccini ·  · 1907–10 opera in three acts a mining-camp drama after belasco, premiered at the metropolitan opera. the card game makes concealed information and orchestral tension work together.

title: La rondine
k: la rondine giacomo puccini ·  · 1914–16; revised later opera in three acts premiered in monte carlo in 1917. waltz and conversational writing preserve traces of the original operetta commission.

title: Il trittico
k: il trittico giacomo puccini ·  · 1913–18 three one-act operas il tabarro, suor angelica and gianni schicchi: murder, religious tragedy and a florentine comedy about a forged will.

title: Turandot
k: turandot giacomo puccini ·  · 1920–24 opera in three acts; unfinished premiered in 1926. the huge chorus, percussion and imported chinese melodies serve a public ritual of riddles and executions; the final duet survives only in sketches and completions.

title: Gustav Mahler
k: gustav mahler 1860–1911 · fin de siecle a conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.

title: Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen
k: lieder eines fahrenden gesellen gustav mahler ·  · 1884–85 voice and orchestra; mahler’s own texts four songs about a jilted journeyman. the second and fourth supply themes for the first symphony.

title: Symphony No. 1 in D major
k: symphony no. 1 in d major gustav mahler ·  · 1888 orchestra begins in a haze of string harmonics and birdcalls; the third movement is the frere jacques funeral march. premiered in budapest in 1889 as a “symphonic poem in two parts”; the nickname “titan” was dropped by mahler himself.

title: Symphony No. 2 “Resurrection”
k: symphony no. 2 “resurrection” gustav mahler ·  · 1888–94 soprano, alto, chorus, orchestra, offstage brass and percussion from a c minor funeral rite to a choral e♭ major. in the finale, the offstage band and an onstage flute and piccolo trade calls — the “great summons” — before the choir enters almost inaudibly.

title: Symphony No. 3 in D minor
k: symphony no. 3 in d minor gustav mahler ·  · 1893–96 alto, women’s and boys’ choirs, orchestra, offstage posthorn six movements, nearly a hundred minutes. the first movement alone, with its brass and percussion march, outlasts many complete symphonies. the finale is a slow movement, a hymn for strings that builds to a blazing d major — an ending mahler would return to, transformed, in the ninth.

title: Symphony No. 4 in G major
k: symphony no. 4 in g major gustav mahler ·  · 1899–1900 soprano and a classically sized orchestra (no trombones) the lightest and most ironic. in the scherzo the leader plays a second violin tuned a tone high, for a scratchy “death strikes up the dance”. the finale is a child’s vision of heaven from des knaben wunderhorn.

title: Kindertotenlieder
k: kindertotenlieder gustav mahler ·  · 1901–04 voice and orchestra; poems by friedrich ruckert five settings of poems ruckert wrote after losing two children. completed three years before mahler lost his own daughter.

title: Symphony No. 5
k: symphony no. 5 gustav mahler ·  · 1901–02 orchestra opens with a solo trumpet’s funeral fanfare in c♯ minor and ends in d major with a contrapuntal rondo. the fourth movement, the adagietto for strings and harp, is his best-known music.

title: Symphony No. 6 in A minor
k: symphony no. 6 in a minor gustav mahler ·  · 1903–04 large orchestra with hammer, cowbells, celesta the most classically built of the symphonies and the bleakest. a march-like motto rhythm and a major-to-minor chord recur like a verdict; the finale is a thirty-minute struggle in which the hammer falls.

title: Symphony No. 7
k: symphony no. 7 gustav mahler ·  · 1904–05 orchestra with tenor horn, mandolin, guitar, cowbells two nachtmusik movements frame a spectral scherzo marked schattenhaft (shadowy). schoenberg admired it above the others, and wrote to mahler about it after hearing it in vienna in 1909.

title: Symphony No. 8 in E♭ major
k: symphony no. 8 in e♭ major gustav mahler ·  · 1906 eight soloists, two mixed choirs, boys’ choir, very large orchestra, organ part i sets the ninth-century hymn veni, creator spiritus; part ii, the last scene of goethe’s faust, ending on the chorus mysticus: “all that is transient is only a likeness.”

title: Das Lied von der Erde
k: das lied von der erde gustav mahler ·  · 1908–09 tenor, alto (or baritone) and orchestra six songs on hans bethge’s free german versions of tang-dynasty poems. the last, der abschied (the farewell), lasts half an hour and ends on the word ewig — forever — repeated into silence. mahler added the final lines himself.

title: Symphony No. 9
k: symphony no. 9 gustav mahler ·  · 1909–10 orchestra begins in d major with a halting, syncopated figure in the cellos and horn and ends in d♭ with an adagio that thins to nothing, marked ersterbend — dying away. berg called the first movement the most heavenly thing mahler ever wrote.

title: Symphony No. 10 (unfinished)
k: symphony no. 10 (unfinished) gustav mahler ·  · 1910 orchestra mahler left the adagio almost fully scored and the rest in a continuous short score covered in anguished notes to alma. deryck cooke’s performing version (final form 1976) is the most often played.

title: Claude Debussy
k: claude debussy 1862–1918 · the french line he made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.

title: Ariettes oubliées
k: ariettes oubliees claude debussy ·  · 1885–87 voice and piano; poems by verlaine six songs in which rain, repetition and speech inflection become pianistic and harmonic processes. il pleure dans mon cœur makes the keyboard’s repeated motion independent of the vocal sentence.

title: Suite bergamasque
k: suite bergamasque claude debussy ·  · 1890; revised 1905 piano four pieces including clair de lune. the collection’s publication history matters: the familiar printed text belongs to the composer’s mature period of revision.

title: String Quartet in G minor
k: string quartet in g minor claude debussy · op. 10 · 1893 two violins, viola and cello an opening idea returns across four movements, altered by rhythm and texture. pizzicato and bowing colour are part of its cyclic construction.

title: Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune
k: prelude a l’apres-midi d’un faune claude debussy ·  · 1894 orchestra with three flutes and two harps; no trumpets or trombones after mallarme’s poem. an unaccompanied flute line begins before the listener has a harmonic foundation; later returns continually reinterpret it.

title: Chansons de Bilitis
k: chansons de bilitis claude debussy ·  · 1897–98 voice and piano; prose poems by pierre louys three settings of invented ancient greek poems, actually written by louys. speech, sparse accompaniment and changing harmonic perspective replace a regular strophic song.

title: Nocturnes
k: nocturnes claude debussy ·  · 1899 orchestra; women’s chorus in sirenes nuages, fetes and sirenes: slow shifts, approaching procession and a human voice used without words. the first two movements were premiered in 1900, the complete triptych in 1901.

title: Pelléas et Mélisande
k: pelleas et melisande claude debussy ·  · 1902 opera in five acts; maeterlinck’s french prose begun in 1893. golaud, pelleas and melisande speak in short phrases while the orchestra carries continuities they cannot articulate; first performed at the opera-comique.

title: Estampes
k: estampes claude debussy ·  · 1903 piano pagodes, la soiree dans grenade, jardins sous la pluie. layered resonance, habanera and transformed nursery songs make three distinct formal designs.

title: La Mer
k: la mer claude debussy ·  · 1905 orchestra three symphonic sketches, composed in 1903–05. returning material and changes in the scale of rhythmic activity connect the movements.

title: Images, Books I and II
k: images, books i and ii claude debussy ·  · 1905–07 piano six pieces including reflets dans l’eau, hommage a rameau and poissons d’or. in book ii, three staves help keep simultaneous registers legible.

title: Children’s Corner
k: children’s corner claude debussy ·  · 1906–08 piano dedicated to chouchou. the final cakewalk interrupts its syncopated dance with an ironic allusion to tristan.

title: Préludes, Book I
k: preludes, book i claude debussy ·  · 1909–10 piano twelve pieces; includes voiles, des pas sur la neige, la cathedrale engloutie and minstrels. titles appear after the music.

title: Préludes, Book II
k: preludes, book ii claude debussy ·  · 1911–13 piano includes brouillards, la terrasse des audiences du clair de lune and feux d’artifice. registral separation and the superposition of distinct note collections become especially exposed.

title: Images for orchestra
k: images for orchestra claude debussy ·  · 1912 orchestra completed after work beginning in 1905. gigues, the three-part iberia and rondes de printemps draw on dance and remembered song.

title: Jeux
k: jeux claude debussy ·  · 1912–13 orchestra; ballet for the ballets russes short figures, unstable pacing and continuously changing instrumental combinations. the tennis scenario belongs to the stage; the score’s changes remain intelligible without it.

title: Études
k: etudes claude debussy ·  · 1915 piano twelve studies dedicated to chopin’s memory. technical restrictions become compositional subjects, from five-finger patterns to repeated notes and contrasted sonorities.

title: Sonata for flute, viola and harp
k: sonata for flute, viola and harp claude debussy ·  · 1915 flute, viola and harp pastorale, interlude and finale. the three instruments can neither blend nor sustain in the same way; changes of partnership determine the texture.

title: Violin Sonata
k: violin sonata claude debussy ·  · 1916–17 violin and piano the third and last completed sonata of a projected six. sudden changes of motion, register and character compress its three movements.

title: Richard Strauss
k: richard strauss 1864–1949 · fin de siecle an orchestral storyteller who took opera to the harmonic edge in salome and elektra, then made conversation and recollection its central events.

title: Don Juan
k: don juan richard strauss · op. 20 · 1888 orchestra after nikolaus lenau; premiered in weimar in 1889. an e major opening rush meets a final collapse into e minor.

title: Till Eulenspiegels lustige Streiche
k: till eulenspiegels lustige streiche richard strauss · op. 28 · 1894–95 orchestra a horn’s long, rhythmically displaced phrase and a clarinet’s short gesture identify the prankster within a rondo design.

title: Also sprach Zarathustra
k: also sprach zarathustra richard strauss · op. 30 · 1896 large orchestra and organ freely after nietzsche. the sunrise fanfare opens a half-hour tonal argument.

title: Don Quixote
k: don quixote richard strauss · op. 35 · 1896–97 orchestra with solo cello and viola “fantastic variations on a theme of knightly character”: ten adventures followed by the knight’s return to reason and death.

title: Ein Heldenleben
k: ein heldenleben richard strauss · op. 40 · 1897–98 large orchestra with extensive solo violin hero, critics, companion, battle, works and withdrawal; quotations from earlier strauss scores make the self-portrait explicit.

title: Salome
k: salome richard strauss · op. 54 · 1903–05 opera in one act oscar wilde in hedwig lachmann’s german translation. a continuous act culminates in salome’s address to jochanaan’s severed head.

title: Elektra
k: elektra richard strauss · op. 58 · 1906–08 opera in one act; very large orchestra premiered in 1909. harmonic collisions and compulsively returning motives organise the tragedy; orest’s recognition scene opens a contrasting lyrical space.

title: Der Rosenkavalier
k: der rosenkavalier richard strauss · op. 59 · 1909–10 opera in three acts premiered in 1911. the silver-rose presentation, the marschallin’s reflections and the final trio coexist with baron ochs’s coarse comedy.

title: Ariadne auf Naxos
k: ariadne auf naxos richard strauss · op. 60 · 1911–12; revised 1916 opera with chamber orchestra in the familiar revision, a backstage prologue explains why a tragedy and a comic troupe must perform simultaneously.

title: Eine Alpensinfonie
k: eine alpensinfonie richard strauss · op. 64 · 1911–15 large orchestra, offstage brass, organ, wind and thunder machines a continuous ascent and descent in twenty-two titled sections; the return to night closes both the itinerary and the tonal design.

title: Metamorphosen
k: metamorphosen richard strauss · trv 290 · 1944–45 twenty-three solo strings a continuous contrapuntal study whose closing bass quotes the funeral march from beethoven’s eroica.

title: Four Last Songs
k: four last songs richard strauss · trv 296 · 1948 soprano and orchestra three hesse settings and eichendorff’s “im abendrot”, assembled under their collective title after strauss’s death; first performed in 1950.

title: Jean Sibelius
k: jean sibelius 1865–1957 · fin de siecle a symphonist who let small figures gather into themes and movements change shape while their underlying pulse continued.

title: Kullervo
k: kullervo jean sibelius · op. 7 · 1891–92 soprano, baritone, male chorus and orchestra five movements after the kalevala; finnish verse governs the choral declamation and the long narrative third movement.

title: Lemminkäinen
k: lemminkainen jean sibelius · op. 22 · 1895–96; revised later orchestra includes the swan of tuonela and lemminkainen’s return. the order and scoring changed during a long revision history.

title: Symphony No. 1 in E minor
k: symphony no. 1 in e minor jean sibelius · op. 39 · 1898–99; revised 1900 orchestra a solitary clarinet over timpani begins a four-movement symphony; the finale brings back the introduction in a transformed string statement.

title: Finlandia
k: finlandia jean sibelius · op. 26 · 1899–1900 orchestra reworked from music for the 1899 press celebrations. the orchestral hymn preceded its familiar sung texts.

title: Symphony No. 2 in D major
k: symphony no. 2 in d major jean sibelius · op. 43 · 1901–02 orchestra fragmentary first-movement ideas and the scherzo’s transition prepare a broad finale.

title: Violin Concerto in D minor
k: violin concerto in d minor jean sibelius · op. 47 · 1903–04; revised 1905 violin and orchestra the first-movement cadenza participates in the development. the revised version is standard, but the substantially different original is also recorded.

title: Symphony No. 3 in C major
k: symphony no. 3 in c major jean sibelius · op. 52 · 1904–07 orchestra three movements; the finale turns dispersed scherzo figures into a firm closing theme.

title: Symphony No. 4 in A minor
k: symphony no. 4 in a minor jean sibelius · op. 63 · 1910–11 orchestra tritones, exposed instrumental lines and interrupted continuity; its slow movement assembles a long melody from incomplete statements.

title: Symphony No. 5 in E♭ major
k: symphony no. 5 in e♭ major jean sibelius · op. 82 · 1915; revised 1916 and 1919 orchestra the final three-movement version joins an opening span and scherzo; the finale’s broad horn figure leads eventually to six chords separated by silence.

title: Symphony No. 6
k: symphony no. 6 jean sibelius · op. 104 · 1918–23 orchestra often described as “in d minor”, though sibelius did not supply a key in the title. dorian inflection, string polyphony and a quiet ending distinguish it.

title: Symphony No. 7 in C major
k: symphony no. 7 in c major jean sibelius · op. 105 · 1918–24 orchestra one continuous movement, first performed as fantasia sinfonica. three appearances of a trombone theme articulate its changing tempos.

title: Tapiola
k: tapiola jean sibelius · op. 112 · 1926 orchestra the forest domain of tapio, expressed through tightly related motives.

title: Erik Satie
k: erik satie 1866–1925 · the french line a cabaret pianist who separated repetition from development, and musical seriousness from ceremonial behaviour.

title: Trois Sarabandes
k: trois sarabandes erik satie ·  · 1887 piano slow triple-time pieces with extended chords. their dates are important to the later debate about satie’s relationship to debussy and ravel.

title: Trois Gymnopédies
k: trois gymnopedies erik satie ·  · 1888 piano bass on the first beat, chord on the second, melody crossing the repeated pattern. debussy later orchestrated nos. 1 and 3.

title: Trois Gnossiennes
k: trois gnossiennes erik satie ·  · c. 1890 piano the first published group uses unbarred notation and verbal directions. additional pieces received the title posthumously, forming the familiar six-piece set.

title: Vexations
k: vexations erik satie ·  · 1893 keyboard a short chromatic motif and harmonisations, with the instruction mentioning 840 repetitions. modern marathon performances began long after satie’s death.

title: Embryons desséchés
k: embryons desseches erik satie ·  · 1913 piano three pieces whose annotations, quotations and inflated cadences parody musical description and the etiquette of a grand ending.

title: Sports et divertissements
k: sports et divertissements erik satie ·  · 1914 piano, with written texts and drawings by charles martin twenty miniature scenes and a prefatory chorale; a combined visual, verbal and musical publication.

title: Parade
k: parade erik satie ·  · 1916–17 orchestra with additional noise-making instruments; ballet cocteau, picasso and massine collaborated on the ballets russes production. repeated popular-style blocks match the parade of competing attractions.

title: Socrate
k: socrate erik satie ·  · 1917–18 female voices and chamber orchestra; version with piano three movements on plato in victor cousin’s french translation, ending with socrates’s death. narration takes the place of operatic impersonation.

title: Relâche, with Cinéma for Entr’acte
k: relache, with cinema for entr’acte erik satie ·  · 1924 orchestra; ballet and film picabia’s ballets suedois production incorporates rene clair’s film. the score for the film uses repeatable units to coordinate music and projected action.

title: Alexander Scriabin
k: alexander scriabin 1872–1915 · fin de siecle a pianist who replaced the need for a resolving tonic with recurring harmonic fields, accelerating figures and carefully organised light.

title: Twenty-four Preludes
k: twenty-four preludes alexander scriabin · op. 11 · 1888–96 piano all twenty-four major and minor keys in a chopin-derived ordering; short pieces already make rhythm and voice-leading disturb their familiar genres.

title: Piano Sonata No. 2 in G♯ minor “Sonata-Fantasy”
k: piano sonata no. 2 in g♯ minor “sonata-fantasy” alexander scriabin · op. 19 · 1892–97 piano two movements: a sustained andante and a fast, continuously active presto. the contrast depends on figuration and register as much as on tempo.

title: Piano Concerto in F♯ minor
k: piano concerto in f♯ minor alexander scriabin · op. 20 · 1896 piano and orchestra three movements, with a central variation set. it provides a useful point of comparison with the later orchestral works in which the piano is no longer a conventional concerto protagonist.

title: Piano Sonata No. 4 in F♯ major
k: piano sonata no. 4 in f♯ major alexander scriabin · op. 30 · 1903 piano an andante followed without a break by prestissimo volando; earlier material returns transformed by speed and dynamic force.

title: The Poem of Ecstasy
k: the poem of ecstasy alexander scriabin · op. 54 · 1905–08 large orchestra with organ a single movement with a prominent trumpet idea and a final c major culmination; premiered in new york in 1908.

title: Piano Sonata No. 5
k: piano sonata no. 5 alexander scriabin · op. 53 · 1907 piano one movement, sharply alternating suspension and propulsion. its printed poetic epigraph connects it with the imaginative world of the poem of ecstasy.

title: Prometheus: The Poem of Fire
k: prometheus: the poem of fire alexander scriabin · op. 60 · 1909–10 piano, large orchestra, organ, optional chorus and colour keyboard premiered in moscow in 1911 without the intended lights. the luce staff contains a locally changing line and a much slower layer.

title: Piano Sonata No. 9
k: piano sonata no. 9 alexander scriabin · op. 68 · 1912–13 piano the nickname “black mass” was not supplied by the composer. short motives and a gathering march-like motion transform the initial material without a key signature.

title: Piano Sonata No. 10
k: piano sonata no. 10 alexander scriabin · op. 70 · 1912–13 piano trills multiply until ornament becomes an organising texture. the single movement repeatedly changes the scale and density of its figuration.

title: Vers la flamme
k: vers la flamme alexander scriabin · op. 72 · 1914 piano a compact study in increasing activity: separated sonorities become repeated attacks and tremulous motion.

title: Sergei Rachmaninoff
k: sergei rachmaninoff 1873–1943 · fin de siecle a composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried russian chant into the concertos and dances of his american exile.

title: Piano Concerto No. 1 in F♯ minor
k: piano concerto no. 1 in f♯ minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 1 · 1891; revised 1917 piano and orchestra dedicated to siloti. the mature revision tightens the orchestration and piano writing of the student concerto; this is the version usually heard.

title: Aleko
k: aleko sergei rachmaninoff ·  · 1892 one-act opera; soloists, chorus and orchestra the conservatory examination opera, after pushkin’s the gypsies. premiered at the bolshoi in 1893; its extended bass cavatina gives the jealous outsider a history before the final murders.

title: Prelude in C♯ minor
k: prelude in c♯ minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 3 no. 2 · 1892 piano from morceaux de fantaisie. three descending pitches, an agitated triplet middle section, and a return enlarged across four staves.

title: Trio élégiaque No. 2 in D minor
k: trio elegiaque no. 2 in d minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 9 · 1893 piano, violin and cello written in memory of tchaikovsky. a substantial variation movement sits between the opening lament and a finale that ultimately returns to funeral music.

title: Symphony No. 1 in D minor
k: symphony no. 1 in d minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 13 · 1895 orchestra a motto and related thematic cells connect all four movements. the failed 1897 premiere obscured a work whose sharp accents and compressed gestures differ markedly from the second symphony; revived in 1945.

title: Six Moments musicaux
k: six moments musicaux sergei rachmaninoff · op. 16 · 1896 piano six contrasted studies in sustained melody, repeated notes, counterpoint and keyboard span. no. 4 in e minor sets its melody above continuous left-hand semiquavers.

title: Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor
k: piano concerto no. 2 in c minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 18 · 1900–01 piano and orchestra dedicated to nikolai dahl. the piano’s opening tolling gives way to an orchestral melody over arpeggios; the finale’s lyrical second subject eventually returns in c major.

title: Sonata in G minor
k: sonata in g minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 19 · 1901 cello and piano four movements with an expansive, independent piano part. the e♭ major andante makes its effect through the exchange of melody and accompaniment.

title: Ten Preludes · Thirteen Preludes
k: ten preludes · thirteen preludes sergei rachmaninoff · opp. 23 and 32 · 1901–03; 1910 piano with op. 3 no. 2, these cover all twenty-four major and minor keys. the g minor march, op. 23 no. 5, and the b minor prelude, op. 32 no. 10, belong to collections ranging from two-part studies to densely voiced chordal writing.

title: Symphony No. 2 in E minor
k: symphony no. 2 in e minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 27 · 1906–07 orchestra premiered in 1908. recurring material connects the slow introduction, scherzo, clarinet-led adagio and e major finale; an uncut performance preserves the scale of these returns.

title: Isle of the Dead
k: isle of the dead sergei rachmaninoff · op. 29 · 1909 orchestra after bocklin’s painting, first encountered as a monochrome reproduction. the recurring 5/8 motion, central expansion and dies irae references make a single continuous movement of about twenty minutes.

title: Piano Concerto No. 3 in D minor
k: piano concerto no. 3 in d minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 30 · 1909 piano and orchestra dedicated to josef hofmann and premiered by the composer under walter damrosch. the unadorned opening theme supplies an unusually large first-movement argument, including two alternative cadenzas.

title: Études-tableaux
k: etudes-tableaux sergei rachmaninoff · opp. 33 and 39 · 1911; 1916–17 piano “study-pictures”: technical problems become dramatic structures. rachmaninoff usually withheld their programmes, but disclosed several to respighi when the latter orchestrated a selection, including the sea and seagulls behind op. 39 no. 2.

title: The Bells
k: the bells sergei rachmaninoff · op. 35 · 1913 soprano, tenor, baritone, chorus and orchestra four movements after poe in balmont’s russian: sleigh, wedding, alarm and funeral bells. the chorus alone provides the vocal part of the third movement; the final lament begins with cor anglais.

title: All-Night Vigil
k: all-night vigil sergei rachmaninoff · op. 37 · 1915 unaccompanied mixed choir, alto and tenor solos fifteen church slavonic settings, ten based on existing chant. divided voices, changing registers and contrapuntal entries give a single melodic line the scale of an orchestral movement.

title: Piano Concerto No. 4 in G minor
k: piano concerto no. 4 in g minor sergei rachmaninoff · op. 40 · 1926; revised 1928 and 1941 piano and orchestra the first concerto completed in exile, dedicated to nikolai medtner. its compressed statements, restless transitions and exposed exchanges between soloist and orchestra resist the continuous melodic breadth expected after the second.

title: Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini
k: rhapsody on a theme of paganini sergei rachmaninoff · op. 43 · 1934 piano and orchestra twenty-four variations on paganini’s last solo-violin caprice. variation 1 precedes the theme; no. 7 introduces the dies irae; no. 18 turns a thematic cell upside down in d♭ major. premiered by rachmaninoff and stokowski in baltimore.

title: Symphonic Dances
k: symphonic dances sergei rachmaninoff · op. 45 · 1940 orchestra, including alto saxophone and piano; also a version for two pianos three dances dedicated to ormandy and philadelphia. the first symphony returns in the first; the vigil and dies irae contend in the last. his final completed composition.

title: Charles Ives
k: charles ives 1874–1954 · modernism a church organist and insurance executive who made hymns, marching bands and incompatible tempos coexist inside concert music.

title: Variations on “America”
k: variations on “america” charles ives ·  · 1891 organ a teenager’s set of variations on the tune also used for god save the king. ives later revised the piece; its orchestral arrangement is by william schuman.

title: Symphony No. 2
k: symphony no. 2 charles ives ·  · 1897–1902 orchestra european symphonic writing and american tunes share the same five-movement structure. leonard bernstein conducted the first performance in 1951.

title: Symphony No. 3 “The Camp Meeting”
k: symphony no. 3 “the camp meeting” charles ives ·  · 1901–04; revised 1909 chamber orchestra three movements draw on hymn tunes and earlier church music. lou harrison conducted the premiere in 1946; the work won the 1947 pulitzer prize.

title: A Symphony: New England Holidays
k: a symphony: new england holidays charles ives ·  · 1904–13 orchestra; chorus in the final movement washington’s birthday, decoration day, the fourth of july and thanksgiving and forefathers’ day. separate occasions retain their distinct musical procedures within the assembled cycle.

title: Central Park in the Dark
k: central park in the dark charles ives ·  · 1906 chamber orchestra, including two pianos quiet strings provide a continuing background beneath accumulating urban sounds and quoted popular music. the foreground disperses without converting the background into its own tempo.

title: The Unanswered Question
k: the unanswered question charles ives ·  · c. 1906–08; revised 1930s trumpet, four woodwinds and strings three layers: the slow strings, the trumpet’s repeated question and increasingly agitated wind answers. early datings differ; the familiar version includes later revisions.

title: Three Places in New England
k: three places in new england charles ives ·  · c. 1908–14; revised 1929 orchestra; also a reduced-orchestra version boston’s shaw memorial, a child at putnam’s camp and the housatonic river. the set reworks earlier material and exists in more than one orchestral version.

title: Symphony No. 4
k: symphony no. 4 charles ives ·  · 1910–25 large orchestra, chorus, keyboards and separately coordinated groups most composition belongs to the 1910s; the wider date range includes revision. its complete premiere took place in 1965, eleven years after ives’s death.

title: Piano Sonata No. 2 “Concord, Mass., 1840–60”
k: piano sonata no. 2 “concord, mass., 1840–60” charles ives ·  · 1911–19; revised to 1947 piano; optional additional flute and viola passages emerson, hawthorne, the alcotts and thoreau, linked by recurrent thematic material. printed in 1920 and circulated in 1921; a substantially revised edition appeared in 1947.

title: 114 Songs
k: 114 songs charles ives ·  · 1922 voice and piano a self-published collection assembling decades of work, with tonal songs beside experimental and political ones.

title: Arnold Schoenberg
k: arnold schoenberg 1874–1951 · modernism a viennese teacher who took motivic development beyond the key signature, then made twelve notes carry the work of a tonal system.

title: Verklärte Nacht
k: verklarte nacht arnold schoenberg · op. 4 · 1899 two violins, two violas and two cellos; later arranged for string orchestra dehmel’s poem supplies five broad sections. d minor becomes d major as the man accepts the woman and her unborn child.

title: Gurre-Lieder
k: gurre-lieder arnold schoenberg ·  · 1900–11 soloists, speaker, choruses and very large orchestra most of the composition dates from 1900–01; the orchestration was completed in 1911. jens peter jacobsen’s danish poems reach schoenberg through robert franz arnold’s german translation.

title: Chamber Symphony No. 1 in E major
k: chamber symphony no. 1 in e major arnold schoenberg · op. 9 · 1906 fifteen solo instruments a continuous movement with scherzo and slow sections, opened by fourth-built and whole-tone harmonies. five solo strings stand against ten wind instruments.

title: String Quartet No. 2
k: string quartet no. 2 arnold schoenberg · op. 10 · 1907–08 string quartet; soprano in movements iii and iv the f♯ minor opening belongs to a work whose george settings move beyond a governing key. the finale nevertheless ends on an f♯ major chord.

title: Five Orchestral Pieces
k: five orchestral pieces arnold schoenberg · op. 16 · 1909 large orchestra; revised scoring 1949 the third piece, farben, makes changes of instrumental colour a structural event. the titles were added after composition.

title: Erwartung
k: erwartung arnold schoenberg · op. 17 · 1909 soprano and orchestra; monodrama to a text by marie pappenheim a single woman’s nocturnal search, in four scenes without a break. first staged in prague in 1924 under alexander zemlinsky.

title: Pierrot lunaire
k: pierrot lunaire arnold schoenberg · op. 21 · 1912 speaking voice and five instrumentalists twenty-one melodramas in three groups of seven. the instrumental changes, strict counterpoint and speech-song deliver different readings of hartleben’s grotesque moon poems.

title: Suite for Piano
k: suite for piano arnold schoenberg · op. 25 · 1921–23 piano one twelve-note row serves every movement, including gavotte, musette, minuet and gigue. the last four notes conceal the b–a–c–h signature in reverse.

title: Variations for Orchestra
k: variations for orchestra arnold schoenberg · op. 31 · 1926–28 orchestra introduction, theme, nine variations and finale. twelve-tone counterpoint is projected across the orchestra; a b–a–c–h figure is explicitly heard in the work.

title: Moses und Aron
k: moses und aron arnold schoenberg ·  · 1930–32 opera for soloists, chorus and orchestra; two acts completed moses’s speech and aron’s tenor singing embody a dispute over thought and representation. the third act survives as text alone.

title: Piano Concerto
k: piano concerto arnold schoenberg · op. 42 · 1942 piano and orchestra four linked sections replace separate movements. the opening waltz-like metre and the closing rondo make the music’s phrase shapes audible before its serial construction is analysed.

title: A Survivor from Warsaw
k: a survivor from warsaw arnold schoenberg · op. 46 · 1947 narrator, men’s chorus and orchestra a brief dramatic account in english and german ends with the hebrew shema yisrael. schoenberg assembled the text himself.

title: Maurice Ravel
k: maurice ravel 1875–1937 · the french line an engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.

title: Pavane pour une infante défunte
k: pavane pour une infante defunte maurice ravel ·  · 1899; orch. 1910 piano; later orchestra a g major processional dance with a recurring refrain. the title imagines a past spanish court; the orchestral opening gives the melody to a solo horn.

title: Jeux d’eau
k: jeux d’eau maurice ravel ·  · 1901 piano dedicated to faure. added-note arpeggios, pedal resonance and widely separated registers make water an exercise in keyboard acoustics; two thematic ideas give the short work its formal organisation.

title: String Quartet in F major
k: string quartet in f major maurice ravel ·  · 1902–03 two violins, viola and cello four movements connected by recurring thematic material. listen for the second movement’s pizzicato attacks and its friction between groups of two and three; the slow movement stretches the same instrumental family across widely separated registers.

title: Shéhérazade
k: sheherazade maurice ravel ·  · 1903 voice and orchestra; poems by tristan klingsor three songs: asie, la flute enchantee and l’indifferent. the first expands a fantasy of travel; the others narrow the frame to overheard music and an unresolved encounter. the earlier orchestral overture shares the title.

title: Miroirs
k: miroirs maurice ravel ·  · 1904–05 piano five pieces dedicated to members of les apaches: moths, birds, a boat, a spanish morning song and bells. ravel later orchestrated two of them: une barque sur l’ocean and alborada del gracioso.

title: Rapsodie espagnole
k: rapsodie espagnole maurice ravel ·  · 1907–08 orchestra four movements: prelude a la nuit, malaguena, habanera and feria. the habanera reuses the 1895 two-piano piece; the opening descending ostinato returns within a score whose colours depend on sharply controlled instrumental registers.

title: Gaspard de la nuit
k: gaspard de la nuit maurice ravel ·  · 1908 piano; after aloysius bertrand ondine, le gibet, scarbo: a water spirit, a hanged man and a nocturnal dwarf. the central movement’s persistent b♭ bell is a test of evenness and balance; the outer pieces demand rapid repeated notes without losing the melodic layer.

title: Ma mère l’Oye
k: ma mere l’oye maurice ravel ·  · 1908–10; ballet 1911–12 piano duet; orchestral suite and expanded ballet five original pieces, from sleeping beauty’s pavane to le jardin feerique. the ballet expands the shorter concert suite with a prelude, a spinning-wheel scene and connecting music.

title: Daphnis et Chloé
k: daphnis et chloe maurice ravel ·  · 1909–12 ballet: large orchestra and wordless mixed chorus a choreographic symphony in three parts for diaghilev. suite no. 2 joins lever du jour, pantomime and danse generale; the complete ballet supplies the abduction, the nocturnal intervention of pan and the thematic connections omitted by the suite.

title: Piano Trio in A minor
k: piano trio in a minor maurice ravel ·  · 1914 piano, violin and cello a 3+2+3 opening, a pantoum scherzo, an eight-bar passacaglia theme and a finale with changing metres. ravel separates the string registers and places piano figuration between them to preserve balance.

title: Le Tombeau de Couperin
k: le tombeau de couperin maurice ravel ·  · 1914–17; orch. 1919 piano; four-movement orchestral version the six piano movements memorialise seven men killed in the war. the orchestral sequence is prelude, forlane, menuet, rigaudon; the fugue and toccata remain piano pieces. the oboe’s rapid opening shows how articulation governs the transfer alongside pitch.

title: La Valse
k: la valse maurice ravel ·  · 1919–20 orchestra; also versions for piano and for two pianos a choreographic poem in which viennese waltz fragments emerge, accumulate and finally lose their equilibrium. ravel resisted the claim that it represented the fall of the habsburg empire; the score’s ballroom is dated around 1855.

title: Pictures at an Exhibition — orchestration
k: pictures at an exhibition — orchestration maurice ravel ·  · 1922 orchestra, including alto saxophone, celesta, two harps and percussion commissioned by serge koussevitzky. compare the saxophone of the old castle, the high tuba of bydło and the brass-and-bell architecture of the finale with mussorgsky’s 1874 piano score.

title: L’Enfant et les sortilèges
k: l’enfant et les sortileges maurice ravel ·  · 1917–25 one-act opera: soloists, chorus and orchestra; libretto by colette furniture, crockery, fire, animals and trees answer a destructive child. a foxtrot, coloratura and older dance styles distinguish the characters. premiered in monte carlo in 1925 under victor de sabata.

title: Boléro
k: bolero maurice ravel ·  · 1928 ballet for large orchestra, including saxophones and two snare drums two melodies, a repeated two-bar rhythm and a sustained crescendo. the near-end shift from c major to e major is a formal event precisely because the preceding repetitions have withheld ordinary modulation and development.

title: Piano Concerto for the Left Hand in D major
k: piano concerto for the left hand in d major maurice ravel ·  · 1929–30 left-hand piano and orchestra written for paul wittgenstein. one continuous movement links slow, low-register music to a fast central section; pedalling and rapid leaps allow one hand to sustain bass, accompaniment and melody.

title: Piano Concerto in G major
k: piano concerto in g major maurice ravel ·  · 1929–31 piano and orchestra the outer movements combine clear forms with jazz inflections and abrupt instrumental exchanges. the e major slow movement gives an extended melody first to the piano, later to the cor anglais. dedicated to marguerite long.

title: Don Quichotte à Dulcinée
k: don quichotte a dulcinee maurice ravel ·  · 1932–33 baritone and piano or orchestra; poems by paul morand three songs: a lover’s pledge, a prayer and a drinking song. originally intended for pabst’s film with chaliapin, but not used in it. ravel’s last completed composition; the film received music by jacques ibert.

title: Béla Bartók
k: bela bartok 1881–1945 · modernism a pianist and fieldworker who turned the modes, rhythms and performance habits of peasant music into new kinds of quartet and orchestral argument.

title: String Quartet No. 1
k: string quartet no. 1 bela bartok · op. 7 · sz. 40 · bb 52 · 1908–09 two violins, viola and cello three connected movements lead from a slow contrapuntal opening towards fast dance. a motif associated with stefi geyer undergoes thematic development.

title: Duke Bluebeard’s Castle
k: duke bluebeard’s castle bela bartok · op. 11 · sz. 48 · bb 62 · 1911 two singers, spoken prologue and orchestra bela balazs’s one-act drama of seven doors. composed in 1911 and revised before the 1918 budapest premiere; the fifth door’s c major expansion shapes the structure.

title: The Miraculous Mandarin
k: the miraculous mandarin bela bartok · op. 19 · sz. 73 · bb 82 · 1918–19 pantomime for large orchestra and wordless mixed chorus orchestrated in 1924; premiered in cologne in 1926. the full stage score extends beyond the familiar concert suite, with a choral sonority in the final part of the drama.

title: Dance Suite
k: dance suite bela bartok · sz. 77 · bb 86 · 1923 orchestra five dances and a finale, with a recurring ritornello. written for budapest’s jubilee, but built from invented melodies reflecting more than one people’s music.

title: Out of Doors
k: out of doors bela bartok · sz. 81 · bb 89 · 1926 solo piano five pieces range from drum-like attacks to the layers of “the night’s music” and the repeated-note pursuit of the final “chase”. the keyboard’s decay is as important as its impact.

title: String Quartet No. 4
k: string quartet no. 4 bela bartok · sz. 91 · bb 95 · 1928 two violins, viola and cello five movements in paired relationships around a slow centre. a muted scherzo is answered by an entirely pizzicato movement; the outer movements share thematic material.

title: Cantata profana
k: cantata profana bela bartok · sz. 94 · bb 100 · 1930 tenor, baritone, double mixed chorus and orchestra the nine sons transformed into stags: a romanian folk narrative refashioned by bartok, with original musical themes. premiered in london in 1934 under aylmer buesst.

title: Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta
k: music for strings, percussion and celesta bela bartok · sz. 106 · bb 114 · 1936 two string orchestras, percussion, piano, harp and celesta paul sacher’s commission for the basle chamber orchestra. a slow opening fugue, two fast movements and a central nocturnal adagio are connected by returning thematic material; the actual order is slow–fast–slow–fast.

title: Sonata for Two Pianos and Percussion
k: sonata for two pianos and percussion bela bartok · sz. 110 · bb 115 · 1937 two pianists and two percussionists three movements for four equal participants. bartok and ditta played the pianos at the basel premiere in january 1938; the ending lets the percussion continue after the pianos withdraw.

title: String Quartet No. 6
k: string quartet no. 6 bela bartok · sz. 114 · bb 119 · 1939 two violins, viola and cello a mesto melody introduces a vivace, march and burletta before occupying the whole last movement. dedicated to the kolisch quartet, which gave the first performance in new york in 1941.

title: Concerto for Orchestra
k: concerto for orchestra bela bartok · sz. 116 · bb 123 · 1943 orchestra koussevitzky commissioned it in memory of his wife natalie and conducted the boston premiere in 1944. instrumental pairs distinguish the second movement; the central elegy recalls the opening movement’s material. bartok revised the finale’s ending in 1945.

title: Piano Concerto No. 3 in E major
k: piano concerto no. 3 in e major bela bartok · sz. 119 · bb 127 · 1945 piano and orchestra written for ditta, with an adagio religioso containing a contrasting bird-call episode. tibor serly orchestrated bartok’s last seventeen bars after the composer’s death.

title: Igor Stravinsky
k: igor stravinsky 1882–1971 · modernism a composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.

title: The Firebird
k: the firebird igor stravinsky ·  · 1909–10 ballet; large orchestra fokine’s fairy tale for diaghilev. hear the full ballet before treating the later suites as its equivalent: the supernatural dances, pantomime and transitions establish the contrast with the human characters’ diatonic tunes.

title: Petrushka
k: petrushka igor stravinsky ·  · 1910–11 ballet in four tableaux; large orchestra with piano a shrovetide fair and three puppets, with a prominent orchestral piano. the 1947 revision reduces and redistributes the orchestration of the 1911 score.

title: The Rite of Spring
k: the rite of spring igor stravinsky ·  · 1911–13 ballet in two parts; large orchestra “adoration of the earth” and “the sacrifice”. repeated chords, short melodic cells and competing periodicities carry the argument; the final dance makes changing metre audible as bodily effort.

title: Les Noces
k: les noces igor stravinsky ·  · 1914–23 four vocal soloists, mixed chorus, four pianos and percussion; dancers russian wedding scenes in four tableaux. started before most of the swiss works but completed in its definitive instrumentation only in 1923, for choreography by bronislava nijinska.

title: Histoire du soldat
k: histoire du soldat igor stravinsky ·  · 1918 narrator, actors, dancers; violin, double bass, clarinet, bassoon, cornet, trombone and percussion ramuz’s soldier trades his violin to the devil. the seven-player ensemble separates treble from bass without the intermediate cushion of violas, cellos or horns.

title: Pulcinella
k: pulcinella igor stravinsky ·  · 1919–20 ballet; soprano, tenor, bass and chamber orchestra eighteenth-century sources, then attributed to pergolesi, recast through changes of accent, instrumental balance and harmony. the complete ballet includes vocal numbers absent from the familiar suite.

title: Symphonies of Wind Instruments
k: symphonies of wind instruments igor stravinsky ·  · 1920 woodwind and brass dedicated to debussy’s memory. contrasting blocks and a final chorale replace sonata development; the 1947 revision changes details of instrumentation and notation.

title: Symphony of Psalms
k: symphony of psalms igor stravinsky ·  · 1930 mixed chorus; orchestra with two pianos and harp, without violins, violas or clarinets three connected movements setting latin psalms. the central movement’s instrumental and vocal fugues combine before the finale alternates animated praise with a slow conclusion.

title: Symphony in Three Movements
k: symphony in three movements igor stravinsky ·  · 1942–45 orchestra with piano and harp the outer movements use forceful repeated figures; the central andante makes the harp prominent. the finale’s counterpoint gathers previously separated instrumental gestures into a more continuous texture.

title: The Rake’s Progress
k: the rake’s progress igor stravinsky ·  · 1948–51 opera in three acts and an epilogue; english libretto by w. h. auden and chester kallman hogarth’s narrative becomes a pact with the demonic nick shadow. recitative and closed musical numbers provide a formal frame for tom’s collapse and anne trulove’s fidelity.

title: Agon
k: agon igor stravinsky ·  · 1953–57 ballet for twelve dancers; orchestra balanchine’s abstract ballet places old dance types, including a saraband and gaillarde, beside twelve-note passages. its successive groups of dancers have counterparts in the changing instrumental combinations.

title: Requiem Canticles
k: requiem canticles igor stravinsky ·  · 1965–66 contralto and bass soloists, mixed chorus and orchestra a compact selection of latin requiem texts with instrumental prelude, interlude and postlude. serial pitch construction serves short, separated utterances.

title: Anton Webern
k: anton webern 1883–1945 · modernism a conductor and scholar of renaissance polyphony who compressed canons and variations into a few exposed notes.

title: Passacaglia in D minor
k: passacaglia in d minor anton webern · op. 1 · 1908 orchestra an eight-bar bass theme and continuous variations conclude webern’s study with schoenberg. the tonal language and orchestral scale distinguish it from his later numbered works.

title: Five Movements
k: five movements anton webern · op. 5 · 1909 string quartet; later arranged for string orchestra short, freely atonal movements in which harmonics, pizzicato and bow position help define the formal divisions.

title: Six Orchestral Pieces
k: six orchestral pieces anton webern · op. 6 · 1909; revised 1928 large orchestra; later reduced scoring the fourth piece is a funeral march with a mounting percussion climax. compare the original and revised versions for webern’s changing treatment of orchestral mass.

title: Six Bagatelles
k: six bagatelles anton webern · op. 9 · 1911–13 string quartet six freely atonal movements lasting only a few minutes altogether.

title: Six Songs after Poems by Georg Trakl
k: six songs after poems by georg trakl anton webern · op. 14 · 1917–21 voice and changing chamber ensemble the three abendland settings stand among poems whose images of twilight and decay are separated by precise instrumental gestures.

title: Symphony
k: symphony anton webern · op. 21 · 1928 clarinet, bass clarinet, two horns, harp and strings two movements: a double canon in contrary motion and a variation movement. its row has retrograde symmetry at the tritone.

title: Concerto for Nine Instruments
k: concerto for nine instruments anton webern · op. 24 · 1934 flute, oboe, clarinet, horn, trumpet, trombone, violin, viola and piano three movements. the opening separates the row into four related three-note cells; the piano’s reply makes the title’s concerto principle audible.

title: Variations for Piano
k: variations for piano anton webern · op. 27 · 1936 piano three movements, the last an explicit variation sequence. symmetries and canons are articulated through register, dynamics, rests and contrasting kinds of attack.

title: Variations for Orchestra
k: variations for orchestra anton webern · op. 30 · 1939–40 orchestra a continuous chain of short sections projects linked motivic shapes through changing instrumental groups. first performed in winterthur in 1943 under hermann scherchen.

title: Cantata No. 2
k: cantata no. 2 anton webern · op. 31 · 1941–43 soprano, bass, mixed chorus and orchestra six movements on texts by hildegard jone. webern’s last numbered work gives serial counterpoint a vocal and choral span far beyond the early miniatures.

title: Alban Berg
k: alban berg 1885–1935 · modernism a composer of operas and coded chamber music who made twelve-tone rows accommodate triads, folk song and a bach chorale.

title: Piano Sonata in B minor
k: piano sonata in b minor alban berg · op. 1 · 1907–08 piano one sonata-form movement. whole-tone and fourth-based materials unsettle its key without preventing a final return to b minor.

title: String Quartet
k: string quartet alban berg · op. 3 · 1910 two violins, viola and cello two linked movements develop shared intervallic material. the work completes berg’s period of formal study with schoenberg.

title: Five Orchestral Songs on Picture-Postcard Texts by Peter Altenberg
k: five orchestral songs on picture-postcard texts by peter altenberg alban berg · op. 4 · 1911–12 voice and large orchestra minute verbal texts are expanded by an exceptionally differentiated orchestra. two songs were heard at the interrupted vienna concert of march 1913.

title: Four Pieces for Clarinet and Piano
k: four pieces for clarinet and piano alban berg · op. 5 · 1913 clarinet and piano brief, sharply contrasted movements in which changes of register, attack and silence carry the formal argument.

title: Three Orchestral Pieces
k: three orchestral pieces alban berg · op. 6 · 1913–15 large orchestra praludium, reigen and marsch: percussion grows out of near-silence, dance rhythms lose their footing, and the march accumulates mahlerian violence.

title: Wozzeck
k: wozzeck alban berg · op. 7 · 1914–22 opera in three acts; voices, orchestra and stage ensembles fifteen scenes after buchner. traditional instrumental forms bind a drama about poverty, military discipline, jealousy and murder.

title: Chamber Concerto
k: chamber concerto alban berg ·  · 1923–25 piano, violin and thirteen wind instruments a piano-led variation movement and violin-led adagio are brought together in the finale. the introduction encodes schoenberg, webern and berg in note names.

title: Lyric Suite
k: lyric suite alban berg ·  · 1925–26 string quartet six movements, some twelve-tone, with a private programme concerning hanna fuchs-robettin. its last movement conceals a vocal setting of baudelaire in george’s translation.

title: Lulu
k: lulu alban berg ·  · 1929–35 opera in three acts; third-act orchestration completed by friedrich cerha after two wedekind plays. related character rows, symmetrical returns and the central film interlude organise the stage action.

title: Violin Concerto
k: violin concerto alban berg ·  · 1935 violin and orchestra two movements, each in two sections. the dedication to manon gropius frames a sequence of dances, crisis, chorale and final withdrawal.

title: Sergei Prokofiev
k: sergei prokofiev 1891–1953 · modernism a pianist who made the keyboard strike like percussion, and a theatre composer whose longest melodies keep their footing through abrupt changes of key.

title: Piano Concerto No. 1 in D♭ major
k: piano concerto no. 1 in d♭ major sergei prokofiev · op. 10 · 1911–12 piano and orchestra a single continuous movement with slow and scherzando sections; the opening orchestral proclamation returns to hold the design together. prokofiev played it to win the conservatory’s anton rubinstein piano prize in 1914.

title: Toccata in D minor
k: toccata in d minor sergei prokofiev · op. 11 · 1912 piano repeated notes shared between the hands become a continuous stream of semiquavers. chromatic movement and changes of register transform the pattern without granting the pianist a conventional lyrical respite.

title: Piano Concerto No. 2 in G minor
k: piano concerto no. 2 in g minor sergei prokofiev · op. 16 · 1912–13; revised 1923 piano and orchestra four movements, including a first-movement cadenza of exceptional structural weight and a scherzo in almost continuous parallel octaves. the performed score is the substantial 1923 reconstruction after the original orchestral manuscript was lost.

title: Scythian Suite
k: scythian suite sergei prokofiev · op. 20 · 1914–15 large orchestra, including expanded brass, percussion, piano and two harps four movements salvaged from the rejected ballet ala and lolli. violent repeating figures give way to the thinner textures of “night”; the last movement builds towards sunrise.

title: Visions fugitives
k: visions fugitives sergei prokofiev · op. 22 · 1915–17 piano twenty miniatures, sometimes only a page long. character comes from a register, an interval or an articulation; the set places quiet diatonic writing beside densely chromatic fragments.

title: Violin Concerto No. 1 in D major
k: violin concerto no. 1 in d major sergei prokofiev · op. 19 · 1915–17 violin and orchestra a fast central scherzo between two more spacious movements. the opening violin line, marked sognando, returns near the end. completed in 1917, but first performed in paris in 1923 by marcel darrieux under koussevitzky.

title: Symphony No. 1 in D major “Classical”
k: symphony no. 1 in d major “classical” sergei prokofiev · op. 25 · 1916–17 orchestra with paired woodwinds, two horns, two trumpets, timpani and strings four movements in roughly fifteen minutes, with a gavotte instead of a minuet. haydn’s formal proportions coexist with wide melodic leaps and sudden tonal displacements; premiered under prokofiev in petrograd in april 1918.

title: The Love for Three Oranges
k: the love for three oranges sergei prokofiev · op. 33 · 1919 opera in a prologue and four acts, after carlo gozzi theatrical factions argue over the kind of opera the audience will receive. rapid declamation, orchestral interjections and the celebrated march propel the fairy tale. premiered in french in chicago in december 1921.

title: Piano Concerto No. 3 in C major
k: piano concerto no. 3 in c major sergei prokofiev · op. 26 · 1917–21 piano and orchestra clarinet song, fast piano passagework and abrupt changes of harmony share the opening movement. a theme and five variations forms the centre; the finale’s broad lyrical episode interrupts its more angular outer material.

title: The Fiery Angel
k: the fiery angel sergei prokofiev · op. 37 · 1919–27 opera in five acts, after valery bryusov renata’s visions and obsession govern an orchestral fabric built from recurrent motifs. not staged during prokofiev’s lifetime; much of its material entered symphony no. 3, op. 44, composed in 1928.

title: Lieutenant Kijé Suite
k: lieutenant kije suite sergei prokofiev · op. 60 · 1933–34 orchestra, with optional baritone in the romance and troika five concert movements derived from the film about an imaginary officer. tenor saxophone, military calls and sleigh bells give his invented biography distinct instrumental settings.

title: Romeo and Juliet
k: romeo and juliet sergei prokofiev · op. 64 · 1935–36; revised 1939–40 full-length ballet after shakespeare; large orchestra with tenor saxophone, cornet, piano and celesta the complete dramatic context matters: the knights’ tread, mercutio’s quick movements and juliet’s changing phrases interact before returning in altered circumstances. first staged in brno in 1938; lavrovsky’s kirov production followed in 1940.

title: Peter and the Wolf
k: peter and the wolf sergei prokofiev · op. 67 · 1936 narrator and orchestra a musical tale written for natalia sats’s children’s theatre. each character has an instrumental identity; their combinations turn an introduction to timbre into a lesson in remembering and recognising themes.

title: Alexander Nevsky
k: alexander nevsky sergei prokofiev · op. 78 · 1938–39 cantata for mezzo-soprano, mixed chorus and orchestra seven movements reworked from eisenstein’s 1938 film. “the battle on the ice” accumulates contrasting layers; “the field of the dead” replaces massed conflict with a solo voice. the film score itself has no opus number.

title: Piano Sonatas Nos. 6–8, the “War Sonatas”
k: piano sonatas nos. 6–8, the “war sonatas” sergei prokofiev · opp. 82–84 · 1939–44 piano no. 6 in a major (1940): four movements, with the opening material returning in the finale. no. 7 in b♭ major (1942): a 7/8 precipitato after the e major slow movement. no. 8 in b♭ major (1944): an extended opening andante dolce and a fast finale.

title: Cinderella
k: cinderella sergei prokofiev · op. 87 · 1940–44 ballet in three acts; scenario by nikolai volkov after charles perrault traditional ballet numbers — waltzes, variations, character dances — support unusually distinct portraits of the sisters and cinderella. the clock turns regular rhythm into the mechanism that ends the ball. premiered at the bolshoi in november 1945.

title: War and Peace
k: war and peace sergei prokofiev · op. 91 · 1941–52 opera in thirteen scenes with choral epigraph; libretto by prokofiev and mira mendelson after tolstoy private scenes of natasha, andrei and pierre lead into the public catastrophe of 1812. extensive revisions enlarged the patriotic and military episodes. the composer never heard the entire opera staged.

title: Symphony No. 5 in B♭ major
k: symphony no. 5 in b♭ major sergei prokofiev · op. 100 · 1944 large orchestra with piano, harp and percussion an andante in sonata form, a motoric scherzo, an adagio and a fast finale. near the end the orchestration abruptly shrinks to an exposed ensemble before the final tutti. prokofiev conducted the premiere in january 1945.

title: Lili Boulanger
k: lili boulanger 1893–1918 · the french line her songs and psalms give a sustained bass, a repeated interval and the weight of a choral unison the force of a large formal argument.

title: Pour les funérailles d’un soldat
k: pour les funerailles d’un soldat lili boulanger ·  · 1912–13 baritone, mixed chorus and piano or orchestra; poem by alfred de musset a pre-war setting of musset’s military funeral poem. the distinction between the solo utterance and collective response anticipates the later large choral scores.

title: Faust et Hélène
k: faust et helene lili boulanger ·  · 1913 mezzo-soprano, tenor, baritone and orchestra the prix de rome cantata, on eugene adenis’s text after goethe. a substantial dramatic score with three characters.

title: Clairières dans le ciel
k: clairieres dans le ciel lili boulanger ·  · 1913–14 voice and piano; thirteen poems by francis jammes recurring ideas and harmonic memories bind a cycle about a remembered young woman. the final song, demain fera un an, gathers earlier material into a longer span.
