title: Psalm 24: La terre appartient à l’Éternel
k: psalm 24: la terre appartient a l’eternel lili boulanger ·  · 1916 tenor, mixed chorus and ensemble including brass and organ a compact ceremonial setting. its massed proclamation provides a useful contrast with the scale and low-register tension of psalm 130.

title: Psalm 130: Du fond de l’abîme
k: psalm 130: du fond de l’abime lili boulanger ·  · 1917 contralto, tenor, mixed chorus, organ and orchestra begun in 1914. a large french-language setting of the prayer from the depths; bass persistence and the alternation of solo and choral writing control its form.

title: Vieille prière bouddhique
k: vieille priere bouddhique lili boulanger ·  · 1917 tenor, mixed chorus and orchestra completed after work begun in 1914. sets a french version of a buddhist prayer for all living beings, with a religious vocabulary distinct from the psalms.

title: D’un soir triste
k: d’un soir triste lili boulanger ·  · 1917–18 chamber versions and orchestra a slow instrumental work whose repeated weight and accumulated sonorities should be heard alongside d’un matin de printemps.

title: D’un matin de printemps
k: d’un matin de printemps lili boulanger ·  · 1917–18 flute or violin and piano; piano trio; orchestra quick articulations and repeated figures exchange between instruments. compare versions to hear what changes when piano resonance becomes sustained orchestral colour.

title: Pie Jesu
k: pie jesu lili boulanger ·  · 1918 solo voice, string quartet, harp and organ her last completed work, dictated to nadia. the compact ensemble separates the vocal prayer from instrumental lines that remain individually audible.

title: Francis Poulenc
k: francis poulenc 1899–1963 · the french line his songs, concertos and church music keep a singable line in view while the harmony changes its footing without warning.

title: Le Bestiaire ou Cortège d’Orphée
k: le bestiaire ou cortege d’orphee francis poulenc · fp 15 · 1919 voice and piano; version with chamber ensemble six settings from apollinaire’s illustrated collection. their brevity leaves little room for a neutral introduction or an unnecessary final cadence.

title: Les Biches
k: les biches francis poulenc · fp 36 · 1923 orchestra and offstage mixed chorus; ballet, later orchestral suite premiered in 1924 with choreography by nijinska and designs by marie laurencin. the suite omits the vocal numbers of the complete ballet.

title: Concert champêtre
k: concert champetre francis poulenc · fp 49 · 1927–28 harpsichord and orchestra written for wanda landowska and premiered in 1929. baroque references and modern harmonic cuts share the same three-movement concerto.

title: Concerto for Two Pianos in D minor
k: concerto for two pianos in d minor francis poulenc · fp 61 · 1932 two pianos and orchestra commissioned by the princesse de polignac. percussive keyboard exchanges, mozartian phrase-making and gamelan-related passages remain deliberately distinguishable.

title: Organ Concerto in G minor
k: organ concerto in g minor francis poulenc · fp 93 · 1934–38 organ, strings and timpani a continuous sequence of contrasting sections. the reduced orchestra makes organ registration, string attack and timpani articulation central to the changes of character.

title: Figure humaine
k: figure humaine francis poulenc · fp 120 · 1943 double mixed choir, unaccompanied; poems by paul eluard eight movements ending with liberte. written during the occupation and first broadcast in london in 1945; its harmonic and registral demands require exceptional choral control.

title: Dialogues des Carmélites
k: dialogues des carmelites francis poulenc · fp 159 · 1953–56 opera in three acts; text after georges bernanos premiered at la scala in 1957. short conversational units and recurring musical ideas lead to the final scene’s progressively diminishing chorus.

title: Gloria
k: gloria francis poulenc · fp 177 · 1959 soprano, mixed chorus and orchestra six movements, first performed in boston in 1961. acclamatory rhythms and the soprano’s extended lines belong to different kinds of liturgical utterance within one score.

title: Clarinet Sonata
k: clarinet sonata francis poulenc · fp 184 · 1962 clarinet and piano dedicated to arthur honegger’s memory. three movements distinguish an unsettled opening, a sustained romanza and a rapid finale; premiered by benny goodman and leonard bernstein in 1963.

title: Dmitri Shostakovich
k: dmitri shostakovich 1906–1975 · modernism fifteen symphonies and fifteen quartets turn marches, fugues and a four-note signature into arguments about public ceremony and individual memory.

title: Symphony No. 1 in F minor
k: symphony no. 1 in f minor dmitri shostakovich · op. 10 · 1924–25 orchestra with piano the conservatory graduation work, first performed in 1926. short wind solos and a prominent orchestral piano interrupt the four-movement design with changes of pace and character.

title: The Nose
k: the nose dmitri shostakovich · op. 15 · 1927–28 opera in three acts; soloists, chorus and chamber orchestra gogol’s story of a civil servant and his independent nose. first staged in 1930; rapid scene changes, speech-derived singing and a percussion interlude carry the satire.

title: Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District
k: lady macbeth of the mtsensk district dmitri shostakovich · op. 29 · 1930–32 opera in four acts; soloists, chorus and orchestra after leskov. successful from its 1934 premiere until the 1936 attack; later revised as katerina izmailova, op. 114.

title: Symphony No. 4 in C minor
k: symphony no. 4 in c minor dmitri shostakovich · op. 43 · 1935–36 large orchestra three movements, with a short central intermezzo between two extended outer movements. withdrawn before its planned 1936 premiere and first heard in 1961; the finale subsides into a quiet, unresolved aftermath.

title: Symphony No. 5 in D minor
k: symphony no. 5 in d minor dmitri shostakovich · op. 47 · 1937 orchestra four movements from a tightly argued opening through a scherzo and string-dominated largo to a d major conclusion. the first performance under mravinsky produced an exceptional public ovation.

title: Symphony No. 7 in C major “Leningrad”
k: symphony no. 7 in c major “leningrad” dmitri shostakovich · op. 60 · 1941 large orchestra with expanded brass and percussion dedicated to leningrad and completed after evacuation to kuibyshev. its accumulating first-movement march is only one part of a four-movement symphony that also contains extended passages of lament.

title: Piano Trio No. 2 in E minor
k: piano trio no. 2 in e minor dmitri shostakovich · op. 67 · 1943–44 violin, cello and piano dedicated to sollertinsky’s memory. high cello harmonics open the work; a repeated piano-chord sequence supports the largo, and a jewish-inflected dance drives the finale.

title: From Jewish Folk Poetry
k: from jewish folk poetry dmitri shostakovich · op. 79 · 1948 soprano, contralto, tenor and piano; orchestral version op. 79a eleven settings of russian translations of jewish folk texts. written during the renewed anti-formalist campaign and first performed publicly in its piano version in january 1955.

title: Twenty-four Preludes and Fugues
k: twenty-four preludes and fugues dmitri shostakovich · op. 87 · 1950–51 solo piano all major and minor keys, ordered by the circle of fifths with relative minors. tatiana nikolayeva’s bach playing at leipzig was a stimulus; the cycle ends in a d minor double fugue.

title: Symphony No. 10 in E minor
k: symphony no. 10 in e minor dmitri shostakovich · op. 93 · 1953 orchestra an extended opening moderato precedes a short, concentrated scherzo. the dsch signature becomes explicit in the later movements and survives the finale’s changes of tempo and character.

title: String Quartet No. 8 in C minor
k: string quartet no. 8 in c minor dmitri shostakovich · op. 110 · 1960 two violins, viola and cello five connected movements built around dsch and quotations from earlier works. the public dedication to victims of fascism and war coexists with the autobiographical explanation in his letter to glikman.

title: Symphony No. 14
k: symphony no. 14 dmitri shostakovich · op. 135 · 1969 soprano, bass, string orchestra and percussion eleven settings concerned with death, using poems by lorca, apollinaire, kuchelbecker and rilke. dedicated to britten; the abrupt ending refuses a conventional symphonic apotheosis.

title: Olivier Messiaen
k: olivier messiaen 1908–1992 · after 1945 an organist who made catholic theology, symmetrical modes, unequal rhythms and transcribed birdsong the materials of a new musical language.

title: L’Ascension
k: l’ascension olivier messiaen ·  · 1932–34 orchestra, 1932–33; organ version, 1933–34 four meditations. the organ version replaces the orchestral third movement with transports de joie, a newly composed toccata; the slow final prayer survives in both versions.

title: La Nativité du Seigneur
k: la nativite du seigneur olivier messiaen ·  · 1935 organ nine meditations on the nativity. modal harmony, added rhythmic values and sharply contrasted registrations lead to the closing dieu parmi nous, whose toccata depends on an active pedal part.

title: Quatuor pour la fin du temps
k: quatuor pour la fin du temps olivier messiaen ·  · 1940–41 clarinet, violin, cello and piano eight movements inspired by revelation 10, premiered at stalag viii-a on 15 january 1941. the changing combinations include solo clarinet, a trio without piano, two string-and-piano duos and full-ensemble unisons.

title: Vingt Regards sur l’Enfant-Jésus
k: vingt regards sur l’enfant-jesus olivier messiaen ·  · 1944 piano written for yvonne loriod. recurring themes connect twenty movements whose techniques include fugue, rhythmic canons, slow chordal meditation and rapidly alternating registers.

title: Turangalîla-Symphonie
k: turangalila-symphonie olivier messiaen ·  · 1946–48 solo piano, ondes martenot and large orchestra ten movements organised around recurring themes and contrasting rhythmic strata. the sixth, jardin du sommeil d’amour, places piano birdsong over sustained love music; the fifth is the violent joie du sang des etoiles.

title: Oiseaux exotiques
k: oiseaux exotiques olivier messiaen ·  · 1955–56 piano, winds, brass and percussion birds from asia and the americas meet in an ensemble without strings. piano cadenzas alternate with ensemble passages; percussion carries greek and indian rhythmic patterns independently of the birdsong.

title: Catalogue d’oiseaux
k: catalogue d’oiseaux olivier messiaen ·  · 1956–58 piano thirteen pieces in seven books, dedicated to loriod. each principal bird belongs to a described french habitat; the central la rousserolle effarvatte expands the reed warbler’s surroundings into a long sequence of changing light and activity.

title: Et exspecto resurrectionem mortuorum
k: et exspecto resurrectionem mortuorum olivier messiaen ·  · 1964 woodwind, brass and metallic percussion five movements commissioned by andre malraux to commemorate the dead of both world wars. biblical inscriptions govern the sequence; deep wind sonorities, bells, gongs and tam-tams require space for their resonance.

title: La Transfiguration de Notre Seigneur Jésus-Christ
k: la transfiguration de notre seigneur jesus-christ olivier messiaen ·  · 1965–69 mixed chorus, seven instrumental soloists and large orchestra fourteen movements in two groups of seven. latin gospel narrative alternates with commentary; the solo group comprises piano, cello, flute, clarinet, xylorimba, vibraphone and marimba.

title: Des canyons aux étoiles…
k: des canyons aux etoiles… olivier messiaen ·  · 1971–74 solo piano, horn, xylorimba and glockenspiel with orchestra twelve movements written for alice tully’s american bicentenary commission. named utah landscapes coexist with birds from other regions, two unaccompanied piano movements and the solo horn’s appel interstellaire.

title: Saint François d’Assise
k: saint francois d’assise olivier messiaen ·  · 1975–83 opera in three acts and eight tableaux; solo voices, chorus and large orchestra with three ondes martenot messiaen’s own libretto follows francis’s spiritual transformation. the angel’s music and the sermon to the birds occupy extended tableaux; the final scene sets the saint’s death and entry into light.

title: Éclairs sur l’Au-Delà…
k: eclairs sur l’au-dela… olivier messiaen ·  · 1988–91 large orchestra eleven movements commissioned for the new york philharmonic’s 150th anniversary. the final completed orchestral cycle includes australian birds and slow string writing; zubin mehta conducted its posthumous premiere on 5 november 1992.

title: Benjamin Britten
k: benjamin britten 1913–1976 · after 1945 an opera composer who made the english speaking voice, the suffolk coast and the repeated bass into instruments of drama.

title: Variations on a Theme of Frank Bridge
k: variations on a theme of frank bridge benjamin britten · op. 10 · 1937 string orchestra ten variations on a theme from bridge’s second idyll. a march, waltz, funeral march and fugue turn a teacher’s material into a study of string techniques and musical character.

title: Les Illuminations
k: les illuminations benjamin britten · op. 18 · 1939 high voice and string orchestra; arthur rimbaud french prose poems set in compact, contrasting movements. written for the soprano sophie wyss and subsequently taken up by tenors including pears.

title: Serenade for Tenor, Horn and Strings
k: serenade for tenor, horn and strings benjamin britten · op. 31 · 1943 tenor, horn and strings six english poems framed by a solo horn prologue and its offstage return. natural harmonics give the frame its deliberately unequal intonation.

title: Peter Grimes
k: peter grimes benjamin britten · op. 33 · 1944–45 opera in a prologue and three acts; libretto by montagu slater a fisherman, his dead apprentices and a community that turns into a pursuing crowd. the four sea interludes, op. 33a, are a concert sequence extracted and reordered from the opera.

title: The Young Person’s Guide to the Orchestra
k: the young person’s guide to the orchestra benjamin britten · op. 34 · 1945 orchestra, with optional narration variations and fugue on a theme of purcell, from his incidental music to abdelazer. made for the educational film instruments of the orchestra, released in 1946.

title: Billy Budd
k: billy budd benjamin britten · op. 50 · 1950–51; revised 1960 opera; all-male cast, chorus and orchestra e. m. forster and eric crozier adapted melville’s novella. the original four acts became two in the revision; captain vere’s retrospective frame remains.

title: The Turn of the Screw
k: the turn of the screw benjamin britten · op. 54 · 1954 six singers and thirteen instrumentalists; libretto by myfanwy piper henry james’s ghost story organised as a theme and fifteen variations. the celesta is associated with peter quint; doubling makes thirteen players supply a much larger range of colours.

title: War Requiem
k: war requiem benjamin britten · op. 66 · 1961–62 three soloists, mixed chorus, boys’ choir, large orchestra, chamber orchestra and organ the latin requiem is interrupted by nine owen poems. in the closing movement two dead soldiers recognise one another before the musical groups are brought together.

title: Curlew River
k: curlew river benjamin britten · op. 71 · 1964 church parable for male singers and seven instrumentalists william plomer’s text adapts the noh play sumidagawa. a mother looking for her son crosses a river and learns that he has died there; chant opens and closes the performance.

title: Death in Venice
k: death in venice benjamin britten · op. 88 · 1971–73 opera; libretto by myfanwy piper after thomas mann aschenbach is a tenor; the boys are dancers. piano-accompanied recitative, a baritone’s multiple roles and percussion associated with tadzio divide the dramatic world.

title: György Ligeti
k: gyorgy ligeti 1923–2006 · after 1945 he packed canons so closely that their lines disappeared, then made competing pulses and unequal tunings audible again.

title: Musica ricercata
k: musica ricercata gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1951–53 piano eleven pieces, progressing from two pitch classes to twelve. the last is a contrapuntal homage to frescobaldi; six movements were recast as the six bagatelles for wind quintet.

title: String Quartet No. 1 “Métamorphoses nocturnes”
k: string quartet no. 1 “metamorphoses nocturnes” gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1953–54 string quartet a continuous sequence of transformations, still close to bartok in its intervallic cells, dance rhythms and contrasting bowing techniques. first performed after ligeti had left hungary.

title: Atmosphères
k: atmospheres gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1961 large orchestra a work of changing density and register in which separate instrumental parts merge into collective sonorities. the opening foregrounds a chromatic mass.

title: Requiem
k: requiem gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1963–65 soprano, mezzo-soprano, mixed chorus and orchestra four movements: introitus, kyrie, de die judicii sequentia and lacrimosa. closely packed choral imitation gives way to extreme registral and dynamic contrasts.

title: Lux aeterna
k: lux aeterna gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1966 sixteen unaccompanied mixed voices quiet canonic entrances create a continuously changing choral blend. breath, vowel and the timing of consonants are as consequential as the pitches.

title: Lontano
k: lontano gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1967 orchestra canonic writing produces changes of harmonic perspective. recognisable intervals seem to emerge at different distances.

title: Le Grand Macabre
k: le grand macabre gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1974–77; revised 1996–97 opera in two acts; libretto by ligeti and michael meschke after michel de ghelderode an apocalypse in breughelland, announced by a figure whose power may be fraudulent. car horns, an extensive percussion section and extreme vocal registers give the comedy its material substance.

title: Trio for Violin, Horn and Piano
k: trio for violin, horn and piano gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1982 violin, horn and piano subtitled ‘hommage a brahms’. four movements bring march, dance and lament into contact with displaced accents and the horn’s unequally tuned natural harmonics.

title: Études pour piano
k: etudes pour piano gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1985–2001 piano; eighteen etudes in three books independent accent cycles, blocked keys, repeated notes and competing registers turn keyboard technique into formal design. ‘desordre’, ‘fanfares’ and ‘l’escalier du diable’ are useful contrasting entrances.

title: Violin Concerto
k: violin concerto gyorgy ligeti ·  · 1989–93 solo violin and chamber orchestra five movements in the final version. retuned orchestral strings, natural harmonics and ocarinas complicate the solo violin’s relation to the ensemble; the second movement recalls material from the early piano music.

title: Pierre Boulez
k: pierre boulez 1925–2016 · after 1945 he extended the series beyond pitch, then spent decades turning its ordered material into proliferating instrumental forms.

title: Douze Notations
k: douze notations pierre boulez ·  · 1945 piano twelve pieces of twelve bars each. their sharply contrasted attacks and registers later became starting points for much larger orchestral compositions.

title: Piano Sonata No. 2
k: piano sonata no. 2 pierre boulez ·  · 1947–48 piano four movements put inherited sonata, scherzo and fugal procedures under pressure. registral leaps and changing rhythmic groupings make the pianist responsible for several simultaneous strands.

title: Structures, Book I
k: structures, book i pierre boulez ·  · 1951–52; revised 1953 two pianos ia, ib and ic explore different degrees of serial control. ia borrows its pitch sequence from messiaen; the complete book was first performed by yvonne loriod and hans alexander kaul in 1955.

title: Le Marteau sans maître
k: le marteau sans maitre pierre boulez ·  · 1952–55; revised 1957 mezzo-soprano and six instrumentalists; rene char nine movements interleave three poem-based cycles. alto flute, viola, guitar, vibraphone, xylorimba and percussion create a deliberately heterogeneous ensemble.

title: Piano Sonata No. 3
k: piano sonata no. 3 pierre boulez ·  · 1955–57; unfinished piano two of the five projected formants were published: trope and constellation–miroir. prescribed alternative routes make the performer’s choice part of the form.

title: Pli selon pli
k: pli selon pli pierre boulez ·  · 1957–62; revised to 1989 soprano and orchestra ‘don’ and ‘tombeau’ surround three improvisations sur mallarme. the cycle moves between clearly projected words and a voice absorbed into instrumental texture.

title: Rituel in memoriam Bruno Maderna
k: rituel in memoriam bruno maderna pierre boulez ·  · 1972–75; later revisions orchestra divided into eight groups a memorial for the composer-conductor who died in 1973. groups of different sizes and their percussion articulate a ceremony of repeated responses.

title: Répons
k: repons pierre boulez ·  · 1980–84; later revisions six instrumental soloists, chamber ensemble and live electronics the central ensemble is surrounded by soloists whose sounds are transformed and redistributed electronically. the distinction between an attack and its response becomes spatial as well as temporal.

title: Dérive 2
k: derive 2 pierre boulez ·  · 1988–2006 eleven instrumentalists begun for elliott carter’s eightieth birthday and expanded into a large continuous span. repeated harmonic material supports instrumental layers with different rates of movement.

title: Anthèmes 2
k: anthemes 2 pierre boulez ·  · 1997 violin and live electronics an expansion of the solo anthemes. sustained harmonic tones and rapid figures are answered by electronic transformations and changes of position in the listening space.

title: Morton Feldman
k: morton feldman 1926–1987 · after 1945 soft attacks, unequal repetitions and lengths beyond ordinary musical memory replace the argument towards a climax.

title: Projection 1
k: projection 1 morton feldman ·  · 1950 cello a graphic score specifying registers and sound types within a temporal grid. the player chooses exact pitches under those constraints.

title: Durations I–V
k: durations i–v morton feldman ·  · 1960–61 five different chamber combinations prescribed pitches, quiet dynamics and independent timing. the changing alignment of parts makes each realisation’s harmonic succession different.

title: The Viola in My Life I–IV
k: the viola in my life i–iv morton feldman ·  · 1970–71 solo viola with different ensembles; no. iv with orchestra short melodic gestures emerge from carefully spaced instrumental events. the solo viola is genuinely a foreground voice, making these pieces useful contrasts to the later all-over patterns.

title: Rothko Chapel
k: rothko chapel morton feldman ·  · 1971 soprano and alto soloists, mixed choir, viola, celesta and percussion wordless music for the houston chapel housing rothko’s paintings. sustained choral sonorities, isolated percussion and a closing viola melody make a sequence of clearly different textures.

title: neither
k: neither morton feldman ·  · 1977 soprano and orchestra; text by samuel beckett an opera without a conventional cast or plot. beckett’s brief text is distributed through repeated orchestral figures and demanding high vocal writing.

title: Crippled Symmetry
k: crippled symmetry morton feldman ·  · 1983 flute/bass flute, piano/celesta, vibraphone/glockenspiel; three players an extended study in repeated patterns whose layers do not remain aligned. similar figures can overlap differently without becoming material for a regular cumulative process.

title: String Quartet No. 2
k: string quartet no. 2 morton feldman ·  · 1983 string quartet performances can extend beyond five hours. quiet articulation, counting and recollection must remain controlled across an exceptional span.

title: For Bunita Marcus
k: for bunita marcus morton feldman ·  · 1985 piano written for the composer and pianist bunita marcus. sparse, very quiet events and carefully measured silences occupy roughly seventy minutes, with changes of metre altering the distances between them.

title: Coptic Light
k: coptic light morton feldman ·  · 1985; premiered 1986 large orchestra, including two pianos feldman’s last orchestral work; the publisher dates it 1986. ancient coptic textiles prompted an investigation of instrumental colour and a continuously changing orchestral equivalent of the sustaining pedal.

title: Palais de Mari
k: palais de mari morton feldman ·  · 1986 piano the last solo piano work. its shorter span offers a concentrated encounter with the late language: quiet recurring sonorities, altered spacing and no conventional climactic destination.

title: György Kurtág
k: gyorgy kurtag b. 1926 · after 1945 a composer of messages, memorials and interrupted sentences, who can make two notes carry the weight of a scene.

title: String Quartet
k: string quartet gyorgy kurtag · op. 1 · 1959 string quartet six short movements; kurtag’s chosen starting point after his paris crisis and work with marianne stein.

title: The Sayings of Péter Bornemisza
k: the sayings of peter bornemisza gyorgy kurtag · op. 7 · 1963–68 soprano and piano a large-scale vocal-instrumental work on hungarian prose, divided into confession, sin, death and spring.

title: Játékok
k: jatekok gyorgy kurtag ·  · 1973 onwards piano solo and piano duet an expanding collection of physical experiments, homages and memorial pieces, rooted in teaching.

title: Messages of the Late Miss R. V. Troussova
k: messages of the late miss r. v. troussova gyorgy kurtag · op. 17 · 1976–80 soprano and chamber ensemble twenty-one russian poems by rimma dalos, concentrated into scenes of isolation, desire and remembered contact.

title: Kafka-Fragmente
k: kafka-fragmente gyorgy kurtag · op. 24 · 1985–87 soprano and violin forty text fragments in four parts; two musicians sustain a cycle of roughly an hour without accompanying ensemble.

title: Officium breve in memoriam Andreae Szervánszky
k: officium breve in memoriam andreae szervanszky gyorgy kurtag · op. 28 · 1988–89 string quartet fifteen movements of remembrance, incorporating material associated with szervanszky and webern.

title: Hommage à R. Sch.
k: hommage a r. sch. gyorgy kurtag · op. 15d · 1990 clarinet, viola and piano, with bass drum six movements refer to schumann’s imagined characters and musical predecessors; the final movement greatly enlarges the preceding miniatures’ scale.

title: Stele
k: stele gyorgy kurtag · op. 33 · 1994 large orchestra three movements, written for claudio abbado and the berlin philharmonic. the title denotes an upright memorial stone.

title: …concertante…
k: …concertante… gyorgy kurtag · op. 42 · 2003 violin, viola and orchestra the two soloists preserve the responsiveness of chamber music within a large orchestral work.

title: Fin de partie
k: fin de partie gyorgy kurtag ·  · 2010–17 four singers and orchestra kurtag’s opera on beckett’s french text, premiered at la scala in 2018 under markus stenz, in pierre audi’s staging.

title: Sofia Gubaidulina
k: sofia gubaidulina 1931–2025 · after 1945 she made the crossing of registers, the pressure of a bow and the breath of an accordion carry the argument of a sacred drama.

title: Chaconne
k: chaconne sofia gubaidulina ·  · 1962 piano a repeated harmonic foundation meets hard attacks, wide registers and increasingly dense keyboard writing.

title: Musical Toys
k: musical toys sofia gubaidulina ·  · 1969 piano fourteen short pieces for children; sound, register and touch are introduced through sharply differentiated miniature forms.

title: Concerto for Bassoon and Low Instruments
k: concerto for bassoon and low instruments sofia gubaidulina ·  · 1975 solo bassoon and low instrumental ensemble the soloist works within, and struggles against, an accompanying body concentrated in the lower register.

title: De profundis
k: de profundis sofia gubaidulina ·  · 1978 solo bayan written for friedrich lips. clusters, sustained pitches and bellows noise turn the psalm’s cry from the depths into instrumental action.

title: Offertorium
k: offertorium sofia gubaidulina ·  · 1980; revised 1982, 1986 violin and orchestra the royal theme from bach’s musical offering is dismantled and reconstructed. gidon kremer gave the premiere in vienna in 1981.

title: Seven Words
k: seven words sofia gubaidulina ·  · 1982 cello, bayan and strings seven movements after christ’s sayings from the cross; written for vladimir tonkha and friedrich lips.

title: Stimmen… verstummen…
k: stimmen… verstummen… sofia gubaidulina ·  · 1986 large orchestra a symphony in twelve movements. stable sonorities alternate with disturbed textures; movement ix is a silent solo for the conductor.

title: Viola Concerto
k: viola concerto sofia gubaidulina ·  · 1996 viola and orchestra written for yuri bashmet, who premiered it with the chicago symphony orchestra in 1997.

title: Johannes-Passion
k: johannes-passion sofia gubaidulina ·  · 2000 vocal soloists, two mixed choirs, organ and orchestra russian texts from the gospel of john and revelation. its companion johannes-ostern followed in 2001.

title: In tempus praesens
k: in tempus praesens sofia gubaidulina ·  · 2007 violin and orchestra without orchestral violins written for anne-sophie mutter. the isolated solo violin confronts a large ensemble whose string section begins with violas.

title: Arvo Pärt
k: arvo part b. 1935 · after 1945 he joined a moving scale to the notes of a single triad, then used that rule to rebuild his musical language.

title: Credo
k: credo arvo part ·  · 1968 piano, mixed choir and orchestra bach’s c major prelude is placed against musical breakdown; the explicit christian text contributed to the work’s suppression after its tallinn premiere.

title: Für Alina
k: fur alina arvo part ·  · 1976 piano the first tintinnabuli work. two lines, limited pitches and exposed decay establish the new technique without a large ensemble.

title: Fratres
k: fratres arvo part ·  · 1977 various authorised instrumental versions a recurrent harmonic and rhythmic design changes register and presentation; the violin-and-piano version dates from 1980.

title: Cantus in Memory of Benjamin Britten
k: cantus in memory of benjamin britten arvo part ·  · 1977 string orchestra and bell descending a minor lines in different durations; the bell measures a separate, slower span.

title: Tabula rasa
k: tabula rasa arvo part ·  · 1977 two violins, prepared piano and string orchestra two movements, ludus and silentium, contrast active figuration with a prolonged slow unfolding.

title: Spiegel im Spiegel
k: spiegel im spiegel arvo part ·  · 1978 violin and piano; later versions for other instruments a scale-based solo line expands around a central pitch while the piano sustains its triadic pattern.

title: Passio
k: passio arvo part ·  · 1982 vocal soloists, mixed choir, instrumental quartet and organ the latin passion according to st john. an ensemble of voices and instruments shares the evangelist’s narration.

title: Te Deum
k: te deum arvo part ·  · 1984–85; revised 1992 three choirs, prepared piano, string orchestra and recorded wind harp an ancient latin hymn organised through recurring pitch centres, choral groups and sustained background sound.

title: Kanon pokajanen
k: kanon pokajanen arvo part ·  · 1997 unaccompanied mixed choir the canon of repentance in church slavonic; language and syllabic structure shape the musical setting.

title: Da pacem Domine
k: da pacem domine arvo part ·  · 2004 four vocal parts; several later arrangements a setting of the old latin antiphon, commissioned by jordi savall and composed in the aftermath of the madrid train bombings.

title: Steve Reich
k: steve reich b. 1936 · after 1945 he made the changing relationship between repeated patterns audible, then brought speech, hebrew psalms and recorded testimony into the process.

title: It’s Gonna Rain
k: it’s gonna rain steve reich ·  · 1965 two-channel tape brother walter’s recorded preaching is looped and displaced; the speech’s own rhythm and pitch become increasingly audible as musical material.

title: Piano Phase
k: piano phase steve reich ·  · 1967 two pianos or two marimbas live performers move through successive alignments of repeating patterns, preserving the gradual transitions between them.

title: Drumming
k: drumming steve reich ·  · 1970–71 percussion ensemble, voices and piccolo four parts move through tuned bongos, marimbas and glockenspiels before combining them; rhythmic construction joins phase shifting.

title: Clapping Music
k: clapping music steve reich ·  · 1972 two performers clapping eight attacks within twelve equal pulses. one player repeats unchanged; the other shifts abruptly through all twelve positions.

title: Music for 18 Musicians
k: music for 18 musicians steve reich ·  · 1974–76 voices, clarinets, violin, cello, pianos and tuned percussion an eleven-chord cycle supports sections articulated by pulse, breath and audible instrumental cues.

title: Tehillim
k: tehillim steve reich ·  · 1981 four women’s voices and ensemble; also orchestral version hebrew psalm excerpts set to newly composed melodies. text rhythm replaces the fixed short metric patterns of the early works.

title: The Desert Music
k: the desert music steve reich ·  · 1984 chorus and orchestra five movements on texts by william carlos williams; the vocal and harmonic writing extends well beyond phase-process form.

title: Electric Counterpoint
k: electric counterpoint steve reich ·  · 1987 electric guitar with prerecorded guitars and basses written for pat metheny. a live player adds a line to a multilayered recording of their own instrument.

title: Different Trains
k: different trains steve reich ·  · 1988 string quartet and prerecorded sound american childhood train journeys and holocaust testimony are linked through speech-derived melodies; written for the kronos quartet.

title: Double Sextet
k: double sextet steve reich ·  · 2007 two sextets, or one sextet with prerecorded counterpart each group comprises flute, clarinet, violin, cello, vibraphone and piano. three movements alternate fast, slow and fast music.

title: John Adams
k: john adams b. 1947 · after 1945 repeated pulses support changing harmonies, long orchestral arguments and operas about the people who make public history.

title: Phrygian Gates
k: phrygian gates john adams ·  · 1977 piano a continuous span of repeating figures organised into changing lydian and phrygian fields. the “gates” are abrupt changes of harmonic state.

title: Shaker Loops
k: shaker loops john adams ·  · 1978 three violins, viola, two cellos and double bass; string-orchestra version 1983 four linked movements: shaking and trembling, hymning slews, loops and verses, a final shaking. bowed oscillations and trills generate a texture that changes density and speed.

title: Harmonium
k: harmonium john adams ·  · 1980–81 mixed chorus and large orchestra donne’s negative love followed by dickinson’s because i could not stop for death and wild nights. the opening repeated note expands into a large-scale choral and orchestral accumulation.

title: Harmonielehre
k: harmonielehre john adams ·  · 1984–85 large orchestra with two tubas, two harps, piano and celesta three movements linking repetitive processes with mahlerian and sibelian harmony. the opening e minor and final e♭ major stand a semitone apart; the middle movement contains a direct compositional homage to mahler’s tenth.

title: Short Ride in a Fast Machine
k: short ride in a fast machine john adams ·  · 1986 large orchestra, woodblock and other percussion; optional synthesizers a four-minute fanfare premiered by michael tilson thomas and the pittsburgh symphony. the clear crotchet pulse remains audible while the orchestra complicates the listener’s sense of its accents.

title: Nixon in China
k: nixon in china john adams ·  · 1987 opera in three acts; soloists, chorus and orchestra goodman’s verse libretto moves from the 1972 diplomatic visit’s public rituals to the participants’ private recollections. four saxophones, synthesizer and piano contribute to the pit’s particular weight and attack.

title: The Wound-Dresser
k: the wound-dresser john adams ·  · 1988 baritone and orchestra whitman’s nursing of wounded civil war soldiers, set for sanford sylvan. the vocal line follows the poem’s changing sentence lengths; solo violin and trumpet carry prominent responses.

title: On the Transmigration of Souls
k: on the transmigration of souls john adams ·  · 2002 adult chorus, children’s chorus, orchestra and prerecorded sounds commissioned by the new york philharmonic in memory of 11 september 2001. recorded names and fragments of remembrance coexist with orchestral and choral writing; awarded the 2003 pulitzer prize.

title: Doctor Atomic
k: doctor atomic john adams ·  · 2004–05 opera in two acts; soloists, chorus, orchestra and sound design oppenheimer and the los alamos community before the trinity test. sellars’s assembled libretto places scientific and military documents beside donne, baudelaire and sacred texts.

title: Antony and Cleopatra
k: antony and cleopatra john adams ·  · 2022 opera in two acts; soloists, chorus and orchestra shakespeare adapted by adams, with consultation from elkhanah pulitzer. premiered by san francisco opera; the public language of empire and the lovers’ private speech occupy the same dramatic space.

title: Kaija Saariaho
k: kaija saariaho 1952–2023 · after 1945 she made the passage between a bowed note and the noise around it into a way of composing harmony, form and opera.

title: Laconisme de l’aile
k: laconisme de l’aile kaija saariaho ·  · 1982 flute, with optional electronics the player moves between spoken words from saint-john perse’s oiseaux, breath and flute tone. a compact introduction to the border between articulation and pitch.

title: Lichtbogen
k: lichtbogen kaija saariaho ·  · 1985–86 nine instruments and live electronics flute, percussion, piano, harp and five strings. analysis of changing cello sounds informs the harmony; the title refers to the northern lights.

title: Nymphéa
k: nymphea kaija saariaho ·  · 1987 string quartet and live electronics written for the kronos quartet. harmonics, friction and electronically extended resonance complicate the distinction between a sustained chord and a sound with an interior motion.

title: Du cristal …à la fumée
k: du cristal …a la fumee kaija saariaho ·  · 1989–90 orchestra; alto flute, cello and electronics in the second work two linked works, also performable separately. …a la fumee extracts solo voices from the orchestral material of du cristal.

title: Graal théâtre
k: graal theatre kaija saariaho ·  · 1994 violin and orchestra; chamber-orchestra version 1997 two movements, delicato and impetuoso. premiered at the 1995 proms by gidon kremer, the bbc symphony orchestra and esa-pekka salonen; no electronics.

title: L’Amour de loin
k: l’amour de loin kaija saariaho ·  · 1999–2000 opera in five acts; three soloists, chorus, orchestra and electronics maalouf’s libretto turns the rudel legend into a drama of imagined love and physical separation. the pilgrim’s mezzo-soprano connects jaufre’s baritone and clemence’s soprano.

title: Orion
k: orion kaija saariaho ·  · 2002 orchestra the three movements are memento mori, winter sky and hunter. slow registral spaces give way to the final movement’s much faster instrumental motion.

title: Laterna magica
k: laterna magica kaija saariaho ·  · 2008 orchestra named after ingmar bergman’s autobiography. the changing speed of images in a magic lantern suggested the relation between rhythmic activity and the perception of continuity; premiered in berlin in 2009.

title: Innocence
k: innocence kaija saariaho ·  · 2018 multilingual opera; singers, actors and orchestra a wedding opens onto the concealed aftermath of a school shooting. oksanen’s text and aleksi barriere’s multilingual dramaturgy separate present conversation from remembered testimony; premiered at aix in 2021.

title: HUSH
k: hush kaija saariaho ·  · 2023 trumpet and orchestra the final completed work, written for verneri pohjola and premiered after saariaho’s death. four movements examine the trumpet’s capacity for breath, muted colour and sustained melodic line.

title: Thomas Adès
k: thomas ades b. 1971 · after 1945 his harmonies move by independent interval cycles, so a familiar chord can become unfamiliar without any voice breaking its rule.

title: Living Toys
k: living toys thomas ades ·  · 1993 chamber ensemble of fourteen players a child’s imagined adventures take instrumental form through rapidly changing textures and registers. the trumpet part and the abrupt contrasts between solo and ensemble writing make this a concentrated introduction to the early style.

title: Arcadiana
k: arcadiana thomas ades ·  · 1994 string quartet seven linked images of lost or threatened idylls. watteau, poussin, mozart and schubert are among the sources; the english chorale o albion precedes the disappearing lines of lethe.

title: Powder Her Face
k: powder her face thomas ades ·  · 1995 chamber opera in two acts; four singers and fifteen players hensher’s libretto draws on the duchess of argyll. period dances and popular-song references are fractured by the chamber ensemble; the four singers cover a much larger set of social roles.

title: Asyla
k: asyla thomas ades · op. 17 · 1997 large orchestra with bass oboe, six percussionists and keyboards four movements, including the dance-club-derived ecstasio. a quarter-tone-flat upright piano belongs to the orchestral palette; first performed in birmingham under simon rattle.

title: The Tempest
k: the tempest thomas ades ·  · 2004 opera in three acts; soloists, chorus and orchestra meredith oakes’s new text after shakespeare. prospero’s baritone, ariel’s high soprano and caliban’s tenor establish different claims on the island; the lovers’ music gradually escapes prospero’s control.

title: Violin Concerto “Concentric Paths”
k: violin concerto “concentric paths” thomas ades ·  · 2005 violin and orchestra three movements, rings, paths and rounds. the central movement carries the most weight, with harmonic cycles beneath multiple-stopped chords and sustained solo lines; written for anthony marwood.

title: The Four Quarters
k: the four quarters thomas ades ·  · 2010 string quartet premiered by the emerson quartet in 2011. a cycle of night, morning, day and a fictive twenty-fifth hour; in the finale, 25/16 metre is grouped 8 + 3 + 8 + 6, giving the recurring dance an unequal internal structure.

title: Totentanz
k: totentanz thomas ades ·  · 2013 mezzo-soprano, baritone and large orchestra death, assigned to the baritone, addresses successive human figures sung by the mezzo. the german text is associated with lubeck’s dance-of-death tradition; the final encounter is with an infant.

title: The Exterminating Angel
k: the exterminating angel thomas ades ·  · 2016 opera in three acts; large cast, chorus and orchestra with ondes martenot cairns’s libretto after bunuel and luis alcoriza’s film. an unexplained inability to leave a room converts social repetitions into a mechanism of confinement; premiered at salzburg under the composer.

title: Concerto for Piano and Orchestra
k: concerto for piano and orchestra thomas ades ·  · 2018 piano and orchestra written for kirill gerstein and premiered in boston in 2019. three movements — allegramente, andante gravemente, allegro giojoso — retain a conventional concerto outline while continuously unsettling its local rhythms.

k: the baroque 1600–1750 figured bass, fugue and the tempered keyboard

title: Classical
k: classical 1750–1827 the sonata principle: drama made of keys

title: Romanticism
k: romanticism 1815–1890 the song, the self and the swelling orchestra

title: Fin de siècle
k: fin de siecle 1880–1918 the late-romantic sunset, at its most extravagant

title: The French Line
k: the french line 1870–1937 colour, clarity and the escape from wagner

title: Modernism
k: modernism 1908–1945 breaking the key, the beat and the frame

title: After 1945
k: after 1945 1945–present total control, chance, texture, pulse — and then everything at once

title: The Music Lesson (Lady at the Virginals with a Gentleman)
k: the music lesson (lady at the virginals with a gentleman) johannes vermeer · c. 1662–65

title: A Dance to the Music of Time
k: a dance to the music of time nicolas poussin · c. 1634–36 father time plays a lyre while four figures dance in a ring. poussin made the picture in rome for giulio rospigliosi, the future pope clement ix, who also wrote opera librettos. the connection to baroque music is both institutional and technical: an educated patron receives an allegory whose cyclical movement is made legible by measured gestures. the wallace collection record gives its date and provenance.

title: A Song for St Cecilia’s Day — opening
k: a song for st cecilia’s day — opening john dryden · 1687 these lines turn the ordering of the elements into a musical act. handel set the poem in his ode for st cecilia’s day, hwv 76, in 1739; later stanzas summon particular instruments and the passions attributed to them. the public-domain text supplies a direct example of musical rhetoric.

title: The Oath of the Horatii
k: the oath of the horatii jacques-louis david · 1784

title: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump
k: an experiment on a bird in the air pump joseph wright of derby · 1768 a scientific demonstration becomes a scene of differentiated attention: the children fear for the bird, one spectator watches the mechanism, and others turn inward or towards one another. the comparison with a mozart ensemble concerns the organisation of simultaneous responses. both give several viewpoints a shared frame. the national gallery identifies the bird as a cockatoo and describes the experiment’s place in public scientific demonstration.

title: An die Freude — first stanza
k: an die freude — first stanza friedrich schiller · 1785; revised c. 1803 schiller’s revised stanza, with spelling modernised, replaces the first version’s explicit pairing of beggars and princes with “all people”. beethoven set selections from the revised poem in the ninth symphony, adding his own introductory appeal, “o freunde, nicht diese tone!” the finale tests fraternity through changes of musical company: bass soloist, quartet, chorus and orchestra. the historical versions record the poem’s revisions.

title: Two Men Contemplating the Moon
k: two men contemplating the moon caspar david friedrich · 1819–20

title: The Abbey in the Oakwood
k: the abbey in the oakwood caspar david friedrich · 1809–10 the funeral procession occupies only a narrow strip beneath the ruined gothic window and leafless oaks. architecture survives as a fragment, while the implied ceremony gives the small figures a temporal direction. the pairing concerns the same romantic interest in ruins, memory and the incomplete that informs the song cycle and character piece. the museum’s friedrich project documents the painting and its pendant, monk by the sea.

title: Erlkönig — opening stanzas
k: erlkonig — opening stanzas johann wolfgang von goethe · 1782 schubert’s 1815 setting, d 328, distributes the speakers by register and harmonic character while the piano’s repeated triplets maintain the ride. the father explains away what the child sees; the accompaniment refuses to relax when he does so. the final interruption of the running texture makes the narrator’s report physically different from everything preceding it. goethe’s original is a ballad.

title: Beethoven Frieze: The Well-Armed Strong One
k: beethoven frieze: the well-armed strong one gustav klimt · 1902

title: The Scream
k: the scream edvard munch · 1893 the rigid diagonal of the walkway meets curves that pass through sky, water and the central figure. munch makes an experience alter the organisation of the visible scene. the comparison with late-romantic music concerns that transfer between individual perception and an enlarged surrounding field: an orchestral texture can change the apparent meaning of a simple melodic figure. this is the national museum’s 1893 version.

title: The midnight song from Also sprach Zarathustra
sub: Friedrich Nietzsche · 1884; repeated in Part IV, 1885
k: the midnight song from also sprach zarathustra friedrich nietzsche · 1884; repeated in part iv, 1885 mahler sets this text for alto in the fourth movement of the third symphony; strauss responds to the larger book in also sprach zarathustra. the words first appear at the end of “das andere tanzlied” in part iii. the intervening numbered strokes of midnight are omitted here. nietzsche’s opposition between grief, delight and recurrence gives the musical return a philosophical subject.

title: Nocturne: Blue and Gold — Old Battersea Bridge
k: nocturne: blue and gold — old battersea bridge james mcneill whistler · c. 1872–75

title: Bathers at Asnières
k: bathers at asnieres georges seurat · 1884, retouched c. 1887 seurat built his colour from separate touches meant to combine in the viewer’s eye, following the colour theory of chevreul and ogden rood; when he reworked this canvas around 1887 he added small dots of complementary colour to the boy’s hat and the water. the affinity with debussy and ravel lies in their orchestral colour: they repeatedly set pure colours side by side — a flute’s low register beside muted horns, a harp harmonic on a string chord — so that the blend happens in the ear.

title: Art poétique — first and fourth stanzas
sub: Paul Verlaine · written 1874; published in Jadis et naguère, 1884
k: art poetique — first and fourth stanzas paul verlaine · written 1874; published in jadis et naguere, 1884 a manifesto in nine-syllable lines — l’impair, the odd count verlaine recommends, which cannot divide into the symmetrical halves of the classical alexandrine. the musical analogue is the french line’s distrust of four-square phrasing and emphatic arrival. verlaine was the poet these composers set most: faure’s la bonne chanson and cinq melodies “de venise”, debussy’s ariettes oubliees and two sets of fetes galantes.

title: Impression III (Concert)
k: impression iii (concert) wassily kandinsky · 1911

title: Fate of the Animals
k: fate of the animals franz marc · 1913 intersecting diagonals break the forest and animals into recognisable planes that disrupt ordinary depth. marc belonged to the blue rider circle whose publications also included schoenberg’s work. the painting predates the first world war. its present surface includes paul klee’s 1919 restoration of damage sustained in a 1917 fire, documented by the kunstmuseum basel.

title: Zone — opening
k: zone — opening guillaume apollinaire · 1913, in alcools the opening gives a steel tower the role of a shepherdess and brings bridges, antiquity and motorcars into successive lines without punctuation. that assembly of incompatible registers offers a concrete literary counterpart to musical collage and abrupt changes of block. the 1913 collection places “zone” first, making its argument with the past the reader’s point of entry.

title: Ad Parnassum
k: ad parnassum paul klee · 1932

title: Broadway Boogie Woogie
k: broadway boogie woogie piet mondrian · 1942–43 the grid provides a stable division while short coloured units interrupt its continuity, making the eye compare repetition and displacement. its musical title refers to boogie-woogie, which mondrian encountered in new york after arriving in 1940. the moma record documents that setting. postwar process music addresses a related technical problem: keeping the underlying unit recognisable while its combinations change. the link to reich is a comparison of technique, with no documented influence.

title: Walden — from “Sounds”
k: walden — from “sounds” henry david thoreau · 1854 the passage makes unallocated time a positive condition. cage drew on thoreau’s journal to construct empty words in 1973–74, progressively removing linguistic units until letters and sounds became the material. this passage from walden offers an earlier statement of a related attention. see digital thoreau’s text and the john cage trust account.

title: Les Plaisirs du bal
k: les plaisirs du bal jean-antoine watteau · c. 1715–17 a dancer performs before a seated company while musicians occupy the architectural setting. the painting dates from the years of couperin’s first two harpsichord books, whose dances and social portraits similarly depend on a small audience’s knowledge of gesture and deportment. the link is their shared parisian culture. watch the difference between the central dance and the spectators’ individual poses; listen for the comparable distinction between a piece’s dance pattern and its local ornaments.

title: Pèlerinage à l’île de Cythère
k: pelerinage a l’ile de cythere jean-antoine watteau · 1717 watteau submitted this painting to the academie royale in 1717; its lovers and theatrical landscape helped establish the category fete galante. couperin’s second harpsichord book appeared in the same year. both works belong to a culture in which pastoral costume and gestures of courtship could be presented as art for private spectators. no documented programme connects this painting with les barricades mysterieuses.

title: Bacino di San Marco, Venice
k: bacino di san marco, venice canaletto · 1738 the basin and its boats place venice’s ceremonial buildings within a working system of transport and trade. canaletto painted such views for an international market that included travellers who also heard the city’s institutional concerts. the pieta stood on the waterfront east of the piazza san marco. this is vivaldi’s urban and commercial setting; the building now called the pieta’s church was erected after his death.

title: La Primavera
sub: Anonymous; sometimes attributed to Vivaldi · Published with Op. 8, 1725
k: la primavera anonymous; sometimes attributed to vivaldi · published with op. 8, 1725 the sonnet’s first eight lines belong to the opening allegro, the next three to the largo, and the final three to the pastoral dance. in the original publication, lettered references connect these events to the parts. the poem documents the programme. the philharmonie de paris’s account of spring follows these correspondences.

title: Title page of Nouveau système de musique théorique
sub: Jean-Philippe Rameau; printed by Jean-Baptiste-Christophe Ballard · 1726
k: title page of nouveau systeme de musique theorique jean-philippe rameau; printed by jean-baptiste-christophe ballard · 1726 the 1726 nouveau systeme followed the traite de l’harmonie of 1722. the title promises principles for accompaniment and composition, linking speculative explanation to the daily tasks of a working musician. rameau continued revising his theoretical account. the library of congress copy preserves the page reproduced here.

title: Phèdre — Act I, scene 3
k: phedre — act i, scene 3 jean racine · 1677 pellegrin’s hippolyte et aricie draws on racine’s tragedy; these lines belong to the play alone. racine makes phedre recount desire through failures of bodily control; the opera redistributes the story among recitative, supernatural scenes, dances and a surviving pair of lovers. pellegrin discusses his debt and his alterations in the 1733 libretto’s preface.

title: Johann Sebastian Bach
k: johann sebastian bach elias gottlob haussmann · 1746 the paper in bach’s hand is the canon triplex a 6 voci, bwv 1076: three written lines generate six sounding parts by canonic imitation. the portrait displays his compositional craft. bach joined lorenz christoph mizler’s corresponding society of the musical sciences in 1747; the canon also belongs to the learned exchange associated with that society. haussmann painted a second version in 1748, now held by the bach-archiv.

title: St Thomas’s Church and School, Leipzig
k: st thomas’s church and school, leipzig johann gottfried krugner · 1723 the view places church and school side by side: bach’s principal musical workplace and the institution that housed and trained his singers. his family lived in the thomasschule. the arrangement matters to the cantatas: the same establishment supplied education, accommodation, rehearsal and the labour of preparing music for the city’s churches. the engraving dates from the year of his arrival in leipzig.

title: Aus tiefer Not schrei ich zu dir — first stanza
k: aus tiefer not schrei ich zu dir — first stanza martin luther · 1524 luther’s paraphrase of psalm 130 supplies the chorale of cantata bwv 38 and two organ settings in clavier-ubung iii. in bwv 686 bach writes six parts, including two for the pedals: the hymn is embedded in a texture whose sustained notes and imitative preparation recall older vocal polyphony. the german text is given in modernised spelling; the published hymn predates bach by two centuries.

title: Wachet auf, ruft uns die Stimme — opening lines
k: wachet auf, ruft uns die stimme — opening lines philipp nicolai · 1599 nicolai published words and melody in 1599. bach’s bwv 140, first performed in 1731, uses all three stanzas of the hymn, with new poetry between them developing the bridal imagery. in the opening chorus the sopranos carry nicolai’s melody in long notes above active lower voices; in the fourth movement the tenors sing the second stanza against an independent string melody. the hymn refers to the parable of the wise and foolish virgins in matthew 25.

title: Captain Thomas Coram
k: captain thomas coram william hogarth · 1740 coram founded the foundling hospital in 1739. hogarth donated this portrait and encouraged other artists to support the institution, helping make it a public destination for painting. handel’s benefit performances added music to the same philanthropic project. his 1749 benefit introduced the foundling hospital anthem; messiah followed there in 1750. the foundling museum’s collection preserves the material connection.

title: Westminster Bridge, with the Lord Mayor’s Procession on the Thames
k: westminster bridge, with the lord mayor’s procession on the thames canaletto · 1747 the procession displays the river as a route for public ceremony, with decorated barges, spectators and the city’s new bridge. painted thirty years after the documented water music excursion, it shows the continuing civic practice that makes a floating royal concert intelligible: the thames could function as an auditorium as well as a commercial waterway.

title: Alexander’s Feast — closing stanza
k: alexander’s feast — closing stanza john dryden · 1697 timotheus has used music to manipulate alexander’s emotions; saint cecilia’s sacred music supplies the final comparison. handel set dryden’s ode in 1736, with adaptations by newburgh hamilton. the closing antithesis becomes a choral judgement after an evening in which musical affects have been demonstrated one by one. the 1697 text supplies the work’s literary source.

title: Bárbara de Braganza as Princess of Asturias
k: barbara de braganza as princess of asturias jean ranc · c. 1729 maria barbara’s marriage carried scarlatti’s employment from portugal to spain. the portrait presents her dynastic position, while the sonatas record a different part of her education: the keyboard skills cultivated through a long association with her teacher. her ownership of instruments and manuscript music directly links the sitter to the repertory.

title: Portrait group: The singer Farinelli and friends
k: portrait group: the singer farinelli and friends jacopo amigoni · c. 1750–52 farinelli appears with the singer teresa castellini, the poet metastasio and amigoni himself. the group is a constructed image of friendship; a joint sitting in madrid remains undocumented. farinelli and scarlatti served the same spanish royal household, and farinelli’s later collection is part of the history of the sonata manuscripts. the ngv’s painting makes the court’s connections among singing, poetry, collecting and painting visible.

title: To the reader of the Essercizi — opening sentence
k: to the reader of the essercizi — opening sentence domenico scarlatti · 1738–39 the preface addresses both kinds of player and names a practical purpose: freedom and assurance at the instrument. the phrase belongs to scarlatti’s own publication; the cat story attached to k. 30 came later. the text is quoted in the treccani account; spelling and capitalisation are normalised here.

title: Flute Concert of Frederick the Great at Sanssouci
k: flute concert of frederick the great at sanssouci adolph menzel · 1850–52 menzel reconstructs the court where bach earned his salary: frederick plays the flute, and bach is seated at the keyboard. painted a century after the events, this is historical theatre. its arrangement makes the employment relationship visible. in the picture, the accompanist watches the royal soloist, while the listeners occupy the room around them.

title: Die Ehre Gottes aus der Natur — first stanza
k: die ehre gottes aus der natur — first stanza christian furchtegott gellert · 1757 bach set gellert’s geistliche oden und lieder in 1758; beethoven returned to six of the same poet’s religious texts in op. 48. gellert’s short clauses and scriptural imagery offer a different task from operatic recitative: clear delivery for a domestic singer without making the accompaniment inert. text: the 1757 collection.

title: Versuch — the performer’s feeling
sub: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach · 1753, Part I, chapter 3, §13
k: versuch — the performer’s feeling carl philipp emanuel bach · 1753, part i, chapter 3, §13 the prose belongs to the eighteenth-century discussion of acting and sensibility as much as to keyboard instruction. bach’s next sentences distinguish languid or sorrowful passages from forceful or cheerful ones: the performer’s expression must change with them. the digital versuch supplies the passage in its original context.

title: Eszterháza Palace, Fertőd
k: eszterhaza palace, fertod unidentified photographer · 1920 a later photograph of the palace complex where haydn composed, rehearsed and directed opera for prince nikolaus. the image records the scale of the establishment. court musicians worked within a household that also maintained servants, gardens, theatres and ceremonial rooms; haydn’s symphonies and baryton trios were part of that system of daily expenditure.

title: The Ancient of Days, frontispiece to Europe a Prophecy
k: the ancient of days, frontispiece to europe a prophecy william blake · 1794 blake’s figure measures the world with compasses while haydn’s oratorio makes an ordered world emerge through harmony. contact is undocumented. blake’s urizen can represent restrictive rational law, whereas haydn’s chorus celebrates creation. the print was made during haydn’s second london visit, placing these opposed accounts of cosmic order in the same decade and city.

title: Paradise Lost, Book VII — before the creation of humanity
k: paradise lost, book vii — before the creation of humanity john milton · 1667; revised edition 1674 milton, genesis and the psalms supplied the english source libretto that van swieten adapted for the creation. the passage moves from populated earth to the upright human figure, the same transition heard before haydn’s tenor aria mit wurd’ und hoheit angetan. text: book vii.

title: The Mozart Family in Paris
k: the mozart family in paris louis carrogis carmontelle · 1763 leopold plays the violin beside wolfgang at the keyboard while maria anna stands with music. the drawing records the family’s paris visit during the long tour of 1763–66. the child composer appears within a working ensemble managed by his father. nannerl’s place in the group also restores the sibling partnership often removed from accounts of the tour.

title: The Hall of Stars in the Palace of the Queen of the Night
sub: Karl Friedrich Thiele, after Karl Friedrich Schinkel · 1847–49, after the 1816 stage design
k: the hall of stars in the palace of the queen of the night karl friedrich thiele, after karl friedrich schinkel · 1847–49, after the 1816 stage design schinkel designed the setting for the berlin magic flute of 1816; this print belongs to a later publication of his designs. the queen occupies a celestial architecture that gives visual form to the separation already audible between her high coloratura and the lower voices of the other characters. it documents the opera’s nineteenth-century staging history, after the 1791 premiere. museum catalogue.

title: Das Veilchen — opening
k: das veilchen — opening johann wolfgang von goethe · 1774; published 1775 mozart set the poem as k. 476 on 8 june 1785. the violet’s imagined speech and the girl’s unknowing destruction of it turn the song into a small dramatic scene; mozart adds the final exclamation das arme veilchen! the excerpt gives goethe’s opening with modernised spelling. kochel catalogue record.

title: Le nozze di Figaro — forgiveness in the final scene
k: le nozze di figaro — forgiveness in the final scene lorenzo da ponte · 1786 the count has just refused the forgiveness that he now needs himself. mozart slows the action for the countess’s answer and then allows the ensemble to take up its harmony. the words establish the reversal of power; the sustained musical response gives it a duration beyond ordinary dialogue. text: the 1786 vienna libretto.

title: Bonaparte Crossing the Great St Bernard Pass
k: bonaparte crossing the great st bernard pass jacques-louis david · 1800–01 david turns the crossing into a public image of command: bonaparte points forward while the names of earlier conquerors appear on the rock. beethoven’s changing relation to bonaparte during the making of the eroica belongs to the same period of heroic image-making. the link is the political icon whose name could be written into, and then removed from, a title page; there is no evidence that the painting supplied the symphony’s programme.

title: Title page of the Eroica score, with Bonaparte’s name erased
sub: Copyist, with alterations by Ludwig van Beethoven · 1804
k: title page of the eroica score, with bonaparte’s name erased copyist, with alterations by ludwig van beethoven · 1804 this is the surviving copyist’s score with beethoven’s corrections; the autograph score is lost. the erasure damages the paper where the title referred to bonaparte. ferdinand ries’s later account supplies the scene of beethoven’s anger; the manuscript supplies independent physical evidence of the changed wording. later annotations record further changes to the leaf. archive account.

title: Heiligenstadt Testament — art and survival
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven · 6 October 1802; postscript 10 October
k: heiligenstadt testament — art and survival ludwig van beethoven · 6 october 1802; postscript 10 october the unsent document addresses beethoven’s brothers and explains conduct that others had interpreted as hostility. this excerpt concerns his decision to continue living and working. the original is held by the staats- und universitatsbibliothek hamburg. spelling and punctuation are lightly regularised here. german text.

title: An die Freude — opening stanza
k: an die freude — opening stanza friedrich schiller · 1785; revised 1803 beethoven selected and reordered parts of schiller’s poem for the ninth. ‘all human beings become brothers’ belongs to the revised wording; the earlier version spoke of beggars becoming brothers of princes. beethoven supplied the bass soloist’s introductory o freunde, nicht diese tone!. textual versions.

title: Ein Schubert-Abend bei Josef von Spaun (A Schubert Evening at Josef von Spaun’s)
k: ein schubert-abend bei josef von spaun (a schubert evening at josef von spaun’s) moritz von schwind · 1868 schwind places schubert at the piano with vogl beside him and the circle of friends arranged as listeners. the drawing was made forty years after the composer’s death; its crowded room commemorates that circle. it identifies the social machinery behind the songs: a pianist-composer, an experienced singer and friends who supplied poems, rooms, introductions and subscriptions. the museum catalogue records the mixed drawing technique.

title: Winter Landscape
k: winter landscape caspar david friedrich · probably 1811 a man has put aside his crutches beside a boulder and prays before a crucifix; beyond the fir trees, a gothic church emerges through mist. the link with winterreise is shared subject matter. friedrich gives his solitary traveller a religious object towards which to turn. muller’s walker in das wirtshaus approaches a cemetery as an inn, finds no room there and must continue. the national gallery’s account identifies the painting’s christian signs of renewal: a different outcome from the song cycle’s unanswered final question.

title: Der Leiermann — first and last stanzas
sub: Wilhelm Müller · Published 1823; collected 1824; set by Schubert 1827
k: der leiermann — first and last stanzas wilhelm muller · published 1823; collected 1824; set by schubert 1827 the three middle stanzas are omitted. the leier here is a hurdy-gurdy, a string instrument sounded by a hand-turned wheel. its drone allows the musical act to persist without a change of harmony. muller ends with two questions, which remain unanswered in schubert’s setting. the 1824 text and publication history distinguish muller’s wording from small changes in the song.

title: Marguerite with the Spinning Wheel, from the Faust illustrations
k: marguerite with the spinning wheel, from the faust illustrations eugene delacroix · 1828 delacroix’s seventeen faust lithographs accompanied albert stapfer’s french translation in 1828. berlioz read gerard de nerval’s translation that year and composed his huit scenes de faust in 1828–29. the two artists approached goethe independently: marguerite’s enclosed room and repetitive labour oppose faust’s restless movement. in la damnation, her solitary songs similarly arrest the succession of public scenes.

title: Romeo and Juliet · Act III, scene 5
k: romeo and juliet · act iii, scene 5 william shakespeare · first published 1597 juliet tries to misidentify the sound that requires romeo to leave. berlioz saw harriet smithson as juliet in 1827. his 1839 dramatic symphony transfers the lovers’ dialogue to the orchestra, asking instruments to distinguish appeal, interruption and consent without words. the play’s dependence on heard signals makes that transfer unusually exact.

title: Aeneid · IV, 651–654
k: aeneid · iv, 651–654 virgil · first century bce dido addresses the objects aeneas has left behind. berlioz read this scene as a child and made her farewell the centre of the final act of les troyens. in his own french adaptation, private leave-taking expands into the carthaginians’ curse and a vision of rome.

title: Fanny Mendelssohn
k: fanny mendelssohn wilhelm hensel · 1829 wilhelm drew fanny in the year they married, with a floral wreath and carefully articulated dress. his drawings later shared the pages of the illustrated manuscript of das jahr. their collaboration belongs to the material history of the music.

title: Nachts · set as Nachtwanderer
sub: Joseph von Eichendorff · Published 1826; Hensel’s setting published 1847
k: nachts · set as nachtwanderer joseph von eichendorff · published 1826; hensel’s setting published 1847 hensel’s op. 7 no. 1 gives the poem a piano part whose continuing motion complicates the repeated claims of stillness. the final ‘rufen’ is a call from dreams. the sung german text supplies a precise point of comparison with robert schumann’s different eichendorff settings.

title: Staffa, Fingal’s Cave
k: staffa, fingal’s cave j. m. w. turner · 1831–32; exhibited 1832 turner visited staffa in 1831, two years after mendelssohn. his painting includes a steamship: romantic access to the apparently remote landscape depended on modern transport. the overture and painting are independent responses to the same hebridean destination. turner blurs sea, smoke and atmosphere; mendelssohn keeps a precisely articulated motif audible while its orchestral surroundings change. collection record.

title: A Midsummer Night’s Dream · Act V, scene 1
k: a midsummer night’s dream · act v, scene 1 william shakespeare · first published 1600 puck’s epilogue supplies a theatrical exit from confusion. mendelssohn’s 1842 incidental score returns to the 1826 overture’s wind chords at the end, making musical recollection serve a comparable closing function. the quick string writing belongs to a play that repeatedly changes the status of what its characters think they have seen.

title: Study for the Double Portrait of Chopin and George Sand
k: study for the double portrait of chopin and george sand eugene delacroix · c. 1838 the drawing preserves the shared composition lost when the unfinished oil painting was cut apart. chopin plays; sand occupies the same space as a listener and working companion. delacroix knew both and later visited nohant. the study records their artistic circle at first hand. louvre catalogue.

title: George Sand
k: george sand eugene delacroix · 1838 the other surviving fragment of the portrait shown above the biography. separating the canvases turned a scene of music-making into two independent images of famous people. sand’s nohant household supplied working conditions for the mature sonatas, barcarolle and polonaise-fantaisie; her accounts of chopin’s revisions are valuable evidence, though they are written by a novelist involved in the events.

title: Wiosna · opening three stanzas
sub: Stefan Witwicki · Set by Chopin in 1838
k: wiosna · opening three stanzas stefan witwicki · set by chopin in 1838 chopin set this poem as wiosna, later published as op. 74 no. 2. these are the first three stanzas; the poem subsequently turns towards an unexplained sorrow and a lark’s ascending song. his small body of polish songs connects his music directly to emigre poetry. polish sung text.

title: Man and Woman Contemplating the Moon
k: man and woman contemplating the moon caspar david friedrich · c. 1824 the two figures share a landscape whose nocturnal world invites comparison with eichendorff’s poems, especially mondnacht, which schumann set in op. 39. the exposed tree roots and interrupted path give the view a physical resistance; in the song, the piano’s continuous movement and the voice’s slower phrases similarly occupy different measures of time.

title: Im wunderschönen Monat Mai
sub: Heinrich Heine · 1822–23; collected in Buch der Lieder, 1827
k: im wunderschonen monat mai heinrich heine · 1822–23; collected in buch der lieder, 1827 schumann opens dichterliebe with this poem in 1840. heine reports the confession but gives no answer from the beloved; schumann makes the absence audible by withholding a final tonic resolution. the simple equation of spring and love is therefore unstable before the cycle has reached its explicit disappointments. 1827 text and scan.

title: Beethovens Instrumentalmusik · from Kreisleriana
sub: E. T. A. Hoffmann · Collected in 1814
k: beethovens instrumentalmusik · from kreisleriana e. t. a. hoffmann · collected in 1814 hoffmann’s essays and fictions give the musician johannes kreisler a voice at once analytical and unstable. schumann borrowed the name for op. 16. the rapid alternation of agitation and inward reflection has a literary counterpart in hoffmann’s changes of speaker and frame. this passage is quoted from the beethoven essay.

title: The Marriage of the Virgin (Lo Sposalizio)
k: the marriage of the virgin (lo sposalizio) raphael · 1504 the direct source for sposalizio, the first piece of the italian annees. raphael’s central temple and radiating pavement give the crowded ceremony a strict perspective. liszt’s small opening idea expands through repetition and harmonic enlargement until it can sustain a ceremonial climax. the connection is named in the score.

title: Lorenzo de’ Medici, called Il Pensieroso
sub: Michelangelo; photograph by an unidentified photographer · Sculpture, c. 1526–34; photograph, c. 1875–1900
k: lorenzo de’ medici, called il pensieroso michelangelo; photograph by an unidentified photographer · sculpture, c. 1526–34; photograph, c. 1875–1900 the helmeted, seated figure from the tomb of lorenzo, duke of urbino, supplied the title of liszt’s il penseroso. its low register, dotted tread and chromatic harmonies make a deliberate contrast with the preceding sposalizio. liszt also printed michelangelo’s four-line answer to a poem about the adjacent figure of night: he connected the chapel’s sculpture with sleep, stone and the wish not to be awakened.

title: Pace non trovo — opening quatrain
sub: Francesco Petrarca · Fourteenth century; Liszt’s Sonetto 104
k: pace non trovo — opening quatrain francesco petrarca · fourteenth century; liszt’s sonetto 104 the opening of sonnet 134 in the modern numbering, called 104 in liszt’s edition. the contradictory verbs give a reason for the music’s changes between declamation, sustained song and sudden agitation. liszt’s piano setting is descended from his vocal one: the decorated right-hand line becomes an instrumental singer.

title: Portrait of Alessandro Manzoni
k: portrait of alessandro manzoni francesco hayez · 1841 the writer whose death prompted verdi’s requiem. hayez portrays the author of i promessi sposi through the sitter’s hands and direct bearing. verdi admired manzoni’s literary and moral standing and conducted the memorial work on the first anniversary of his death. the connection is a named dedication and public act of remembrance. brera collection record.

title: Othello and Desdemona in Venice
k: othello and desdemona in venice theodore chasseriau · 1850 chasseriau depicts othello telling desdemona his life, a subject drawn from shakespeare’s first act. boito removed that venetian act when adapting otello, but its account of their courtship returns in the love duet at the end of verdi’s act i. the lovers remember that she loved him for his suffering and he loved her for her pity. the painting supplies a visible setting for a past that the opera reconstructs through sung recollection. louvre collection record.

title: Macbeth, Act V, scene 5 — “Tomorrow”
k: macbeth, act v, scene 5 — “tomorrow” william shakespeare · c. 1606; first published 1623 macbeth speaks after learning of his wife’s death. verdi and piave compress the response into brief declamation; macbeth’s principal late aria, “pieta, rispetto, amore”, has already occurred. the comparison shows adaptation as a change of dramatic timing. shakespeare suspends the battle for an argument about time, while the opera must decide how much musical duration that suspension can bear.

title: The Frolic of the Rhine-Maidens
k: the frolic of the rhine-maidens arthur rackham · 1910 rackham’s illustration belongs to an edition of wagner’s own dramas. the swimming figures and curling water answer the beginning of rheingold, where the stage is submerged and the orchestra is still emerging from its sustained e♭. the book makes visible the physical setting from which the gold is stolen; wagner’s later motifs keep recalling that loss after the scene has changed.

title: Tristram and Isolde
