sub: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: haydn learns at the keyboard from emanuel carl philipp emanuel bach → joseph haydn · documented haydn recalled playing emanuel bach’s sonatas repeatedly during his early years of independent study. the testimony names actual keyboard works as models; it does not say that haydn was emanuel’s personal pupil or identify one particular sonata as the source of a later haydn theme. c. p. e. bach’s keyboard sonatas haydn’s independent keyboard studies

title: Palestrina becomes a counterpoint teacher on paper
sub: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina → Johann Joseph Fux · documented
k: palestrina becomes a counterpoint teacher on paper giovanni pierluigi da palestrina → johann joseph fux · documented fux’s gradus ad parnassum presents counterpoint through a dialogue between aloysius, representing palestrina, and josephus, representing fux. the imagined lesson became a route from the older contrapuntal ideal into the studies of haydn and beethoven; it is not a historical claim that fux met palestrina. palestrina’s reputation as a contrapuntal model gradus ad parnassum (1725)

title: Haydn works Fux’s problems more than once
sub: Johann Joseph Fux → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: haydn works fux’s problems more than once johann joseph fux → joseph haydn · documented griesinger’s account, reproduced by nohl, describes haydn solving fux’s counterpoint problems, putting them aside, then returning to check them. the method was repeated written work rather than a single encounter with a famous treatise, and haydn retained a worn copy. gradus ad parnassum (1725) haydn’s self-directed counterpoint exercises

title: Accompanying singing lessons teaches Haydn declamation
sub: Nicola Antonio Porpora → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: accompanying singing lessons teaches haydn declamation nicola antonio porpora → joseph haydn · documented in vienna, haydn accompanied pupils in porpora’s singing lessons and received instruction in return. porpora’s teaching connected composition with singing and italian declamation, a practical complement to haydn’s independent keyboard and counterpoint studies. porpora’s vocal and compositional teaching in vienna haydn’s lessons in the early 1750s

title: Haydn hears Handel’s London festival scale
sub: George Frideric Handel → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: haydn hears handel’s london festival scale george frideric handel → joseph haydn · documented during his first london visit, haydn attended the handel commemoration at the end of may 1791. hearing handel’s choral music in this setting preceded haydn’s later english-inspired oratorios; the encounter is firmer evidence than treating every large haydn chorus as a borrowing from messiah. handel’s music at the london commemoration haydn’s london experience in 1791

title: Haydn hears Mozart’s new quartets at home
sub: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: haydn hears mozart’s new quartets at home wolfgang amadeus mozart → joseph haydn · documented mozart played his six new quartets for haydn in vienna on 15 january 1785; the newest three were heard again at mozart’s home on 12 february. leopold’s report of the second gathering preserves haydn’s strong approval, documenting direct listening rather than an inferred general kinship between their quartet styles. quartets k. 387, 421, 428, 458, 464 and 465 haydn’s hearings in vienna, january–february 1785

title: Six quartets are entrusted to Haydn
sub: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart → Joseph Haydn · documented
k: six quartets are entrusted to haydn wolfgang amadeus mozart → joseph haydn · documented artaria’s first edition of mozart’s six quartets carries an italian dedication to haydn. the dedication is a separate piece of evidence from possible op. 33 modelling: it is an explicit published acknowledgement, while the precise extent of that musical modelling is left open in the critical edition’s foreword. six string quartets, k. 387–465 dedication to joseph haydn in artaria’s 1785 edition

title: Bach’s keyboard sonatas become Mozart concertos
sub: Johann Christian Bach → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: bach’s keyboard sonatas become mozart concertos johann christian bach → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented mozart’s three concertos k. 107 transform johann christian bach’s op. 5 nos. 2, 3 and 4 into works for keyboard with strings. the surviving manuscript contains work by both wolfgang and leopold, so these arrangements document a practical family workshop in concerto writing as well as wolfgang’s admiration for the london bach. keyboard sonatas op. 5 nos. 2–4 three keyboard concertos, k. 107 (after 1770)

title: Emanuel’s miniature supplies a concerto finale
sub: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: emanuel’s miniature supplies a concerto finale carl philipp emanuel bach → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented the finale of mozart’s k. 40 reworks emanuel bach’s keyboard piece la boehmer. leopold dated the concerto manuscript july 1767, and the critical edition identifies this specific source: the bach connection here is an actual pasticcio movement, not a general claim about mozart’s expressive style. la boehmer, published in musikalisches allerley (1761) keyboard concerto in d major, k. 40, finale (july 1767)

title: Bach’s keyboard fugues acquire string voices
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: bach’s keyboard fugues acquire string voices johann sebastian bach → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented mozart arranged five bach fugues for two violins, viola and cello in the group traditionally numbered k. 405. the critical edition places the bach arrangements beside the quartet work of 1782; the arrangement itself is secure evidence of study, without proving that every later contrapuntal mozart passage came from bach. fugues from the well-tempered clavier five fugues for string quartet, k. 405 (1782)

title: Sunday sessions bring Bach and Handel home
sub: Gottfried van Swieten → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: sunday sessions bring bach and handel home gottfried van swieten → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented in his letter to nannerl of 20 april 1782, mozart explains that van swieten lent him bach and handel works after he had played them at the baron’s sunday gatherings. constanze’s enthusiasm for fugues then helped prompt the prelude and fugue k. 394: the letter supplies a named intermediary and a particular compositional result. van swieten’s bach and handel repertory mozart’s prelude and fugue in c, k. 394 (1782)

title: Mozart recolours Messiah for Viennese winds
sub: George Frideric Handel → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · documented
k: mozart recolours messiah for viennese winds george frideric handel → wolfgang amadeus mozart · documented at van swieten’s initiative, mozart arranged handel’s messiah for german-language performances in vienna in 1789. his version adds wind colouring to handel’s texture rather than composing a new oratorio; the arrangement was made for particular performances and appeared in print only after mozart’s death. messiah, hwv 56 (1741) der messias, k. 572 (1789)

title: A Mozart suite looks towards Handel
sub: George Frideric Handel → Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · inferred
k: a mozart suite looks towards handel george frideric handel → wolfgang amadeus mozart · inferred the critical edition identifies handel’s suites as the principal stylistic model for mozart’s incomplete suite k. 399. its overture, allemande and courante belong to mozart’s 1782 engagement with older keyboard music; the unfinished sarabande also prevents the fragment from being presented as a completed four-movement suite. handel’s keyboard suites suite k. 399, overture and dances (1782)

title: Haydn teaches Beethoven counterpoint in Vienna
sub: Joseph Haydn → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: haydn teaches beethoven counterpoint in vienna joseph haydn → ludwig van beethoven · documented beethoven’s lessons with haydn began in early 1793 after his move from bonn to vienna. the exercises drew on fux’s gradus ad parnassum; when haydn left for london in january 1794, beethoven continued contrapuntal study with albrechtsberger. haydn’s counterpoint teaching, based on fux beethoven’s viennese studies, 1793–94

title: Fugue and canon follow Haydn’s departure
sub: Johann Georg Albrechtsberger → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: fugue and canon follow haydn’s departure johann georg albrechtsberger → ludwig van beethoven · documented after haydn’s january 1794 departure for london, beethoven took lessons from johann georg albrechtsberger. the subjects were counterpoint, fugue and canon, making this a different documented stage of training from the italian vocal work he later undertook with salieri. albrechtsberger’s teaching of counterpoint, fugue and canon beethoven’s studies in 1794

title: Salieri teaches Beethoven Italian vocal style
sub: Antonio Salieri → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: salieri teaches beethoven italian vocal style antonio salieri → ludwig van beethoven · documented beethoven studied italian vocal and operatic style with antonio salieri around 1800–02. these lessons concerned writing for the voice, rather than replacing the counterpoint training beethoven had already received from haydn and albrechtsberger. salieri’s instruction in italian vocal writing beethoven’s lessons, around 1800–02

title: Beethoven copies fugues to teach an archduke
sub: Johann Joseph Fux → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: beethoven copies fugues to teach an archduke johann joseph fux → ludwig van beethoven · documented beethoven’s autograph hcb mh 45 copies two four-part fugues from fux’s gradus ad parnassum. beethoven-haus relates the copy, probably, to the compendium he prepared for archduke rudolph’s theoretical lessons: the older textbook passes through beethoven to another pupil. gradus ad parnassum: two four-part fugues beethoven’s autograph study material, hcb mh 45

title: The Well-Tempered Clavier enters Beethoven’s early training
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: the well-tempered clavier enters beethoven’s early training johann sebastian bach → ludwig van beethoven · documented neefe’s communication to cramer’s magazin der musik, dated 2 march 1783, identifies bach’s well-tempered clavier as central to the young beethoven’s keyboard repertory and says neefe supplied it. the same report describes instruction in thoroughbass and composition, locating bach’s music inside beethoven’s practical education rather than merely linking two later reputations for fugue. the well-tempered clavier beethoven’s keyboard studies in bonn

title: Beethoven copies Emanuel while studying with Haydn
sub: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: beethoven copies emanuel while studying with haydn carl philipp emanuel bach → ludwig van beethoven · documented during his viennese studies in 1793–94, beethoven copied keyboard sonatas by emanuel bach. other surviving extracts come from emanuel’s versuch uber die wahre art das clavier zu spielen, which beethoven also used when teaching his own pupils. c. p. e. bach’s keyboard sonatas and versuch beethoven’s copies and theoretical extracts

title: Handel’s conquering hero becomes chamber variations
sub: George Frideric Handel → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: handel’s conquering hero becomes chamber variations george frideric handel → ludwig van beethoven · documented beethoven used handel’s ‘see, the conqu’ring hero comes’ as the theme of twelve variations for cello and piano, woo 45, in 1796. his surviving study copies also include passages from handel’s messiah in mozart’s arrangement: borrowing a recognisable tune and copying a score are two separately documented forms of his engagement with handel. see, the conqu’ring hero comes, judas maccabaeus twelve variations for cello and piano, woo 45 (1796)

title: Beethoven studies Mozart’s ensembles for Fidelio
sub: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: beethoven studies mozart’s ensembles for fidelio wolfgang amadeus mozart → ludwig van beethoven · documented while beginning work on fidelio, beethoven copied passages from mozart’s don giovanni to study the handling of vocal ensembles. beethoven-haus exhibited this study manuscript: the mechanism is written compositional analysis, not the unverified story that mozart personally taught beethoven in 1787. don giovanni: ensemble passages beethoven’s study copy during work on fidelio

title: Schiller’s ode enters a symphonic finale
sub: Friedrich Schiller → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: schiller’s ode enters a symphonic finale friedrich schiller → ludwig van beethoven · documented beethoven incorporated schiller’s an die freude in the choral finale of the ninth symphony, first performed in vienna on 7 may 1824. the literary connection belongs to the sung finale, not to a retrospective programme imposed on the instrumental movements. an die freude symphony no. 9, finale (1824) ode-to-joy

title: Goethe’s tragedy receives Beethoven’s stage music
sub: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: goethe’s tragedy receives beethoven’s stage music johann wolfgang von goethe → ludwig van beethoven · documented beethoven composed music for goethe’s egmont in 1809–10, including songs, entr’actes and music for the tragedy’s final act. he announced the work to goethe by letter in 1811, before their personal meetings in 1812; the setting therefore did not result from a collaboration begun at teplitz. egmont incidental music to egmont, op. 84 (1809–10)

title: Schubert’s early compositions lead to Salieri lessons
k: schubert’s early compositions lead to salieri lessons antonio salieri → franz schubert · documented schubert’s early compositional gifts led to study with antonio salieri in vienna. the link joins schubert to a working vocal composer and teacher, rather than to the fictional account of salieri as mozart’s murderer. salieri’s compositional teaching in vienna schubert’s early musical training

title: Faust’s spinning scene becomes a piano song
sub: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe → Franz Schubert · documented
k: faust’s spinning scene becomes a piano song johann wolfgang von goethe → franz schubert · documented schubert set goethe’s gretchen text as gretchen am spinnrade, d. 118, in 1814. gibbs places it beside erlkonig among the early goethe settings that made the piano an active interpreter of the poem, rather than treating it as a neutral support for the voice. faust: gretchen’s song gretchen am spinnrade, d. 118 (1814)

title: Goethe’s ballad becomes Schubert’s first published opus
sub: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe → Franz Schubert · documented
k: goethe’s ballad becomes schubert’s first published opus johann wolfgang von goethe → franz schubert · documented schubert composed his setting of goethe’s erlkonig, d. 328, in 1815; it later became his op. 1. the pairing of a specific poem, catalogue number and publication identity makes this a direct literary inheritance, not a loose association with german romantic poetry. erlkonig erlkonig, d. 328, op. 1 (1815)

title: Spanish strumming enters a keyboard sonata
sub: Spanish guitar and dance traditions → Domenico Scarlatti · inferred
k: spanish strumming enters a keyboard sonata spanish guitar and dance traditions → domenico scarlatti · inferred giulio d’amore’s santa cecilia programme note hears andalusian guitar attack and dance energy in the dense, dissonant chords of scarlatti’s k. 175. this is a stylistic reading of music written for keyboard, not evidence that scarlatti quoted a recoverable folk tune or originally composed the sonata for guitar. spanish plucked-string and dance gestures keyboard sonata in a minor, k. 175

title: Schubert carries a torch for Beethoven
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Franz Schubert · documented
k: schubert carries a torch for beethoven ludwig van beethoven → franz schubert · documented schubert was a torchbearer in beethoven’s funeral procession on 29 march 1827. this public act of homage is documented separately from uncertain stories of bedside visits, and does not imply that the two men had enjoyed a sustained personal friendship. beethoven’s public memorial in vienna schubert at the funeral, 29 march 1827

title: Bach signs the unfinished fugue in notes
sub: The B–A–C–H signature → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: bach signs the unfinished fugue in notes the b–a–c–h signature → johann sebastian bach · documented the unfinished fugue printed with the art of fugue introduces b♭–a–c–b♮ as its third subject, spelling bach’s name in german note names. the signature is visible in the score; the familiar story that bach died at precisely this point is not needed to identify it. b♭–a–c–b♮, bach’s name in german notation the art of fugue, fuga a 3 soggetti, third subject bach-motif

title: The nymph laments over a falling fourth
sub: The descending lament bass → Claudio Monteverdi · documented
k: the nymph laments over a falling fourth the descending lament bass → claudio monteverdi · documented monteverdi’s lamento della ninfa places the abandoned nymph’s lament over the descending tetrachord associated with the lament-bass tradition. published in his eighth book of madrigals in 1638, it shows that this expressive device belonged to secular vocal drama as well as later sacred music. the descending minor tetrachord as a ground lamento della ninfa, sv 163, published in madrigals book viii (1638) lament-bass

title: A solo violin carries the descending ground
sub: The descending lament bass → Heinrich Ignaz Franz Biber · documented
k: a solo violin carries the descending ground the descending lament bass → heinrich ignaz franz biber · documented biber’s unaccompanied violin passacaglia repeatedly returns to g–f–e♭–d, descending from tonic to dominant. sometimes exposed and sometimes absorbed into chords or rapid figuration, the four-note ground gives the listener a point of continuity without a separate bass instrument. descending minor tetrachord, g–f–e♭–d passacaglia in g minor, c. 105, concluding the mystery sonatas (c. 1676) lament-bass

title: Dido’s farewell circles a chromatic descent
sub: The descending lament bass → Henry Purcell · documented
k: dido’s farewell circles a chromatic descent the descending lament bass → henry purcell · documented purcell’s when i am laid in earth repeats a chromatically descending ground in g minor beneath dido’s farewell. the bass keeps returning while the voice renews its plea to be remembered, making repetition part of the drama rather than a merely convenient accompaniment. the chromatic descending fourth and ground-bass convention when i am laid in earth, dido and aeneas, z. 626 lament-bass

title: Bach’s chorus of tears descends chromatically
sub: The descending lament bass → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: bach’s chorus of tears descends chromatically the descending lament bass → johann sebastian bach · documented the opening chorus of bach’s bwv 12 lays sighing vocal entries over a repeating chromatic descent. first performed in weimar on 22 april 1714, this music returns from a more hopeful middle section to the same sorrowful ground, and later supplies the basis of the b-minor mass’s crucifixus. the chromatic lament-bass convention weinen, klagen, sorgen, zagen, bwv 12, opening chorus (1714) lament-bass

title: The lament ground returns at the Crucifixion
sub: The descending lament bass → Johann Sebastian Bach · documented
k: the lament ground returns at the crucifixion the descending lament bass → johann sebastian bach · documented for the crucifixus, bach reworked the lamenting chorus of bwv 12 in e minor, placing the recurring ground beneath the words of the crucifixion and burial. near the end, its altered course leads to g major before the resurrection movement: the ground’s eventual change matters as much as its repetitions. the chromatic ground of bwv 12 and the lament-bass convention mass in b minor, bwv 232, crucifixus (assembled c. 1748–49) lament-bass

title: A falling bass powers thirty-two variations
sub: The descending lament bass → Ludwig van Beethoven · documented
k: a falling bass powers thirty-two variations the descending lament bass → ludwig van beethoven · documented beethoven’s woo 80 theme sets a chromatically descending bass beneath its melody, reusing the familiar lament-bass framework. thirty-two piano variations then make that short harmonic scheme a basis for changing figuration rather than an explicitly narrated funeral. the chromatic descending-fourth bass convention thirty-two variations in c minor, woo 80, theme (1806) lament-bass

title: Corelli makes an old Folia his finale
sub: La Folia tradition → Arcangelo Corelli · documented
k: corelli makes an old folia his finale la folia tradition → arcangelo corelli · documented corelli closed his op. 5 violin sonatas, published in rome in 1700, with variations headed follia. the set became a particularly influential vehicle for the inherited tune, but neither its title nor its later fame makes corelli the melody’s original composer. the inherited la folia theme and harmonic scheme sonata in d minor, op. 5 no. 12, follia (1700) la-folia

title: Marais answers the Folia on the viol
sub: La Folia tradition → Marin Marais · documented
k: marais answers the folia on the viol la folia tradition → marin marais · documented marais included couplets de folies in his second book of viol pieces in 1701, with a theme and thirty-one variations for bass viol and continuo. the familiar d-minor framework thus belonged to the viol’s repertory as well as corelli’s violin and vivaldi’s trio sonata. la folia / les folies d’espagne couplets de folies, pieces de viole, livre ii, no. 20 (1701) la-folia

title: Corelli’s Folia becomes a concerto grosso
k: corelli’s folia becomes a concerto grosso arcangelo corelli → francesco geminiani · documented geminiani expanded corelli’s solo-violin folia into music for a string ensemble in 1729. alternation between concertino and ripieno gives the variations a new kind of contrast: this is an identifiable arrangement of corelli, not simply another independent setting of the same traditional tune. violin sonata op. 5 no. 12, follia concerto grosso arrangement of corelli’s folia (1729) la-folia

title: Emanuel strips the Folia back to essentials
sub: La Folia tradition → Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach · documented
k: emanuel strips the folia back to essentials la folia tradition → carl philipp emanuel bach · documented emanuel bach’s twelve variations on les folies d’espagne present the old tune in a notably plain melodic and rhythmic form. the critical edition places the set among his technically ambitious works for professional players, rather than his simpler teaching variations. les folies d’espagne / la folia twelve variations, wq 118/9 (1778) la-folia

title: A folk poem interrupts the symphony
sub: Des Knaben Wunderhorn → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: a folk poem interrupts the symphony des knaben wunderhorn → gustav mahler · documented mahler set urlicht, a poem from the folk-poetry anthology des knaben wunderhorn, before placing it between the second symphony’s scherzo and finale. the alto’s intimate appeal for release is a new vocal presence after three instrumental movements: the borrowed material is the poem, not a documented traditional tune. des knaben wunderhorn: urlicht urlicht; symphony no. 2, movement iv

title: The fish sermon loses its words
sub: Des Knaben Wunderhorn → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: the fish sermon loses its words des knaben wunderhorn → gustav mahler · documented in mahler’s wunderhorn song, saint anthony preaches to attentive fish who return unchanged to their usual behaviour. its musical material also supplies the second symphony’s instrumental scherzo, so the poem’s circular, unsuccessful sermon has an afterlife without a singer to explain it. des knaben wunderhorn: des antonius von padua fischpredigt des antonius von padua fischpredigt; symphony no. 2, movement iii

title: A child’s heaven becomes the destination
sub: Des Knaben Wunderhorn → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: a child’s heaven becomes the destination des knaben wunderhorn → gustav mahler · documented mahler composed das himmlische leben in 1892, well before the fourth symphony, and subsequently reorchestrated it for that work’s finale. the soprano describes a childlike heaven of food, saints and music; the apparently simple conclusion is therefore an older song around which a new symphonic destination was built. des knaben wunderhorn: das himmlische leben symphony no. 4, finale

title: Bruckner’s Third passes through four hands
k: bruckner’s third passes through four hands anton bruckner → gustav mahler · documented mahler and rudolf krzyzanowski prepared a piano-duet arrangement of bruckner’s third symphony. reducing the orchestral work to four hands was practical, detailed engagement with bruckner’s construction, not merely admiration from a distance; the precise division of work between the two arrangers should not be treated as settled. symphony no. 3, 1877 version piano-duet arrangement, 1878–1880

title: Parsifal heard at Bayreuth
k: parsifal heard at bayreuth richard wagner → gustav mahler · documented mahler heard parsifal at bayreuth in 1883 under hermann levi and reported the experience to fritz lohr. this is a documented encounter with wagner’s music in its purpose-built theatre, rather than evidence that any particular later mahler theme was copied from it. parsifal mahler’s bayreuth visit and letter to fritz lohr

title: Bruder Martin walks into a funeral
sub: Frère Jacques / Bruder Martin → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: bruder martin walks into a funeral frere jacques / bruder martin → gustav mahler · documented over the timpani’s tread, the first symphony’s third movement introduces bruder martin, the round also known as frere jacques, in d minor and builds a canon from it. mahler’s opening includes a small f–e eighth-note turn: it is not a note-for-note transcription of the familiar classroom version. minor-mode versions of the round already circulated in austria, so the transformation should not be advertised as mahler’s invention. bruder martin / frere jacques, traditional round symphony no. 1, movement iii, opening canon frere-jacques

title: Titan was a title, not a plot
k: titan was a title, not a plot jean paul → gustav mahler · documented mahler attached the name titan, borrowed from jean paul’s novel, to the first symphony for its hamburg performance in 1893. the title does not establish a movement-by-movement setting of the novel: mahler subsequently withdrew the programme and title, leaving a four-movement symphony. titan, novel symphony no. 1: hamburg programme, 1893

title: Reading the symphonies beside The Brothers Karamazov
k: reading the symphonies beside the brothers karamazov fyodor dostoevsky → gustav mahler · inferred celeste belknap’s study places mahler’s third and fourth symphonies beside the brothers karamazov, a novel mahler admired, especially around faith, nihilism and childhood. this offers a specific interpretative lens for the fourth’s childlike heaven, not proof that mahler secretly composed a dostoevsky programme. the brothers karamazov symphonies nos. 3 and 4

title: Rott’s scherzo: resemblance is not proof
k: rott’s scherzo: resemblance is not proof hans rott → gustav mahler · inferred hans rott’s e-major symphony contains landler-like scherzo writing that has been compared with mahler’s first and fifth symphonies. mahler knew rott as a fellow student and later praised his music, but the securely reported loan of rott’s score in 1900 comes after the first symphony’s composition. similarity, friendship and later possession of a score do not by themselves prove when mahler first knew that passage or that he copied it. symphony in e major, scherzo, 1878–1880 symphony no. 1, scherzo; comparison with symphony no. 5

title: The garrison town enters the orchestra
sub: Bohemian military-band tradition → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: the garrison town enters the orchestra bohemian military-band tradition → gustav mahler · documented mahler grew up in iglau, a bohemian garrison town where military bands were part of everyday listening alongside church bells, synagogue music and street musicians. michael tilson thomas’s keeping score account connects that mixed soundscape with the marches and fanfares of mahler’s orchestral world; it does not identify every march as a quotation of a particular regimental tune. military bands and street music in iglau mahler’s childhood listening; later marches and fanfares

title: Bach on the composing-hut desk
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: bach on the composing-hut desk johann sebastian bach → gustav mahler · documented records of the bach-gesellschaft edition place mahler among its subscribers during his hamburg years, and recollections by natalie bauer-lechner and alma mahler describe his sustained study of bach. the report that bach scores accompanied him to his composing retreat makes this a working relationship with counterpoint, not merely a name on a list of favourite composers. bach-gesellschaft collected edition; contrapuntal works mahler’s bach study during the hamburg years

title: Two Bach suites become one programme
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: two bach suites become one programme johann sebastian bach → gustav mahler · documented mahler assembled his performing suite from movements of bach’s second and third orchestral suites. here the connection can be followed into an actual arrangement: selected bach movements were reorganised for mahler’s own concert practice rather than simply imitated in a new composition. orchestral suites nos. 2 and 3, bwv 1067–1068 suite aus den orchesterwerken von j. s. bach

title: China reaches Mahler through several translators
k: china reaches mahler through several translators hans bethge → gustav mahler · documented mahler drew the texts of das lied von der erde from hans bethge’s die chinesische flote, combining seven poems into six songs. bethge’s german poems were paraphrases mediated by earlier european translations, including those of judith gautier and the marquis d’hervey-saint-denys, not direct translations made by mahler from chinese. the chain of transmission is part of the work’s history, not an inconvenience to erase. die chinesische flote, 1907 das lied von der erde

title: Rückert’s private grief becomes five songs
k: ruckert’s private grief becomes five songs friedrich ruckert → gustav mahler · documented friedrich ruckert wrote his kindertotenlieder after losing two children in 1833–1834; mahler selected five poems for his song cycle. mahler composed the settings before his own daughter maria died in 1907, so the cycle is neither a diary of that later loss nor evidence of supernatural prediction. kindertotenlieder, poems written after the deaths of two children kindertotenlieder, 1901–1904

title: A memorial service unlocks the finale
sub: Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: a memorial service unlocks the finale friedrich gottlieb klopstock → gustav mahler · documented at the memorial service for hans von bulow in 1894, mahler heard klopstock’s resurrection hymn and found the textual starting point for his second symphony’s finale. he did not simply set the complete hymn: his finale joins part of klopstock’s poem to verses of his own. die auferstehung symphony no. 2, finale

title: Faust answers Veni creator spiritus
sub: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe → Gustav Mahler · documented
k: faust answers veni creator spiritus johann wolfgang von goethe → gustav mahler · documented the eighth symphony’s second part sets the closing scene of goethe’s faust ii, following a first part built on the latin hymn veni creator spiritus. mahler links these apparently distant texts through returning musical material, making goethe’s final ascent the continuation of the opening invocation rather than a separate cantata appended to it. faust, part ii, closing scene symphony no. 8, part ii

title: Zarathustra sings at midnight
k: zarathustra sings at midnight friedrich nietzsche → gustav mahler · documented after three instrumental movements, the third symphony introduces an alto singing nietzsche’s midnight poem from also sprach zarathustra. the sparse, slow setting changes the scale of listening from the preceding orchestral world to a single voice contemplating sorrow and eternity; this is an actual text setting, not a claim that the whole symphony illustrates nietzsche’s philosophy. also sprach zarathustra: midnight song symphony no. 3, movement iv

title: Mahler’s orchestra behind Berg’s three pieces
k: mahler’s orchestra behind berg’s three pieces gustav mahler → alban berg · documented mark devoto’s account identifies mahler’s ninth as a profound influence on berg’s three pieces for orchestra, composed in 1914–1915. the central reigen turns around dance material including a landler, while the final marsch magnifies the orchestra into a destructive march: the inheritance is a way of organising orchestral drama, not a single asserted quotation. symphony no. 9 three pieces for orchestra, op. 6

title: Teenage Britten hears Mahler’s Fourth
k: teenage britten hears mahler’s fourth gustav mahler → benjamin britten · documented the teenage britten heard mahler’s fourth at a london prom in september 1930 and recorded a response that combined impatience at its length with admiration for its beauty. david matthews relates this encounter, and britten’s subsequent purchase of the lieder eines fahrenden gesellen score, to the mahlerian orchestral world of plymouth town; the diary establishes the encounter more securely than any proposed bar-by-bar borrowing. symphony no. 4, london prom, september 1930 britten’s diary; early orchestral work including plymouth town

title: Zverev’s household was also a conservatory
k: zverev’s household was also a conservatory nikolai zverev → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff entered nikolai zverev’s moscow household as a piano pupil in 1885. its musical gatherings also brought him into contact with tchaikovsky, so the teacher provided both intensive pianistic training and access to the professional circle in which the young composer was first heard. nikolai zverev’s residential piano teaching rachmaninoff’s moscow training, from 1885

title: A cousin takes over the piano lessons
k: a cousin takes over the piano lessons alexander siloti → sergei rachmaninoff · documented in 1888 rachmaninoff moved into the senior stage of his moscow conservatory training and studied piano with his cousin alexander siloti. this pianistic relationship ran alongside, rather than replaced, the separate composition and counterpoint instruction he received from arensky and taneyev. alexander siloti’s piano teaching rachmaninoff’s senior moscow studies

title: Tchaikovsky recommends advanced counterpoint
k: tchaikovsky recommends advanced counterpoint sergei taneyev → sergei rachmaninoff · documented on tchaikovsky’s recommendation, rachmaninoff studied advanced counterpoint with sergei taneyev. naming the subject matters: this was technical training in combining independent voices, not simply a vague personal influence attributed retrospectively to an older russian master. sergei taneyev’s advanced counterpoint teaching rachmaninoff’s moscow conservatory studies

title: Arensky teaches the composer’s working tools
k: arensky teaches the composer’s working tools anton arensky → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff’s senior moscow studies included composition, harmony and instrumentation with anton arensky. arensky’s place in this history is therefore an identifiable teaching relationship, distinct from taneyev’s counterpoint lessons and siloti’s piano instruction. anton arensky’s harmony, instrumentation and composition classes rachmaninoff’s moscow conservatory studies

title: Tchaikovsky champions the graduation opera
sub: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky → Sergei Rachmaninoff · documented
k: tchaikovsky champions the graduation opera pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky → sergei rachmaninoff · documented tchaikovsky publicly praised rachmaninoff’s graduation opera aleko, attended its bolshoi premiere in 1893 and proposed pairing it with his own iolanta. this was concrete patronage of a younger composer’s work, not simply a later listener’s comparison of their melodies. tchaikovsky’s support and proposed iolanta double bill aleko, composed 1892; bolshoi premiere, 1893

title: A memorial trio answers a memorial trio
sub: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky → Sergei Rachmaninoff · documented
k: a memorial trio answers a memorial trio pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky → sergei rachmaninoff · documented after tchaikovsky’s death, rachmaninoff composed his second trio elegiaque in his memory, completing it in december 1893. the choice of a large piano trio as a memorial follows the precedent of tchaikovsky’s own trio for nikolai rubinstein: the younger composer mourned his patron in a form that patron had already made commemorative. piano trio in a minor, op. 50, in memory of nikolai rubinstein trio elegiaque no. 2 in d minor, op. 9

title: Grieg provides a concerto starting point
k: grieg provides a concerto starting point edvard grieg → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff used grieg’s concerto as a model while composing the original version of his first piano concerto in 1891. this belongs to the student work’s genesis; it should not obscure how extensively rachmaninoff later revised his own concerto in 1917. piano concerto in a minor, op. 16 piano concerto no. 1 in f-sharp minor, op. 1, original version

title: Dies irae crosses the dark water
k: dies irae crosses the dark water gregorian chant → sergei rachmaninoff · documented in the isle of the dead, rachmaninoff quotes both fragments and fuller statements of dies irae. the medieval death chant and the painting are different kinds of source: one supplies recognisable musical material, the other the visual stimulus for the work. dies irae, requiem sequence the isle of the dead, op. 29 dies-irae

title: The death chant interrupts Paganini
k: the death chant interrupts paganini gregorian chant → sergei rachmaninoff · documented variation vii of the paganini rhapsody brings dies irae into a work nominally based on a violin caprice. the piano’s chant meets fragments of paganini’s theme in bassoons and pizzicato cellos, letting the listener hear two inherited materials interacting rather than treating the rhapsody as twenty-four independent decorations. dies irae, requiem sequence rhapsody on a theme of paganini, op. 43, variation vii dies-irae

title: Dies irae returns in the last dance
k: dies irae returns in the last dance gregorian chant → sergei rachmaninoff · documented the final symphonic dance repeatedly invokes dies irae, returning to a melody rachmaninoff had already used in the isle of the dead and the paganini rhapsody. it is set against music recalled from his own all-night vigil, turning the movement into an encounter between a western death chant and his russian sacred repertory. dies irae, requiem sequence symphonic dances, op. 45, movement iii dies-irae

title: Old chant becomes a choral orchestra
k: old chant becomes a choral orchestra znamenny chant → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff’s all-night vigil incorporates inherited orthodox chants rather than inventing all its melodies in an antique style. david bray’s account identifies znamenny chant in movements including no. 8, where altos and basses carry it in octaves, and no. 12; the surrounding choral texture gives a monodic tradition a many-voiced setting. russian orthodox znamenny chant all-night vigil, op. 37, including nos. 8 and 12

title: The Vigil’s Alleluia survives in exile
k: the vigil’s alleluia survives in exile znamenny chant → sergei rachmaninoff · documented near the end of the symphonic dances, rachmaninoff recalls the ninth movement of his all-night vigil and marks the passage with an alleluia indication. the russian sacred melody reaches the orchestral work through his own earlier choral setting: it is both inherited chant and self-quotation. all-night vigil, op. 37, no. 9, based on znamenny chant symphonic dances, op. 45, movement iii, coda

title: Böcklin’s island becomes a symphonic poem
k: bocklin’s island becomes a symphonic poem arnold bocklin → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff’s encounter with a black-and-white reproduction of arnold bocklin’s isle of the dead stimulated his tone poem; he later found the painting in colour less compelling than the reproduction. the music’s recurring 5/8 motion accompanies an imagined crossing towards the island, but the illustration here is identified as a particular version, not asserted to be the exact reproduction he saw. die toteninsel / isle of the dead, series of paintings the isle of the dead, op. 29

title: Chopin’s miniature becomes twenty-two variations
k: chopin’s miniature becomes twenty-two variations frederic chopin → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff chose chopin’s c-minor prelude as the theme for twenty-two piano variations, written in 1902–1903. the excerpts isolate the opening upper voice of chopin’s chordal theme and its restatement by rachmaninoff; hearing that plain outline first makes the later virtuoso transformations easier to follow. prelude in c minor, op. 28 no. 20 variations on a theme of chopin, op. 22

title: The pianist writes inside Liszt’s rhapsody
k: the pianist writes inside liszt’s rhapsody franz liszt → sergei rachmaninoff · documented by january 1919, rachmaninoff was performing liszt’s second hungarian rhapsody with his own cadenza, explicitly identified in a carnegie hall programme. this is a particularly literal meeting of pianist-composers: rather than merely adopting a virtuoso manner, rachmaninoff inserted newly composed material into his performance of an older pianist-composer’s work. hungarian rhapsody no. 2 rachmaninoff’s cadenza, documented in a concert programme of 23 january 1919

title: Paganini’s theme arrives after its first variation
k: paganini’s theme arrives after its first variation niccolo paganini → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff built his rhapsody on the theme of paganini’s twenty-fourth caprice, but placed a skeletal first variation before the theme itself. the famous eighteenth variation later turns the theme upside down and into the major mode: its lyricism is a transformation of the same source, not an unrelated tune dropped into the work. caprice no. 24 in a minor, op. 1 rhapsody on a theme of paganini, op. 43

title: Poe’s bells arrive through Balmont
sub: Edgar Allan Poe → Sergei Rachmaninoff · documented
k: poe’s bells arrive through balmont edgar allan poe → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff’s choral symphony the bells sets konstantin balmont’s free russian adaptation of poe, not poe’s english poem directly. its four movements pass through sleigh bells, wedding bells, alarm bells and funeral bells; balmont’s changes, including an earlier presence of death, are part of the text rachmaninoff actually composed. the bells, in konstantin balmont’s russian adaptation the bells, op. 35

title: Mahler rehearses Rachmaninoff’s Third
k: mahler rehearses rachmaninoff’s third gustav mahler → sergei rachmaninoff · documented mahler conducted rachmaninoff as soloist in the third piano concerto in new york in january 1910, after its premiere under walter damrosch. rachmaninoff later singled out mahler’s painstaking rehearsal work: this connection between two favourites is documented collaboration over a new score, not a hypothetical stylistic resemblance. mahler’s conducting in new york piano concerto no. 3, january 1910 performances

title: Fauré’s classroom hears the young Ravel
k: faure’s classroom hears the young ravel gabriel faure → maurice ravel · documented ravel studied composition with faure from 1897, and his early single-movement violin sonata belongs to that classroom world. bru zane identifies a probable performance in faure’s class in 1897–1898 and hears the older composer’s chamber-music example in it; the classroom performance is reported as probable, not certain. faure’s paris conservatoire composition class ravel’s studies; early sonata for violin and piano

title: Gédalge teaches the contrapuntal craft
k: gedalge teaches the contrapuntal craft andre gedalge → maurice ravel · documented alongside faure’s composition class, ravel took private counterpoint lessons with andre gedalge. keeping the two teachers distinct avoids attributing every part of ravel’s technical education to faure alone: gedalge supplied a separate, specifically contrapuntal apprenticeship. andre gedalge’s private counterpoint instruction ravel’s conservatoire-period training

title: Chabrier behind the grotesque serenade
k: chabrier behind the grotesque serenade emmanuel chabrier → maurice ravel · documented in his autobiographical account, ravel explicitly associated his early serenade grotesque with chabrier’s influence. this is the composer identifying a model for a particular piece, a stronger connection than a later critic hearing a general family likeness between two french piano styles. chabrier’s piano music serenade grotesque

title: Ravel names Satie as an early model
k: ravel names satie as an early model erik satie → maurice ravel · documented ravel’s autobiographical sketch names satie as an influence on the early ballade de la reine morte d’aimer. the piece is not available for a reliable musical comparison, so the evidence here is ravel’s own retrospective statement rather than a reconstructed passage or an invented quotation. satie’s early music ballade de la reine morte d’aimer

title: The Pavane’s Satie-like wrong-note chords
k: the pavane’s satie-like wrong-note chords erik satie → maurice ravel · inferred peter jost compares the pavane’s calmly sustained dissonances and unexpected bass support with satie’s early piano writing. this is a harmonic comparison, not a claim that ravel copied the gymnopedie melody; the excerpt isolates ravel’s tune so that the listener can distinguish melody from the accompaniment where the proposed resemblance lies. gymnopedies and early piano harmony pavane pour une infante defunte, original piano version

title: Poe offers a method, not a programme
sub: Edgar Allan Poe → Maurice Ravel · documented
k: poe offers a method, not a programme edgar allan poe → maurice ravel · documented ravel identified poe’s the philosophy of composition as an important guide to his thinking about making a work. emily kilpatrick places that reading beside ravel’s concern with deliberate construction and artistic originality; it is evidence about a declared method, not permission to attach a hidden poe story to every instrumental score. the philosophy of composition, through baudelaire’s translations ravel’s account of his compositional method

title: Pictures gains a saxophone and an orchestra
k: pictures gains a saxophone and an orchestra modest mussorgsky → maurice ravel · documented serge koussevitzky commissioned ravel’s orchestration of mussorgsky’s piano pictures at an exhibition, first performed in paris in october 1922. the trumpet’s opening promenade and the alto saxophone of the old castle are ravel’s instrumental decisions: the melodies and suite belong to mussorgsky, while the familiar orchestral colours belong to the arranger. pictures at an exhibition, piano suite, 1874 pictures at an exhibition, orchestration, 1922

title: An old French suite mourns modern soldiers
k: an old french suite mourns modern soldiers francois couperin → maurice ravel · documented le tombeau de couperin invokes the older french keyboard tradition rather than quoting a single identified couperin work. ravel gave its movements separate memorial dedications to men killed in the first world war; the toccata remembers joseph de marliave, whose widow marguerite long gave the complete suite’s premiere in 1919. couperin and the french keyboard-suite tradition le tombeau de couperin, piano suite, 1914–1917

title: Spanish songs remembered from his mother
sub: Spanish song tradition → Maurice Ravel · documented
k: spanish songs remembered from his mother spanish song tradition → maurice ravel · documented ravel’s mother sang spanish songs to him, giving his later fascination with spain a family setting as well as a concert-hall one. the connection helps explain why spanish subjects recur in his music, including rapsodie espagnole; it does not identify every ostensibly spanish melody as an actual childhood song quotation. spanish songs sung by ravel’s mother ravel’s spanish musical world, including rapsodie espagnole

title: The Trio sways in three-two-three
sub: Basque dance tradition → Maurice Ravel · documented
k: the trio sways in three-two-three basque dance tradition → maurice ravel · documented the first movement of ravel’s piano trio groups its eight eighth notes as 3 + 2 + 3, a rhythm the library of congress programme note connects with basque dance. listen for unequal lengths rather than a conventional four-square pulse: the regional connection is rhythmic and need not imply a verbatim folk-tune quotation. basque dance rhythm piano trio in a minor, movement i

title: Ravel’s Blues predates the American tour
sub: Jazz and blues → Maurice Ravel · documented
k: ravel’s blues predates the american tour jazz and blues → maurice ravel · documented ravel called the middle movement of his 1927 violin sonata blues, before his celebrated american visit and meeting with gershwin in 1928. the chronology matters: american music was already a compositional resource for him, not a revelation that began at gershwin’s piano in new york. jazz and blues idioms sonata for violin and piano, movement ii, blues

title: Gershwin plays at Ravel’s birthday party
k: gershwin plays at ravel’s birthday party george gershwin → maurice ravel · documented at eva gauthier’s new york party for ravel’s birthday on 7 march 1928, gershwin played music including rhapsody in blue and the man i love. the meeting is well documented, but it did not make gershwin ravel’s pupil; colourful versions of the refused-lessons anecdote should not be mistaken for a completed course of instruction. rhapsody in blue and the man i love ravel’s new york encounter with gershwin, 7 march 1928

title: Russian orchestral colour reaches Paris
k: russian orchestral colour reaches paris nikolai rimsky-korsakov → maurice ravel · documented ravel heard russian music associated with rimsky-korsakov at the paris exposition of 1889. this gives a dated encounter behind his interest in russian orchestral colour; it does not prove that a particular instrument in a later ravel score was copied from a particular rimsky-korsakov bar. rimsky-korsakov’s music at the paris exposition ravel’s youthful orchestral listening

title: Gaspard renews Lisztian virtuosity
k: gaspard renews lisztian virtuosity franz liszt → maurice ravel · inferred emily kilpatrick places gaspard de la nuit in the virtuoso pianist-composer tradition of liszt, with scarbo as a particularly conspicuous example. the relationship concerns how extreme keyboard technique becomes a dramatic resource; it is not a verified quotation from a named liszt composition. liszt’s virtuoso piano tradition gaspard de la nuit, especially scarbo

title: Scarbo aims beyond Islamey
k: scarbo aims beyond islamey mily balakirev → maurice ravel · documented ravel’s stated ambition for scarbo was to go beyond the technical difficulty of balakirev’s islamey. the russian work functions here as a challenge to surpass, not a theme to quote: repeated notes, leaps and rapid transformations become means of conjuring bertrand’s elusive goblin. islamey gaspard de la nuit: scarbo

title: Three prose poems become piano scenes
k: three prose poems become piano scenes aloysius bertrand → maurice ravel · documented ravel printed aloysius bertrand’s prose poems with the three movements of gaspard de la nuit. ondine, le gibet and scarbo therefore have specific textual companions, from the water spirit’s address to the tolling bell and the disappearing goblin; the poems are not programmes invented by later annotators. gaspard de la nuit: ondine, le gibet and scarbo gaspard de la nuit, three poems for piano

title: Schubert lends two waltz titles
k: schubert lends two waltz titles franz schubert → maurice ravel · documented ravel explicitly linked the title valses nobles et sentimentales with schubert’s two named waltz collections. the title establishes a conscious historical conversation, but it is not evidence that ravel’s harmonically abrasive waltzes reproduce a particular schubert melody. valses nobles and valses sentimentales valses nobles et sentimentales

title: Vaughan Williams comes to Paris for clarity
sub: Maurice Ravel → Ralph Vaughan Williams · documented
k: vaughan williams comes to paris for clarity maurice ravel → ralph vaughan williams · documented ralph vaughan williams studied with ravel in paris for about three months in 1907–1908. tom service’s account of the surviving correspondence describes lessons directed at craft and clarity, including work with a mozart minuet; the encounter did not require vaughan williams to abandon his own musical identity and become a french imitator. ravel’s lessons in composition and orchestral craft vaughan williams’s paris study, 1907–1908

title: Rimsky’s crowded orchestration classroom
k: rimsky’s crowded orchestration classroom nikolai rimsky-korsakov → sergei prokofiev · documented prokofiev studied orchestration in rimsky-korsakov’s classes at the st petersburg conservatory. david nice’s publisher biography also records his dissatisfaction with their crowded conditions, an important qualification to the easy picture of an intimate, contented master-and-disciple relationship. rimsky-korsakov’s st petersburg conservatory orchestration classes prokofiev’s student training

title: Lyadov’s rules meet an impatient modernist
k: lyadov’s rules meet an impatient modernist anatoly lyadov → sergei prokofiev · documented prokofiev studied harmony and counterpoint with anatoly lyadov, whose teaching he found uninspiring. the publisher’s chronology records lyadov’s alarm at the scriabinesque tendencies of his pupil’s 1909 examination pieces: this was instruction accompanied by aesthetic friction, not agreement about what new music should sound like. anatoly lyadov’s harmony and counterpoint teaching prokofiev’s st petersburg conservatory studies

title: Conducting lessons plant the Classical Symphony
k: conducting lessons plant the classical symphony nikolai tcherepnin → sergei prokofiev · documented nikolai tcherepnin taught prokofiev conducting and encouraged his close study of haydn and mozart. prokofiev dedicated his first piano concerto to him, while the tcherepnin society’s account connects those classical studies with the later conception of the classical symphony. nikolai tcherepnin’s conducting classes and haydn/mozart study prokofiev’s training; piano concerto no. 1 dedication

title: Glière visits the child composer at home
k: gliere visits the child composer at home reinhold gliere → sergei prokofiev · documented before the st petersburg conservatory, prokofiev received two summers of teaching from reinhold gliere at sontsovka. taneyev’s recommendation helped arrange the lessons, giving the child composer a concrete route from home composition towards systematic professional training. reinhold gliere’s summer composition teaching prokofiev’s lessons at sontsovka, 1902–1903

title: Haydn’s orchestra, with modern wrong turns
k: haydn’s orchestra, with modern wrong turns joseph haydn → sergei prokofiev · documented prokofiev imagined how haydn might compose in the modern world when making his classical symphony in 1916–1917. a compact orchestra, four-movement outline and lucid textures supply the historical frame, while abrupt harmonic turns prevent it from becoming an anonymous eighteenth-century imitation; the third movement is a gavotte rather than haydn’s usual minuet. haydn’s symphonic style and orchestral practice symphony no. 1 in d major, op. 25, classical

title: Diaghilev rejects one ballet and orders another
k: diaghilev rejects one ballet and orders another sergei diaghilev → sergei prokofiev · documented diaghilev commissioned ala et lolly after meeting prokofiev in 1914, then rejected the result and commissioned the russian folk-tale ballet chout instead. prokofiev salvaged music from the rejected project as the scythian suite, so the impresario’s refusal helped redirect rather than simply terminate the material’s life. diaghilev’s ballets russes commissions ala et lolly; chout; scythian suite

title: A piano audition turns into a quarrel
k: a piano audition turns into a quarrel igor stravinsky → sergei prokofiev · documented at a 1922 piano presentation of the love for three oranges for diaghilev, stravinsky objected to the opera and the two composers quarrelled. the episode records rivalry and disagreement, not a securely demonstrated musical borrowing; their relationship also included earlier collaboration at the piano, playing petrushka together. stravinsky’s criticism at diaghilev’s 1922 audition the love for three oranges and prokofiev’s response

title: Film follows music; music follows film
k: film follows music; music follows film sergei eisenstein → sergei prokofiev · documented for alexander nevsky, eisenstein and prokofiev worked in both directions: some images were shaped to music, while some music was written to images. prokofiev subsequently recast the 1938 film score as a 1939 concert cantata, so the familiar concert work is an adaptation of a collaborative audiovisual construction, not the film soundtrack unchanged. sergei eisenstein’s alexander nevsky, film alexander nevsky film score; concert cantata, op. 78

title: Romeo and Juliet nearly survived the ballet
k: romeo and juliet nearly survived the ballet william shakespeare → sergei prokofiev · documented prokofiev’s 1935 ballet project initially allowed romeo to arrive in time and the lovers to survive, before the ending was changed back to shakespeare’s tragedy. the adaptation was therefore not inevitable note-for-note storytelling: its authors actively negotiated what a shakespearean ending should become on the ballet stage. romeo and juliet romeo and juliet, ballet, op. 64

title: Prokofiev’s Onegin is not Tchaikovsky’s opera
k: prokofiev’s onegin is not tchaikovsky’s opera alexander pushkin → sergei prokofiev · documented prokofiev wrote eugene onegin music for alexander tairov’s planned stage production in 1936, using spoken voices with orchestra. the production was cancelled, leaving a substantial pushkin adaptation that should not be confused with tchaikovsky’s opera of the same name. eugene onegin, verse novel eugene onegin, incidental music, op. 71

title: Christian Science enters the composer’s own account
sub: Mary Baker Eddy → Sergei Prokofiev · documented
k: christian science enters the composer’s own account mary baker eddy → sergei prokofiev · documented prokofiev’s diaries document his engagement with christian science from 1924, including reading mary baker eddy’s science and health. in a 1933 letter preserved by the mary baker eddy library, he connected that faith with his work as a composer; this establishes a stated intellectual and spiritual influence, not a demonstrable source for particular harmonies or a claim that religious practice cured an illness. science and health with key to the scriptures; christian science teaching prokofiev’s diaries and 31 january 1933 letter to eve crain

title: Dostoevsky’s obsession becomes an opera
k: dostoevsky’s obsession becomes an opera fyodor dostoevsky → sergei prokofiev · documented prokofiev made dostoevsky’s the gambler into an opera during 1915–1917 and revised it a decade later. unlike a conjectural literary influence on an instrumental score, the novel supplies the named dramatic source; its first planned production fell through while prokofiev was still in russia. the gambler the gambler, opera, op. 24, 1915–1917; revised 1927–1928

title: Tolstoy’s invasion meets a second invasion
k: tolstoy’s invasion meets a second invasion leo tolstoy → sergei prokofiev · documented prokofiev turned to tolstoy’s war and peace as an operatic project after the german invasion of the soviet union in 1941. his work with mira mendelson selected scenes from the novel rather than attempting to reproduce the entire book, and repeated revisions made the opera a continuing project rather than a score fixed once in 1941. war and peace war and peace, opera, op. 91, begun 1941

title: Rachmaninoff’s Corelli theme is the older Folia
k: rachmaninoff’s corelli theme is the older folia arcangelo corelli → sergei rachmaninoff · documented rachmaninoff’s op. 42, composed in may and june 1931, takes its theme from the folia familiar through corelli’s op. 5 finale. the title names an important transmitter rather than the tune’s inventor: the theme was already older than corelli. corelli, sonata op. 5 no. 12, follia (1700), inherited theme variations on a theme of corelli, op. 42 (1931) la-folia

title: A Javanese gamelan in Paris reshapes Debussy’s ear
k: a javanese gamelan in paris reshapes debussy’s ear javanese gamelan → claude debussy · documented debussy heard a javanese gamelan at the paris exposition universelle of 1889, and its scales, melodies, rhythms and layered textures appealed to him. their echoes are heard in pagodes, the first piece of the piano suite estampes, which uses pentatonic scales and mimics gamelan melodies. he later wrote that javanese music “obeys laws of counterpoint which make palestrina seem like child’s play”. javanese gamelan at the exposition universelle, paris (1889) pagodes, from estampes (1903)

title: Mallarmé’s faun finds its music
k: mallarme’s faun finds its music stephane mallarme → claude debussy · documented debussy’s orchestral prelude, first performed in paris on 22 december 1894 under gustave doret, takes mallarme’s poem as its subject; debussy called it “a very free illustration” of the poem, not a synthesis of it. mallarme had doubted that music should be set beside poetry, but after attending the premiere at debussy’s invitation he wrote that the music went further than his text “into nostalgia and into light”. l’apres-midi d’un faune (poem, 1876) prelude a l’apres-midi d’un faune (1894)

title: Hokusai’s wave on the cover of La mer
k: hokusai’s wave on the cover of la mer katsushika hokusai → claude debussy · documented the first edition of the orchestral score of la mer (durand, 1905) carried a detail of hokusai’s great wave off kanagawa on its cover: roughly the left half of the print, the great wave with a smaller wave in front of it. the choice of the print is credited to debussy and is read as a sign of how much japanese art meant to him. what is documented is the cover; how far the picture shaped the music is a matter of interpretation. the great wave off kanagawa (c. 1831) la mer, first edition of the orchestral score (durand, 1905)

title: Debussy mocks Tristan in a cakewalk
k: debussy mocks tristan in a cakewalk richard wagner → claude debussy · documented in golliwogg’s cakewalk, debussy alludes satirically to wagner’s tristan und isolde: the opening bars turn the tristan chord into a jaunty, syncopated arpeggio, and the middle section is interrupted several times by a tristan phrase marked avec une grande emotion. debussy had heard the first act of tristan at the concerts lamoureux in 1887 and judged it “decidedly the finest thing i know”, so the joke is aimed at a work he knew well. tristan und isolde, prelude (1859) golliwogg’s cakewalk, from children’s corner (1908) tristan-chord

title: Debussy orchestrates two Gymnopédies
k: debussy orchestrates two gymnopedies claude debussy → erik satie · documented in february 1897, when satie’s popularity was waning and his finances deteriorating, debussy orchestrated the third and first gymnopedies to draw public attention to his friend’s music. when debussy published the scores two years later he reversed the numbering, so that satie’s first became his third. the two had met in 1890 and found each other kindred spirits in their experimental approach to composition. debussy’s orchestration of gymnopedies nos. 3 and 1 (1897) gymnopedies (1888)

title: Péladan makes Satie composer to the Rose+Croix
k: peladan makes satie composer to the rose+croix josephin peladan → erik satie · documented sar josephin peladan, founder of the ordre de la rose-croix catholique, invited satie to become the order’s official composer. for peladan’s first salon de la rose-croix (10 march–10 april 1892), each gathering opened with a solemn mass of the holy ghost, preceded by three fanfares for harp and trumpet that satie composed. they were published as sonneries de la rose+croix, music written for the order’s ceremonies rather than the concert hall. salon de la rose+croix, paris (10 march–10 april 1892) sonneries de la rose+croix (1892)

title: Strauss answers Nietzsche in a tone poem
k: strauss answers nietzsche in a tone poem friedrich nietzsche → richard strauss · documented strauss conducted the first performance of his tone poem in frankfurt on 27 november 1896, and named its sections after chapters of nietzsche’s book (“of the backworldsmen”, “of the great longing”). strauss insisted that he had not meant to write philosophical music or to portray nietzsche’s work, but “to convey in music an idea of the evolution of the human race” up to nietzsche’s idea of the ubermensch. also sprach zarathustra (1883–85) also sprach zarathustra, op. 30 (1896)

title: Strauss ends Metamorphosen on Beethoven’s funeral march
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Richard Strauss · documented
k: strauss ends metamorphosen on beethoven’s funeral march ludwig van beethoven → richard strauss · documented at the end of metamorphosen, strauss quotes the first four bars of the marcia funebre from beethoven’s eroica symphony and writes beneath them “in memoriam!”. a direct quotation from bar 3 of the march also appears earlier in the score as one of the work’s themes, so the funeral march is present throughout the piece before it is named at the close. symphony no. 3, “eroica”, marcia funebre (1804) metamorphosen (1945)

title: A rune singer teaches Sibelius how Finnish sings
k: a rune singer teaches sibelius how finnish sings larin paraske → jean sibelius · disputed at the end of 1891 sibelius travelled with the aesthetician yrjo hirn to porvoo to hear the izhorian rune singer larin paraske. sibelius recalled that he mainly noticed how a rune singer uses finnish, prolonging and stressing the last syllables of words, and that he did not yet realise how famous she was. kullervo, whose vocal movements set runos of the kalevala, followed in 1892. larin paraske’s rune singing, porvoo (1891) kullervo, op. 7 (1892)

title: Scriabin’s 24 Preludes follow Chopin’s plan
k: scriabin’s 24 preludes follow chopin’s plan frederic chopin → alexander scriabin · inferred scriabin’s op. 11 keeps strictly to the circle of fifths to cover every major and minor key, the plan of chopin’s op. 28 set. both cycles are built alike, with pieces arranged in relative major and minor pairs, and the resemblance sits beside a wider spiritual kinship with chopin that runs through scriabin’s early music. chopin, 24 preludes, op. 28 (1839) scriabin, 24 preludes, op. 11 (1888–96)

title: Tolstoy’s Kreutzer Sonata becomes a string quartet
k: tolstoy’s kreutzer sonata becomes a string quartet leo tolstoy → leos janacek · documented janacek wrote his first string quartet between 13 and 28 october 1923, inspired by tolstoy’s novella the kreutzer sonata, which had itself been inspired by beethoven’s violin sonata of that name. he had used the novella once before, in a piano trio of 1908–09 that is lost; surviving fragments suggest similarities to the quartet. the czech quartet gave the first performance in prague on 17 october 1924. the kreutzer sonata (novella) string quartet no. 1, “kreutzer sonata” (1923)

title: Elgar sets Newman’s poem of a dying soul
sub: John Henry Newman → Edward Elgar · documented
k: elgar sets newman’s poem of a dying soul john henry newman → edward elgar · documented elgar had owned a copy of newman’s poem since at least 1885, and in 1889 he was given another as a wedding present; that copy carried handwritten transcriptions of notes made by general gordon. he thought of the text in musical terms for years before setting it for the birmingham triennial festival, where the dream of gerontius was first performed on 3 october 1900. the dream of gerontius (poem, 1865) the dream of gerontius, op. 38 (1900)

title: Nimrod hints at Beethoven’s Pathétique slow movement
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Edward Elgar · documented
k: nimrod hints at beethoven’s pathetique slow movement ludwig van beethoven → edward elgar · documented elgar said nimrod came from a day when he was ready to give up composing and his publisher august jaeger urged him on, pointing to beethoven, who wrote more and more beautiful music despite his worries, and singing the theme of the pathetique sonata’s slow movement. elgar told dora penny that the opening bars of nimrod were made to suggest that theme: “only a hint, not a quotation”. piano sonata no. 8, “pathetique”, slow movement (1799) enigma variations, variation ix “nimrod” (1899)

title: Puccini walks to Pisa to hear Aida
k: puccini walks to pisa to hear aida giuseppe verdi → giacomo puccini · documented in 1876, aged eighteen, puccini walked about twenty kilometres from lucca to pisa to hear the first local performance of verdi’s aida. he said later that when he heard it in pisa he felt “a musical window had opened for me”, and the experience is credited with turning him from church music towards the theatre. aida (1871) puccini’s career in the opera house

title: A Chinese music box gives Turandot its tunes
sub: Chinese folk melody (Mòlìhuā) → Giacomo Puccini · documented
k: a chinese music box gives turandot its tunes chinese folk melody (molihua) → giacomo puccini · documented baron edoardo fassini-camossi, a former italian diplomat in china, gave puccini a music box that played four chinese melodies. puccini worked three of them into turandot, the most memorable being the folk melody “molihua” (“jasmine flower”), which serves as a leitmotif for the princess’s splendour. in all, eight of the opera’s themes appear to be based on traditional chinese music. chinese melodies on a music box owned by baron fassini-camossi turandot (1920–24, unfinished)

title: George’s poems bring a voice into the quartet
k: george’s poems bring a voice into the quartet stefan george → arnold schoenberg · documented in the last two movements of his second string quartet, schoenberg set poems by stefan george for soprano, adding a voice to a genre that had never had one. the rose quartet and the soprano marie gutheil-schoder gave the first performance, and a critic of 1914 called the innovation beethovenian, alluding to the choral finale of the ninth symphony. stefan george, litanei and entruckung (der siebente ring) string quartet no. 2, op. 10, movements iii–iv (1908)

title: Schoenberg dedicates Harmonielehre to Mahler’s memory
k: schoenberg dedicates harmonielehre to mahler’s memory gustav mahler → arnold schoenberg · documented schoenberg wrote his harmonielehre in the summer of 1910 and published it in 1911 with the dedication “dem andenken gustav mahlers ist dieses buch geweiht” (“this book is dedicated to the memory of gustav mahler”). mahler died on 18 may 1911, and the dedication makes the book schoenberg’s memorial to him. gustav mahler, who died in may 1911 harmonielehre (1911)

title: Kandinsky draws Schoenberg into the Blaue Reiter
k: kandinsky draws schoenberg into the blaue reiter wassily kandinsky → arnold schoenberg · documented after hearing schoenberg’s music at a munich concert on 2 january 1911, kandinsky wrote to him on 18 january: “in your works, you have realized what i, albeit in uncertain form, have so greatly longed for in music.” schoenberg visited kandinsky, gabriele munter and franz marc in murnau, and the painters planned an exhibition and an almanac that drew in artists of every medium. the two corresponded until the first world war broke contact in 1914. kandinsky’s letters to schoenberg, from 18 january 1911 schoenberg’s contributions to the blaue reiter exhibition and almanac (1911–12)

title: A Schoenberg concert becomes Impression III
k: a schoenberg concert becomes impression iii arnold schoenberg → wassily kandinsky · documented kandinsky’s painting impression iii (concert) was inspired by a concert of schoenberg’s works in munich on 2 january 1911, which kandinsky attended. he was so enthralled by the music that he wrote to schoenberg within days, beginning an exchange of letters that lasted until 1914. concert of schoenberg’s music, munich (2 january 1911) impression iii (concert) (1911)

title: Berg begins seven years of lessons with Schoenberg
k: berg begins seven years of lessons with schoenberg arnold schoenberg → alban berg · documented berg studied counterpoint, music theory and harmony with schoenberg between 1904 and 1911. he adopted his teacher’s principle of developing variation and, later, the twelve-tone technique, which shapes the lyric suite and the violin concerto. schoenberg’s teaching in vienna (1904–11) berg’s early works, from the piano sonata, op. 1

title: Berg sees Woyzeck on stage and begins an opera
k: berg sees woyzeck on stage and begins an opera georg buchner → alban berg · documented in may 1914 berg attended a performance in vienna of buchner’s play, left unfinished at the author’s death in 1837, and was moved to set it. the opera that followed, wozzeck, kept the play’s fragmentary scenes in order and was completed after the first world war. woyzeck (play, 1837) wozzeck (opera, completed 1922)

title: Berg ends the Violin Concerto on Bach’s chorale
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Alban Berg · documented
k: berg ends the violin concerto on bach’s chorale johann sebastian bach → alban berg · documented berg wrote his violin concerto “to the memory of an angel” after the death of manon gropius, and built its last section on the chorale “es ist genug” from bach’s cantata o ewigkeit, du donnerwort. the last four notes of berg’s tone row, rising by whole tones, are also the first four notes of the chorale, and in the score a footnote explains the marking ch as the chorale motif. berg sets the tune a semitone above bach’s a major, the solo violin giving the first phrase before the clarinets state bach’s harmonisation. cantata bwv 60, closing chorale “es ist genug” violin concerto, part ii, adagio (1935)

title: Berg hides Tristan inside the Lyric Suite
k: berg hides tristan inside the lyric suite richard wagner → alban berg · documented the last movement of berg’s lyric suite develops the tristan motif along with the rest of its material, by berg’s own analysis, through strict adherence to the twelve-note series. in january 1977 george perle was shown a copy of the first printed score annotated in red, blue and green by berg, which revealed a secret programme about berg’s love for hanna fuchs-robettin; the suite was publicly dedicated to zemlinsky, whose lyric symphony it also quotes. tristan und isolde, prelude (1859) lyric suite, last movement (1926) tristan-chord

title: Webern re-scores Bach’s six-part Ricercar
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Anton Webern · documented
k: webern re-scores bach’s six-part ricercar johann sebastian bach → anton webern · documented between december 1934 and early 1935 webern orchestrated the six-voice ricercar from bach’s musical offering for a chamber orchestra of single winds, harp, timpani and strings. the first performance was in london on 25 april 1935. webern keeps bach’s notes and divides the lines among the instruments, so that melodies pass between colours: the principle he called klangfarbenmelodie. musical offering, bwv 1079: ricercar a 6 (1747) fuga (ricercata) a 6 voci, bach–webern (1934–35)

title: Webern edits Isaac and learns the interplay of parts
k: webern edits isaac and learns the interplay of parts heinrich isaac → anton webern · documented for his musicology doctorate under guido adler, webern edited the second part of heinrich isaac’s choralis constantinus. as a composer he would emulate its “subtle organization in the interplay of parts”, a discipline he carried from the study of renaissance polyphony into his own writing. choralis constantinus ii (early 16th century) webern’s doctoral edition and his later counterpoint

title: Bartók records peasant songs on the phonograph
sub: Hungarian peasant song → Béla Bartók · documented
k: bartok records peasant songs on the phonograph hungarian peasant song → bela bartok · documented bartok’s first year of substantial folk-song collecting was 1906: that summer he used a phonograph on his first systematic trip, to bekes county, and over the year he collected more than a thousand hungarian songs and some three hundred slovak ones. in 1907–08 he went on to felsoireg and to the transylvanian regions of csik and gyergyo. following bela vikar, he used the phonograph from the beginning to complete his written notes with sound recordings. peasant songs recorded in bekes county and elsewhere (1906–08) bartok’s folk-song collections and the music built on them

title: Kodály brings Debussy’s scores to Bartók
k: kodaly brings debussy’s scores to bartok claude debussy → bela bartok · documented beginning in 1907 bartok came under the influence of debussy, whose compositions his friend kodaly had brought back from paris. the discovery came as bartok was already absorbed in collecting peasant music, so french harmony and hungarian folk material reach his work together. debussy’s scores, brought from paris by kodaly bartok’s works from 1907

title: Stravinsky studies with Rimsky-Korsakov until 1908
k: stravinsky studies with rimsky-korsakov until 1908 nikolai rimsky-korsakov → igor stravinsky · documented while studying law at the university of saint petersburg, stravinsky met rimsky-korsakov and studied music under him until the older composer’s death in 1908. soon afterwards stravinsky met sergei diaghilev, who commissioned the ballets for the ballets russes that made his name. rimsky-korsakov’s teaching, st petersburg fireworks and the early works (to 1908)

title: The Rite’s opening bassoon sings a Lithuanian tune
sub: Lithuanian folk song → Igor Stravinsky · documented
k: the rite’s opening bassoon sings a lithuanian tune lithuanian folk song → igor stravinsky · documented stravinsky acknowledged that the opening bassoon melody of the rite of spring was derived from an anthology of lithuanian folk songs, but maintained that this was his only borrowing from such sources. later scholars have identified several more melodies in part i that came from the same lithuanian collection, and richard taruskin’s study of the sketches traced further russian folk sources. anthology of lithuanian folk songs (warsaw) the rite of spring, opening bassoon solo (1913)

title: Stravinsky recomposes music then thought to be Pergolesi’s
sub: Giovanni Battista Pergolesi → Igor Stravinsky · documented
