k: stravinsky recomposes music then thought to be pergolesi’s giovanni battista pergolesi → igor stravinsky · documented pulcinella, first danced in paris in may 1920 with designs by picasso, is a ballet on a commedia dell’arte libretto and music then believed to be by pergolesi. the attribution has since been shown to be spurious: some of the music may be by domenico gallo, unico wilhelm van wassenaer, carlo ignazio monza and alessandro parisotti. stravinsky’s score recomposes it, so the influence is of an eighteenth-century idiom rather than of pergolesi himself. pieces then attributed to pergolesi pulcinella (1920)

title: Stravinsky hears Pierrot lunaire in Berlin
k: stravinsky hears pierrot lunaire in berlin arnold schoenberg → igor stravinsky · documented in the winter of 1912 stravinsky was in berlin for performances of his ballets by the ballets russes, and attended a performance of schoenberg’s pierrot lunaire, conducted by the composer, less than two months after its premiere. he had already composed the first of his three japanese lyrics as a song with piano, but after hearing pierrot he decided to give the songs a somewhat similar coat of instrumental colour. pierrot lunaire, op. 21 (1912) three japanese lyrics (1912–13)

title: Hymn tunes and town bands become Ives’s material
sub: American hymn tunes and town bands → Charles Ives · documented
k: hymn tunes and town bands become ives’s material american hymn tunes and town bands → charles ives · documented the sources of ives’s tonal imagery included hymn tunes and traditional songs. he also incorporated the melodies of town bands at holiday parades, fiddlers at saturday-night dances, patriotic songs, sentimental parlour ballads and the tunes of stephen foster. hymn tunes, town-band music, stephen foster ives’s songs, symphonies and sonatas

title: Beethoven’s Fifth motif runs through the Concord Sonata
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Charles Ives · documented
k: beethoven’s fifth motif runs through the concord sonata ludwig van beethoven → charles ives · documented the opening bars of beethoven’s fifth symphony are quoted in each movement of ives’s concord sonata, whose four movements portray emerson, hawthorne, the alcotts and thoreau. ives drew on material dating back to 1904, began substantial work around 1909 and largely completed the sonata by 1915; it was first published in 1920. symphony no. 5, opening motif (1808) piano sonata no. 2, “concord, mass., 1840–60” (completed by 1915)

title: Leipzig’s Bach competition prompts Shostakovich’s 24 Preludes and Fugues
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Dmitri Shostakovich · documented
k: leipzig’s bach competition prompts shostakovich’s 24 preludes and fugues johann sebastian bach → dmitri shostakovich · documented in 1950 shostakovich sat on the jury of the first international johann sebastian bach competition at leipzig, held for the bicentenary of bach’s death. the young tatiana nikolayeva from moscow, who had come prepared to play any of the 48 preludes and fugues on request, won the gold medal. inspired by the competition and her playing, he returned to moscow and began his own cycle of 24 preludes and fugues, which nikolayeva premiered in leningrad on 23 december 1952. the well-tempered clavier (1722, 1742) 24 preludes and fugues, op. 87 (1950–51)

title: Sollertinsky teaches Shostakovich to love Mahler
k: sollertinsky teaches shostakovich to love mahler gustav mahler → dmitri shostakovich · documented shostakovich’s close friendship with the musicologist and theatre critic ivan sollertinsky began in 1927. shostakovich later said that sollertinsky “taught [him] to understand and love such great masters as brahms, mahler, and bruckner”. mahler’s music left a lasting mark on his style, which combines the grotesque with ambivalent tonality. mahler’s symphonies, introduced by ivan sollertinsky shostakovich’s symphonies

title: Shostakovich tells Gubaidulina to continue her “mistaken” way
k: shostakovich tells gubaidulina to continue her “mistaken” way dmitri shostakovich → sofia gubaidulina · documented gubaidulina’s music was judged “irresponsible” during her studies at the moscow conservatory because it explored alternative tunings. when shostakovich evaluated one of her examinations he encouraged her to continue on her path, although others, among them tikhon khrennikov, called it “mistaken”. she went on to the breakthrough of her violin concerto offertorium in 1980. shostakovich’s verdict on a conservatoire examination gubaidulina’s early music at the moscow conservatory

title: Gubaidulina scores Bach’s royal theme in Webern’s manner
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Sofia Gubaidulina · documented
k: gubaidulina scores bach’s royal theme in webern’s manner johann sebastian bach → sofia gubaidulina · documented offertorium is centred on the theme that frederick the great gave to bach, the basis of the musical offering. gubaidulina orchestrates the theme with a klangfarbenmelodie technique reminiscent of webern, passing it around different instruments to exploit their timbres. the piece was her first major breakthrough. musical offering, bwv 1079: the royal theme (1747) offertorium, violin concerto (1980)

title: Shostakovich dedicates his Fourteenth Symphony to Britten
k: shostakovich dedicates his fourteenth symphony to britten dmitri shostakovich → benjamin britten · documented shostakovich dedicated his fourteenth symphony, a song cycle on poems about death, to his close friend britten, who conducted its western premiere at the 1970 aldeburgh festival. symphony no. 14 (1969) western premiere, aldeburgh festival (1970)

title: Britten builds his Young Person’s Guide on Purcell
k: britten builds his young person’s guide on purcell henry purcell → benjamin britten · documented britten’s young person’s guide to the orchestra, subtitled variations and fugue on a theme of purcell, is based on the second movement, a rondeau, of purcell’s abdelazer suite. it was commissioned for the british educational documentary film instruments of the orchestra, released on 29 november 1946. abdelazer, rondeau (1695) the young person’s guide to the orchestra, op. 34 (1945)

title: Auden writes Britten’s first music drama
sub: W. H. Auden → Benjamin Britten · documented
k: auden writes britten’s first music drama w. h. auden → benjamin britten · documented britten’s first music drama, the operetta paul bunyan (1941), has a libretto by w. h. auden. the partnership had begun earlier, in the small group of regular contributors to the gpo film unit that britten joined in the 1930s, where auden was another of the writers. libretto for paul bunyan (1941) paul bunyan (1941)

title: Colin McPhee’s Balinese transcriptions reach Britten
k: colin mcphee’s balinese transcriptions reach britten balinese gamelan → benjamin britten · documented while in the united states, britten first encountered balinese gamelan music through transcriptions for piano duo by the canadian composer colin mcphee, who had lived in bali from 1931 to 1938. the two met in the summer of 1939 and performed some of the transcriptions for a recording. britten later built many gamelan elements into the ballet the prince of the pagodas, including a simulation of the seven-tone pelog tuning on western instruments. mcphee’s piano-duo transcriptions of balinese gamelan the prince of the pagodas (1957)

title: Poulenc writes a harpsichord concerto for Landowska
k: poulenc writes a harpsichord concerto for landowska wanda landowska → francis poulenc · documented poulenc composed his concert champetre for the harpsichordist wanda landowska, a friend and colleague from 1923. she gave the first performance with the orchestre symphonique de paris under pierre monteux at the salle pleyel on 3 may 1929. wanda landowska’s pleyel harpsichord concert champetre (1927–28)

title: Francis Jammes’s poems become Lili Boulanger’s song cycle
k: francis jammes’s poems become lili boulanger’s song cycle francis jammes → lili boulanger · documented boulanger’s song cycle clairieres dans le ciel is set to poems by francis jammes. it stands with her three psalms for chorus and orchestra, the diptych d’un soir triste and d’un matin de printemps, and her prix de rome cantata faust et helene among the works that made her reputation. poems by francis jammes clairieres dans le ciel (1914)

title: Messiaen notates birdsong and writes it into music
k: messiaen notates birdsong and writes it into music birdsong → olivier messiaen · documented messiaen was fascinated by birdsong and notated it around the world. birds had appeared in several earlier works, but the flute piece le merle noir was based entirely on the song of the blackbird; the orchestral reveil des oiseaux (1953) took the idea further, its material consisting almost entirely of the birdsong one might hear between midnight and noon in the jura. from then on he incorporated birdsong transcriptions into his compositions. birdsong, notated in the field le merle noir (1952); reveil des oiseaux (1953)

title: A gift of Pelléas becomes “a thunderbolt” for Messiaen
k: a gift of pelleas becomes “a thunderbolt” for messiaen claude debussy → olivier messiaen · documented at nantes, one of messiaen’s teachers, jehan de gibon, gave him a score of debussy’s opera pelleas et melisande. messiaen called it “a thunderbolt” and “probably the most decisive influence on me”. he entered the paris conservatoire in 1919, aged eleven. pelleas et melisande (1902) messiaen’s early music

title: Ligeti discovers Nancarrow’s player-piano Studies
k: ligeti discovers nancarrow’s player-piano studies conlon nancarrow → gyorgy ligeti · documented ligeti first met nancarrow’s name through a berlin festival of mechanical music in january 1980, and was fascinated by the complexity and temporal layering of a score page of study no. 36 in its catalogue. he called nancarrow’s music “the greatest discovery since webern and ives”. his piano etudes draw on sources that include gamelan, african polyrhythms, bartok, monk, bill evans and nancarrow. studies for player piano ligeti’s piano etudes and piano concerto (1980s)

title: Boulez joins Messiaen’s advanced harmony class
k: boulez joins messiaen’s advanced harmony class olivier messiaen → pierre boulez · documented in june 1944 boulez approached messiaen and asked to study harmony with him. messiaen invited him to attend the private seminars he gave to selected students, and in january 1945 boulez joined his advanced harmony class at the conservatoire de paris. he also studied counterpoint privately with andree vaurabourg and, with rene leibowitz, twelve-note technique. messiaen’s private seminars and conservatoire class boulez’s earliest published works

title: Boulez declares “Schoenberg is Dead”
k: boulez declares “schoenberg is dead” arnold schoenberg → pierre boulez · documented a 1952 article in the british journal the score, published shortly after schoenberg’s death, first brought boulez international attention as a writer. in it he attacked schoenberg for conservatism, contrasting him with the radicalism of webern. the article caused widespread controversy, although boulez had learned twelve-note technique privately with rene leibowitz, a champion of schoenberg. schoenberg’s twelve-note music “schoenberg is dead”, the score (1952)

title: Boulez folds Mallarmé’s sonnets into Pli selon pli
k: boulez folds mallarme’s sonnets into pli selon pli stephane mallarme → pierre boulez · documented boulez’s pli selon pli (“fold by fold”), subtitled portrait de mallarme, is a work in five movements for solo soprano and orchestra whose text is drawn from sonnets by mallarme. it was first performed in 1960 at baden-baden, sixty-six years after debussy answered another mallarme poem with the prelude a l’apres-midi d’un faune. sonnets by stephane mallarme pli selon pli, “portrait de mallarme” (first performed 1960)

title: Cage opens publishers’ doors to Boulez
k: cage opens publishers’ doors to boulez john cage → pierre boulez · documented boulez’s friendship with john cage began in 1949, when cage was visiting paris. cage introduced him to two publishers, heugel and amphion, who agreed to take his recent pieces, and boulez helped arrange a private performance of cage’s sonatas and interludes for prepared piano. sonatas and interludes for prepared piano (1946–48) boulez’s early publications

title: Feldman meets Cage after Webern’s Symphony
k: feldman meets cage after webern’s symphony john cage → morton feldman · documented in january 1950 feldman met john cage walking out of carnegie hall, where both had gone to hear the new york philharmonic under dimitri mitropoulos play webern’s symphony, op. 21. feldman soon moved into cage’s apartment building on grand street, and through cage met jackson pollock, philip guston and frank o’hara. webern’s symphony, op. 21 at carnegie hall (january 1950) feldman’s graph pieces and projections

title: Rothko’s paintings inspire Feldman’s Rothko Chapel
k: rothko’s paintings inspire feldman’s rothko chapel mark rothko → morton feldman · documented in the 1970s feldman wrote a number of pieces about twenty minutes long, among them rothko chapel (1971), written for the building in houston that houses paintings by mark rothko. he found inspiration in abstract expressionist painting and knew its painters through cage, who introduced him to jackson pollock, philip guston and frank o’hara. mark rothko’s paintings in the rothko chapel, houston rothko chapel (1971)

title: Pärt studies chant and Notre Dame polyphony before tintinnabuli
k: part studies chant and notre dame polyphony before tintinnabuli gregorian chant → arvo part · documented after credo (1968), part entered a creative crisis that lasted eight years. during that time he joined the orthodox church and studied gregorian chant, the notre dame school and classic vocal polyphony. in 1976 he emerged with a new and highly original musical language that he called tintinnabuli, first heard in the piano piece fur alina. gregorian chant and the notre dame school fur alina (1976) and the tintinnabuli style

title: Pärt mourns Britten in a descending cantus
k: part mourns britten in a descending cantus benjamin britten → arvo part · documented part composed cantus in memoriam benjamin britten for string orchestra and bell as an elegy for britten, who died in december 1976. part greatly admired him, describing in britten the “unusual purity” that he himself sought as a composer. the work is an early example of part’s tintinnabuli style. britten’s music and example cantus in memoriam benjamin britten (1977)

title: Reich studies Ewe drumming in Ghana
sub: Ewe drumming of Ghana → Steve Reich · documented
k: reich studies ewe drumming in ghana ewe drumming of ghana → steve reich · documented in june 1970 reich travelled to the university of ghana to study polyrhythmic music for five weeks with the ewe master drummer gideon alorwoyie. from this experience, and from a. m. jones’s studies in african music on the ewe, he drew inspiration for drumming (1970–71), which he began composing shortly after his return. ewe drumming taught by gideon alorwoyie, legon (june 1970) drumming (1970–71)

title: Reich studies Balinese gamelan in Seattle and Berkeley
k: reich studies balinese gamelan in seattle and berkeley balinese gamelan → steve reich · documented in the summers of 1973 and 1974 reich studied balinese gamelan, the semar pegulingan and the gambang, at seattle and berkeley. the experience influenced his music for mallet instruments, voices and organ (1973); in 1974 he began writing music for 18 musicians. gamelan semar pegulingan and gambang, studied in summer 1973 and 1974 music for mallet instruments, voices and organ (1973)

title: Kurtág sets Kafka’s fragments for soprano and violin
k: kurtag sets kafka’s fragments for soprano and violin franz kafka → gyorgy kurtag · documented kurtag’s kafka-fragmente, op. 24 (1985–87), for soprano and violin, takes extracts from kafka’s journals and letters and is broken into forty brief settings organised in four sections. kurtag was fascinated by the bareness of kafka’s language, by its sadness and despair, its humour and its depth. the soprano adrienne csengery and the violinist andras keller gave the first performance at the witten festival of contemporary chamber music in 1987. kafka’s diaries, letters and notebooks kafka-fragmente, op. 24 (1985–87)

title: Cage’s Silence loosens Adams’s modernist training
k: cage’s silence loosens adams’s modernist training john cage → john adams · inferred adams’s early work was aligned with modernist music, but he began to disagree with its tenets on reading john cage’s silence: lectures and writings. teaching at the san francisco conservatory of music, he went on to develop a style of his own. silence: lectures and writings (1961) adams’s music from the 1970s

title: A troubadour’s love from afar becomes Saariaho’s opera
k: a troubadour’s love from afar becomes saariaho’s opera jaufre rudel → kaija saariaho · documented saariaho became familiar in 1993 with the twelfth-century troubadour jaufre rudel, the poet of far-off love (amor de lonh). she did not think herself capable of writing an opera until she saw peter sellars’s staging of messiaen’s saint francois d’assise at the 1992 salzburg festival. with a libretto by amin maalouf, l’amour de loin (“love from afar”) was first performed at the salzburg festival on 15 august 2000. jaufre rudel, 12th-century troubadour poet l’amour de loin (2000)

title: Adès re-scores three Couperin harpsichord pieces
k: ades re-scores three couperin harpsichord pieces francois couperin → thomas ades · documented ades’s three studies from couperin (2006), written for the basle chamber orchestra, reconfigure keyboard pieces by couperin — les amusemens, les tours de passe-passe and l’ame-en-peine — for two string ensembles with solo winds and percussion. because couperin’s style involves a great deal of repetition, ades varies it by altering the orchestration or adding shadows and haloes to the parts. pieces de clavecin: les amusemens, les tours de passe-passe, l’ame-en-peine three studies from couperin (2006)

title: Reger builds an organ monument on BACH
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Max Reger · documented
k: reger builds an organ monument on bach johann sebastian bach → max reger · documented reger made b–a–c–h the named subject of his large organ fantasy and fugue, op. 46, composed in february 1900. its dedication is to josef rheinberger: the bach homage in its musical material should not be confused with the person named on the dedication page. the b–a–c–h musical signature fantasie und fuge uber b-a-c-h, op. 46 (1900) bach-motif

title: Bach’s four notes begin Webern’s twelve-tone row
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Anton Webern · documented
k: bach’s four notes begin webern’s twelve-tone row johann sebastian bach → anton webern · documented webern’s op. 28 row begins b♭–a–c–b♮, and its three four-note groups are transformations of that same b–a–c–h cell. the quartet therefore carries an identifiable bach signature inside its twelve-tone organisation rather than quoting a whole bach tune. the b–a–c–h musical signature string quartet, op. 28 (1936–38) bach-motif

title: Pärt places Bach beside twelve-tone dissonance
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Arvo Pärt · documented
k: part places bach beside twelve-tone dissonance johann sebastian bach → arvo part · documented part’s collage uber b-a-c-h begins its ten-note sequence with bach’s four-note signature. in the sarabande, passages from the d-minor english suite alternate with dense clusters, and harpsichord and piano help distinguish inherited baroque music from the modern material set against it. the b–a–c–h signature; english suite in d minor, sarabande collage uber b-a-c-h (1964), especially sarabande bach-motif

title: The chant haunts an amplified string quartet
k: the chant haunts an amplified string quartet gregorian chant → george crumb · documented crumb acknowledged the dies irae among the musical allusions in black angels, alongside schubert’s death and the maiden and tartini’s devil’s trill. the chant’s appearance in a work for amplified string quartet extends its afterlife beyond romantic orchestral spectacle into an intimate, unsettling modern sound-world. dies irae, the requiem plainchant black angels, thirteen images from the dark land (1970) dies-irae

title: The Ode becomes an anthem without words
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → The European anthem · documented
k: the ode becomes an anthem without words ludwig van beethoven → the european anthem · documented the council of europe adopted beethoven’s ode to joy melody as its anthem in 1972; european community leaders adopted it in 1985. the official anthem has no words, allowing the music to serve as a shared symbol without choosing one language for schiller’s poem. symphony no. 9, finale, ode to joy european anthem: council of europe adoption (1972), european community adoption (1985) ode-to-joy

title: Bernstein changes joy to freedom in Berlin
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Leonard Bernstein · documented
k: bernstein changes joy to freedom in berlin ludwig van beethoven → leonard bernstein · documented at the christmas day 1989 concert in east berlin, bernstein conducted beethoven’s ninth with singers substituting freiheit for freude in the finale. the alteration answered the opening of the berlin wall; it is a documented performance decision, not evidence that schiller originally wrote the poem with that word. symphony no. 9, finale, schiller’s an die freude berlin freedom concert, schauspielhaus, 25 december 1989 ode-to-joy

title: A children’s round enters Paperback Writer
sub: Frère Jacques / Bruder Martin → The Beatles · documented
k: a children’s round enters paperback writer frere jacques / bruder martin → the beatles · documented the beatles sing frere jacques in the backing vocals of paperback writer, recorded in april 1966. unlike mahler’s minor-key funeral transformation, this is a brief vocal quotation tucked into a pop recording: the same familiar round travels into a different musical setting. frere jacques, traditional round paperback writer, backing vocals (1966) frere-jacques

title: Zelter teaches Fanny Mendelssohn counterpoint and Bach
sub: Carl Friedrich Zelter → Fanny Hensel · documented
k: zelter teaches fanny mendelssohn counterpoint and bach carl friedrich zelter → fanny hensel · documented hensel and her brother mendelssohn received composition lessons from carl friedrich zelter, head of the berlin sing-akademie, starting in 1819; ludwig berger had earlier taught them piano. in 1816 zelter had written to goethe that her father’s eldest daughter “could give you something of sebastian bach”. at fourteen she played all twenty-four preludes of the well-tempered clavier from memory for her father’s birthday in 1819. carl friedrich zelter, composition lessons from 1819; letter to goethe, 1816 fanny mendelssohn playing the 24 preludes of the well-tempered clavier from memory (1819)

title: Chopin hears village musicians at Szafarnia, 1825
sub: Polish folk music → Frédéric Chopin · disputed
k: chopin hears village musicians at szafarnia, 1825 polish folk music → frederic chopin · disputed chopin spent the summers of 1824 and 1825 at szafarnia, the dziewanowski estate, where he met authentic folk music at first hand: he wrote down songs he heard, joined in rural amusements, and in a letter home of 26 august 1825 describes accompanying a fiddler on a one-stringed cello. his first published mazurkas, op. 6 and op. 7, date from 1830–31 and appeared in 1832. in 1852 liszt wrote that chopin’s mazurkas grew directly out of polish national music, and later writers read “national” as “folk”; recent scholarship holds instead that the likelier source is the national music chopin heard in the towns. folk songs and dances of the dobrzyn land, heard at szafarnia, summers 1824 and 1825 chopin’s mazurkas, from op. 6 and op. 7 (composed 1830–31, published 1832)

title: Mendelssohn reads Shakespeare in German and writes an overture
k: mendelssohn reads shakespeare in german and writes an overture william shakespeare → felix mendelssohn · documented after reading august wilhelm schlegel’s german translation of a midsummer night’s dream, made with ludwig tieck’s help, mendelssohn finished the concert overture, op. 21, on 6 august 1826, at seventeen years and six months. it was first played at stettin on 20 february 1827. in 1843 he added the incidental music for a potsdam production, first performed on 14 october, and incorporated the overture; that score includes the wedding march. shakespeare, a midsummer night’s dream, in the schlegel–tieck german translation mendelssohn, overture, op. 21 (finished 6 august 1826); incidental music, op. 61 (1842–43)

title: Chopin varies Mozart’s Là ci darem; Schumann cheers
sub: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart → Frédéric Chopin · documented
k: chopin varies mozart’s la ci darem; schumann cheers wolfgang amadeus mozart → frederic chopin · documented at seventeen chopin wrote a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the duet sung by don giovanni and zerlina in mozart’s opera, and dedicated it to his schoolfriend tytus woyciechowski; it was published in 1830. schumann, who practised it for months, answered it through his alter ego eusebius in the allgemeine musikalische zeitung of 7 december 1831 with the cry “hats off, gentlemen”. chopin’s own view of the leipzig reviews was cooler: of friedrich wieck’s notice in caecilia he wrote that wieck, “instead of being clever, is very stupid”. mozart, don giovanni, act i duet “la ci darem la mano” (1787) chopin, variations on “la ci darem la mano”, op. 2, piano and orchestra (1827)

title: Berlioz sees Hamlet at the Odéon, 1827
k: berlioz sees hamlet at the odeon, 1827 william shakespeare → hector berlioz · documented on 11 september 1827 berlioz saw hamlet at the odeon with harriet smithson as ophelia; on 15 september he saw her as juliet. he calls the evening, in the memoires (chapter 18), the “greatest drama” of his life and says shakespeare, arriving unawares, struck him like a thunderbolt. he married smithson in 1833, and the plays stayed with him: romeo et juliette (1839) and beatrice et benedict (1862, after much ado about nothing) are the largest results. hamlet and romeo and juliet, odeon, paris, 11 and 15 september 1827 romeo et juliette, op. 17 (1839); beatrice et benedict (1862)

title: Berlioz hears Habeneck’s Beethoven at the Conservatoire
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Hector Berlioz · documented
k: berlioz hears habeneck’s beethoven at the conservatoire ludwig van beethoven → hector berlioz · documented the societe des concerts du conservatoire, directed by francois habeneck, gave its first concert on 9 march 1828, and from then on paris heard beethoven’s symphonies played regularly. in his memoires (chapter 20) berlioz says the shock was almost equal to shakespeare’s: beethoven opened a new world in music as the poet had opened one in poetry. from 1828 he also studied and copied beethoven’s scores in the conservatoire library. two years later habeneck conducted the premiere of the symphonie fantastique in the same hall. beethoven’s symphonies, societe des concerts du conservatoire (first concert 9 march 1828) symphonie fantastique, op. 14 (premiere 5 december 1830)

title: Mendelssohn conducts the St Matthew Passion, Berlin, 1829
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Felix Mendelssohn · documented
k: mendelssohn conducts the st matthew passion, berlin, 1829 johann sebastian bach → felix mendelssohn · documented mendelssohn’s grandmother bella salomon had given him a copy of the st matthew passion score in the mid-1820s, and his teacher carl friedrich zelter, head of the sing-akademie, held a store of bach scores but would not perform the work in public. on 11 march 1829, aged twenty, mendelssohn conducted the passion at the sing-akademie in berlin, the first performance outside leipzig. he cut about a third of the arias and half the choruses but few chorales, and the revival is usually counted as the start of the bach revival. bach, st matthew passion, bwv 244 mendelssohn’s revival, berlin sing-akademie, 11 march 1829

title: Berlioz reads Nerval’s Faust and sets eight scenes
sub: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe → Hector Berlioz · documented
k: berlioz reads nerval’s faust and sets eight scenes johann wolfgang von goethe → hector berlioz · documented berlioz first read goethe’s faust in gerard de nerval’s prose translation and says in the memoires (chapter 26) that he could not put it down, reading it at table, in the theatre and in the street. he set the translation’s verse fragments as huit scenes de faust, had them engraved at his own expense in 1829, then collected and destroyed the copies; the “concert des sylphes” was sung at his conservatoire concert of 1 november 1829. twenty years later he reworked those ideas into la damnation de faust, first given at the opera-comique on 6 december 1846. goethe, faust part one, in gerard de nerval’s french translation (1828) huit scenes de faust (1828–29); la damnation de faust (1846)

title: Schumann’s Papillons retell the masked ball in Flegeljahre
k: schumann’s papillons retell the masked ball in flegeljahre jean paul → robert schumann · documented in april 1832 schumann explained to the editor ludwig rellstab how his papillons arose: he asked him to recall the last scene of jean paul’s flegeljahre, the masked ball, the dancing, the exchange of masks, the confessions and the brother’s departure. he said he kept turning to the last page, “almost unconsciously” found himself at the piano, and one piece after another came into being. in november 1829 he had written to friedrich wieck that schubert was “my only schubert” just as jean paul was “my only jean paul”. jean paul, flegeljahre (1804–05), final masked-ball chapters schumann, papillons, op. 2 (1829–31)

title: Liszt hears Paganini at the Opéra, April 1832
k: liszt hears paganini at the opera, april 1832 niccolo paganini → franz liszt · documented liszt, not yet twenty-one, first heard paganini on 22 april 1832 at an opera benefit for victims of the cholera epidemic (some sources give 20 april). on 2 may he wrote to pierre wolff that he was practising exercises “four or five hours” a day and studying a long shelf of authors and composers at once. the first result was the grande fantaisie de bravoure sur la clochette (1832); the six paganini etudes were published in 1838 and revised in 1851, with five of them based on paganini’s caprices. paganini, benefit concert at the paris opera, 22 april 1832; caprices op. 1 liszt, etudes d’execution transcendante d’apres paganini (1838); grandes etudes de paganini (1851)

title: Chopin dedicates his Op. 10 études to Liszt
k: chopin dedicates his op. 10 etudes to liszt frederic chopin → franz liszt · documented chopin dedicated his twelve op. 10 etudes, published in 1833, “to my friend franz liszt”; the second set, op. 25, went to liszt’s companion marie d’agoult. that june, in a letter to ferdinand hiller, chopin wrote that he did not know what his pen was scribbling because liszt was playing his etudes at that moment, and that he wished he could steal from liszt the way to play them. chopin, 12 etudes, op. 10 (1833), “a mon ami franz liszt” liszt playing the op. 10 etudes (joint letter to hiller, june 1833)

title: Paganini’s viola request becomes Byron’s Harold in Italy
k: paganini’s viola request becomes byron’s harold in italy lord byron → hector berlioz · documented paganini asked berlioz for a showpiece for his stradivari viola, then rejected the first movement because the viola rested too long. berlioz kept the plan but made the solo a “melancholy dreamer in the manner of byron’s childe harold”, set among his memories of the abruzzi, and named the symphony harold en italie. as in the fantastique, a theme recurs, but the viola theme is laid over the orchestra’s tunes instead of interrupting them; the first performance was at the conservatoire on 23 november 1834. byron, childe harold’s pilgrimage (1812–18) harold en italie, op. 16, for viola and orchestra (premiere 23 november 1834)

title: Mendelssohn learns Chopin’s new nocturne by ear
k: mendelssohn learns chopin’s new nocturne by ear frederic chopin → felix mendelssohn · documented in september 1835 chopin visited leipzig, where he played at friedrich wieck’s house and met both schumann and mendelssohn. he played the d♭ nocturne, which was then new; mendelssohn wrote to his sister hensel that chopin “has also such a lovely new notturno, a considerable part of which i learnt by ear”. the two op. 27 nocturnes were published the following year in leipzig, paris and london. chopin, nocturne in d♭, op. 27 no. 2, played at friedrich wieck’s house, leipzig, september 1835 mendelssohn’s letter to his sister fanny

title: Mendelssohn conducts Clara Wieck’s piano concerto, 1835
k: mendelssohn conducts clara wieck’s piano concerto, 1835 felix mendelssohn → clara schumann · documented clara wieck began her piano concerto at thirteen, in january 1833. robert schumann revised the orchestration of its first movement in 1834; she later undid his changes, orchestrated it herself, and finished the three-movement concerto on 1 september 1835, twelve days before her sixteenth birthday. mendelssohn conducted the leipzig gewandhaus orchestra at the first performance of the complete work on 9 november 1835, with clara as soloist. mendelssohn conducting the leipzig gewandhaus orchestra, 9 november 1835 clara wieck, piano concerto in a minor, op. 7 (1833–35)

title: Schumann hides a Beethoven song in his Fantasie
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Robert Schumann · documented
k: schumann hides a beethoven song in his fantasie ludwig van beethoven → robert schumann · documented schumann began the fantasie in 1836 as ruines, a piece written in his distress at being parted from clara wieck. he expanded it into a work to raise money for the beethoven monument in bonn, offering 100 presentation copies to the publisher kistner. the last bars of the first movement quote the phrase “nimm sie hin denn, diese lieder” (“accept, then, these songs”) from beethoven’s song cycle, a quotation schumann did not acknowledge and which apparently went unnoticed until 1910. he dedicated the published score, of 1839, to liszt. beethoven, an die ferne geliebte, op. 98 (1816), last song “nimm sie hin denn, diese lieder” schumann, fantasie in c, op. 17, first movement, closing bars (1836; published 1839)

title: Liszt puts all nine Beethoven symphonies on the piano
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Franz Liszt · documented
k: liszt puts all nine beethoven symphonies on the piano ludwig van beethoven → franz liszt · documented liszt began transcribing the fifth symphony around the end of 1835, and by mid-1837 had finished nos. 5, 6 and 7 for solo piano; the fifth and sixth were published in 1840 with a dedication to the painter ingres. after twenty-three years breitkopf & hartel asked him to go on, and the nine appeared together in 1865, dedicated to hans von bulow. he had made a two-piano version of the ninth in 1850 and at first doubted that its finale could be arranged effectively for one piano. beethoven, symphonies nos. 1–9 liszt, symphonies de beethoven, s. 464 (nos. 5–7 by 1837; the nine complete in 1865) ode-to-joy

title: Chopin sings Bellini’s line at the piano
k: chopin sings bellini’s line at the piano vincenzo bellini → frederic chopin · documented bellini’s friendship with chopin dates from his stay in paris, which began in 1833. on 31 march 1837 chopin contributed the largo sixth variation to hexameron, the set of variations on “suoni la tromba” from i puritani that princess belgiojoso commissioned from six pianists for a benefit in her paris salon. chopin told pupils to study the great opera singers and to imitate them, and a programme note on the op. 27 nocturnes hears a “bel canto melody over rippling broken chords” in the d♭ nocturne. bellini, i puritani (1835), march “suoni la tromba”; the bel canto vocal line chopin, variation vi (largo) in hexameron (1837); nocturne in d♭, op. 27 no. 2 (1835)

title: Clara’s mazurka opens Schumann’s Davidsbündlertänze
k: clara’s mazurka opens schumann’s davidsbundlertanze clara schumann → robert schumann · documented clara wieck and schumann became secretly engaged on 14 august 1837, against her father’s opposition; within a week he began the davidsbundlertanze. the opening bars, headed “motto by c. w.”, quote the start of the mazurka that is no. 5 of her soirees musicales, op. 6, and he began to sketch a whole piece on her theme. schumann later said that these pieces were more urgently addressed to her than anything else he had written; the published set is inscribed to walther von goethe, the poet’s grandson. clara wieck, soirees musicales, op. 6, no. 5, mazurka (1836) schumann, davidsbundlertanze, op. 6, no. 1, “motto by c. w.” (1837)

title: Clara Wieck plays Beethoven; Grillparzer writes a poem
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Clara Schumann · documented
k: clara wieck plays beethoven; grillparzer writes a poem ludwig van beethoven → clara schumann · documented clara wieck reached vienna in december 1837 and, once sure of her audience, added chopin, bach and beethoven to her programmes, which was rare then. her playing of beethoven’s appassionata moved the poet franz grillparzer to write “clara wieck und beethoven” in january 1838. schumann called it the most beautiful poem ever written about her and printed it in the neue zeitschrift fur musik that month. beethoven, piano sonata in f minor, op. 57 (“appassionata”) clara wieck’s vienna concerts, december 1837–april 1838; grillparzer, “clara wieck und beethoven” (january 1838)

title: Hoffmann’s mad Kapellmeister becomes Schumann’s Kreisleriana
sub: E. T. A. Hoffmann → Robert Schumann · documented
k: hoffmann’s mad kapellmeister becomes schumann’s kreisleriana e. t. a. hoffmann → robert schumann · documented schumann’s eight kreisleriana take their title from johannes kreisler, the eccentric, wild and witty kapellmeister in e. t. a. hoffmann’s fantasy pieces in callot’s manner and in kater murr. schumann told clara in 1838 that she and one of her ideas played the main role in the work, and that he wanted to dedicate it to her alone; the printed dedication is to chopin. he said he wrote it in four days in april 1838, a claim one biographer dates differently, to between may and september. e. t. a. hoffmann, “kreisleriana”, fantasy pieces in callot’s manner (1814–15); kater murr schumann, kreisleriana, op. 16 (1838)

title: Paganini’s 20,000 francs pay for Roméo et Juliette
k: paganini’s 20,000 francs pay for romeo et juliette niccolo paganini → hector berlioz · documented paganini, by then voiceless, heard harold en italie for the first time at berlioz’s conservatoire concert of 16 december 1838, and had his son achille relay his admiration. two days later he wrote that with beethoven dead only berlioz could revive him, and sent 20,000 francs through the baron de rothschild. the money cleared berlioz’s debts and left him free to compose: romeo et juliette was given three times, on 24 november, 1 and 15 december 1839. paganini’s letter and gift, paris, 18 december 1838 romeo et juliette, op. 17 (first given 24 november 1839)

title: Chopin finishes 24 Preludes with Bach’s Forty-Eight at hand
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Frédéric Chopin · documented
k: chopin finishes 24 preludes with bach’s forty-eight at hand johann sebastian bach → frederic chopin · documented chopin spent the winter of 1838–39 at valldemossa, majorca, where he had a copy of the well-tempered clavier and finished his op. 28 preludes, a cycle through all twenty-four keys. he ordered them differently from bach, by the circle of fifths with each major key followed by its relative minor, and wrote no fugues. jean-jacques eigeldinger’s study of chopin’s markings in the wtc copy of his pupil pauline chazaren shows that by 1838 he knew a paris edition of the work thoroughly. bach, the well-tempered clavier (24 preludes and fugues in each of two books) chopin, 24 preludes, op. 28 (1835–39; published 1839)

title: Wagner attends Berlioz’s Roméo et Juliette in Paris
k: wagner attends berlioz’s romeo et juliette in paris hector berlioz → richard wagner · documented on 15 december 1839 wagner, newly arrived in paris, was present at the third performance of romeo et juliette at the conservatoire, conducted by berlioz; the programme also had two movements of harold en italie and a movement of the requiem. in may 1841 wagner published an article that had a great deal to say about berlioz, and in early 1860 he sent berlioz the score of tristan inscribed to “the dear and great author of romeo and juliet”, from “the grateful author of tristan”. the editor of the berlioz website takes the inscription as wagner’s open acknowledgement of berlioz’s influence on his work. berlioz, romeo et juliette, third performance, paris conservatoire, 15 december 1839 wagner’s article on berlioz (dresdner abendzeitung, may 1841); tristan inscription (1860)

title: Schumann finds Schubert’s Great C major in Vienna
k: schumann finds schubert’s great c major in vienna franz schubert → robert schumann · documented the gesellschaft der musikfreunde in vienna, to whom schubert had sent the score, tried it briefly and rejected it for its length and difficulty. in january 1839 schumann visited schubert’s brother ferdinand in vienna and discovered a copy of the manuscript among the composer’s papers; he took a copy back to leipzig and sent it to mendelssohn, who conducted the first complete public performance with the gewandhaus orchestra on 21 march 1839. schumann’s article in the neue zeitschrift fur musik praised the symphony’s “heavenly length”, likening it to a four-volume novel, perhaps by jean paul. schubert, symphony in c major, d. 944 (“great”, 1825–26), manuscript held by his brother ferdinand schumann’s copy sent to leipzig; first complete performance, gewandhaus, 21 march 1839, conducted by mendelssohn

title: Did Mickiewicz’s poems inspire Chopin’s Ballades?
k: did mickiewicz’s poems inspire chopin’s ballades? adam mickiewicz → frederic chopin · disputed in 1841 robert schumann reported in the neue zeitschrift fur musik that chopin had told him poems by the polish poet adam mickiewicz inspired his ballades. chopin left no statement of his own, and schumann’s remark concerned the second ballade in particular. a tradition links the first ballade with konrad wallenrod, a poem about a lithuanian raised among the teutonic knights who leads them to defeat; no document ties either piece to a particular poem. when schumann visited leipzig in 1836 he told chopin that the g minor ballade was his favourite of chopin’s works, and chopin replied that it was his too. adam mickiewicz, ballady i romanse (1822) and konrad wallenrod (1828) chopin, ballades nos. 1–4 (no. 1, op. 23, composed 1835–36)

title: Wilhelm Hensel draws each month of Fanny’s Das Jahr
k: wilhelm hensel draws each month of fanny’s das jahr wilhelm hensel → fanny hensel · documented hensel composed das jahr, twelve piano pieces depicting the months, in 1841 and gave it to her husband, the painter wilhelm hensel, as a christmas present. they then reworked it together: the music was written on tinted paper, wilhelm drew a vignette into the score for each month, and each piece carries a short poem by a german poet. the image shown is the opening of april. wilhelm hensel, pen vignettes for each month, in the manuscript of das jahr (1842) fanny hensel, das jahr, twelve piano pieces, one for each month (1841)

title: Mendelssohn invites Berlioz to Leipzig and swaps batons
k: mendelssohn invites berlioz to leipzig and swaps batons felix mendelssohn → hector berlioz · documented mendelssohn had been berlioz’s guide in rome in 1831: each morning he played a beethoven sonata, berlioz wrote home, and they sang gluck’s armide. it was through mendelssohn that berlioz was invited to leipzig in 1843, where he gave gewandhaus concerts on 4 and 22 february. the two exchanged batons “as a token of friendship”, but berlioz noted that mendelssohn praised his romances and said nothing of the symphonies, overtures or requiem. mendelssohn’s invitation and gewandhaus concerts, leipzig, february 1843 berlioz’s gewandhaus concerts of 4 and 22 february 1843

title: Schumann writes six fugues on B–A–C–H, 1845
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Robert Schumann · documented
k: schumann writes six fugues on b–a–c–h, 1845 johann sebastian bach → robert schumann · documented both schumann and liszt wrote works on the four-note motif that spells bach’s name in german notation, and both helped found the bach-gesellschaft in 1850. schumann finished his six fugues on the name bach in november 1845, calling them the work that would, he believed, outlive his others, and saying he had tried to make them worthy of the great name they bear. the first fugue introduces the four notes slowly and builds from a sombre exposition; the second compresses the subject and adds baroque semiquaver figures. bach, third subject of the unfinished fugue of the art of fugue (b♭–a–c–b♮) schumann, six fugues on the name bach, op. 60 (organ or pedal piano), 1845 bach-motif

title: Wagner conducts Beethoven’s Ninth in Dresden, 1846
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Richard Wagner · documented
k: wagner conducts beethoven’s ninth in dresden, 1846 ludwig van beethoven → richard wagner · documented wagner made a piano transcription of beethoven’s ninth in 1830, aged seventeen. on palm sunday, 5 april 1846, he conducted it in dresden, where robert schumann was living and, on christopher reynolds’s evidence, also studying the work: reynolds traces a more contrapuntal, motivic style in both composers to their study of the ninth, including beethoven’s gradual development of the “ode to joy” melody. wagner conducted the ninth at bayreuth’s margravial opera house in 1872 to mark the laying of the festspielhaus foundation stone, not the opening of the completed theatre. beethoven, symphony no. 9, op. 125 wagner’s dresden performance, palm sunday, 5 april 1846; bayreuth foundation-stone concert, 1872 ode-to-joy

title: Verdi sets Macbeth, his first Shakespeare opera
k: verdi sets macbeth, his first shakespeare opera william shakespeare → giuseppe verdi · documented verdi’s macbeth, first given at the teatro della pergola in florence on 14 march 1847, was the first shakespeare play he adapted for the stage. he told his librettist piave that the tragedy was “one of the greatest creations of man” and that if they could not make something great of it they should at least make something out of the ordinary. in 1865 he wrote that shakespeare was “one of my favorite poets”, whom he had had “in my hands from my earliest youth”. for the revised version, given in french in paris on 21 april 1865, he insisted that the witches rule the drama. shakespeare, macbeth (c. 1606) verdi, macbeth, premiere 14 march 1847, florence; revised french version, 21 april 1865, paris

title: From Berlioz’s Witches’ Sabbath to Liszt’s Totentanz
k: from berlioz’s witches’ sabbath to liszt’s totentanz hector berlioz → franz liszt · inferred in the finale of the symphonie fantastique, berlioz gives the dies irae chant to four bassoons and two ophicleides in c minor from bar 127, a funeral rite turned into a parody at the witches’ sabbath. liszt met berlioz the day before the premiere on 5 december 1830 and in 1833 made the piano transcription of the symphony. his totentanz, planned in 1838, completed in 1849 and revised in 1853 and 1859, is a set of variations for piano and orchestra on the same chant. a second recorded source is the triumph of death fresco in the campo santo at pisa, which liszt saw in 1838. berlioz, symphonie fantastique, v: dies irae from bar 127, bassoons and ophicleides (1830) liszt, totentanz: paraphrase on dies irae, s. 126, piano and orchestra (completed 1849) dies-irae

title: Liszt conducts Lohengrin while Wagner is in exile
k: liszt conducts lohengrin while wagner is in exile franz liszt → richard wagner · documented wagner had fled saxony after the may 1849 uprising in dresden, in which he took part, and could not attend the first production of lohengrin. liszt conducted it at weimar on 28 august 1850, a date he chose to honour goethe, who was born there in 1749; david trippett’s study calls the decision politically as well as artistically risky for the weimar court. wagner did not see a complete performance until vienna in 1861; in the meantime he conducted extracts in zurich, london, paris and brussels. liszt’s weimar production, court theatre, 28 august 1850 wagner, lohengrin, wwv 75

title: Verdi sees La Dame aux camélias and writes Traviata
sub: Alexandre Dumas fils → Giuseppe Verdi · documented
k: verdi sees la dame aux camelias and writes traviata alexandre dumas fils → giuseppe verdi · documented in february 1852 verdi and giuseppina strepponi attended a performance in paris of alexandre dumas fils’s la dame aux camelias, a play adapted from his own 1848 novel. his biographer mary jane phillips-matz reports that he began composing at once, though julian budden notes that verdi had probably read the book earlier. francesco maria piave wrote the libretto, and la traviata was first performed at la fenice, venice, on 6 march 1853. alexandre dumas fils, la dame aux camelias (novel 1848; play, paris, 1852) verdi, la traviata, venice, 6 march 1853; act i prelude

title: Did Brahms fall asleep during Liszt’s B minor Sonata?
k: did brahms fall asleep during liszt’s b minor sonata? franz liszt → johannes brahms · disputed in 1853 brahms and the violinist ede remenyi visited weimar, where brahms met liszt, peter cornelius and joachim raff, and liszt played brahms’s scherzo, op. 4, at sight. remenyi later claimed that brahms then slept while liszt played his own b minor sonata. this and other disagreements led remenyi and brahms to part company; that autumn brahms went instead to the schumanns in dusseldorf. liszt, piano sonata in b minor, s. 178 (completed 1853), played at weimar brahms’s visit to weimar with ede remenyi, june 1853

title: Schumann’s “Neue Bahnen” launches the 20-year-old Brahms
k: schumann’s “neue bahnen” launches the 20-year-old brahms robert schumann → johannes brahms · documented in october 1853, with a letter of introduction from joseph joachim, the twenty-year-old brahms called on the schumanns in dusseldorf and played his works from memory. robert is said to have broken off to fetch clara, saying she must hear music “as you have never heard it before”; she noted in her diary that the visitor seemed “specially sent by god”. on 28 october schumann published “neue bahnen” in the neue zeitschrift fur musik, naming brahms as the one fated to give the age its highest and most ideal expression; publishers began to take an interest at once. schumann, “neue bahnen”, neue zeitschrift fur musik, 28 october 1853 brahms’s first publications (opp. 1–6) and his ties to robert and clara schumann

title: Wagner finds Schopenhauer and plans Tristan, 1854
k: wagner finds schopenhauer and plans tristan, 1854 arthur schopenhauer → richard wagner · documented on 16 december 1854 wagner wrote from zurich to liszt that he had been absorbed in a “gift from heaven”, arthur schopenhauer, “the greatest philosopher since kant”; the poet georg herwegh had urged him to read the world as will and representation. in the same letter he announces tristan und isolde: never having known the true bliss of love, he would “erect a monument to the most beautiful of all my dreams”, a conception he calls the simplest but most full-blooded imaginable, ending under a black flag. the first musical sketches date from 19 december 1856, and on 9 august 1857 he broke off siegfried to compose it. schopenhauer, die welt als wille und vorstellung (1819; 2nd ed. 1844) wagner, tristan und isolde (composed 1857–59); letter to liszt, 16 december 1854 tristan-chord

title: Brahms varies the same Schumann theme as Clara
k: brahms varies the same schumann theme as clara robert schumann → johannes brahms · documented brahms wrote his op. 9 variations in dusseldorf in may and june 1854, with variations 10 and 11 added in september, while robert schumann was confined in the asylum at endenich near bonn. he took the theme from the fourth piece of schumann’s bunte blatter, op. 99, the same theme that schumann had chosen for her own variations, op. 20, in 1853. clara is the dedicatee, and brahms brought each variation to show her as he wrote it. schumann, bunte blatter, op. 99, no. 4 (1838–41); clara schumann, variations op. 20 (1853) brahms, variations on a theme by robert schumann, op. 9 (may–june and september 1854)

title: Brahms signs against Wagner’s party, then helps Wagner
k: brahms signs against wagner’s party, then helps wagner richard wagner → johannes brahms · documented in 1860 a manifesto against the “pursuits of a certain party” whose organ was brendel’s neue zeitschrift fur musik circulated with the signatures of brahms, joseph joachim and others; its author was almost certainly brahms. it leaked, the neue zeitschrift parodied it on 4 may, and it appeared in the echo on 6 may with more than twenty names. yet in vienna brahms helped prepare wagner’s concerts of 1862–63, was given a manuscript of part of tannhauser (wagner demanded it back in 1875), and in january 1863 played wagner his handel variations; the meeting was cordial. the new german school’s organ, brendel’s neue zeitschrift fur musik; wagner’s vienna concerts of 1862–63 the 1860 manifesto, almost certainly drafted by brahms; brahms’s help with wagner’s concerts

title: Berlioz “reads and re-reads” the Tristan prelude, baffled
k: berlioz “reads and re-reads” the tristan prelude, baffled richard wagner → hector berlioz · documented wagner’s paris concerts of january–february 1860 included the tristan prelude, and berlioz reviewed them in the journal des debats on 9 february. he describes a slow piece that starts pianissimo, swells to fortissimo and falls back, with “no theme other than a sort of chromatic moaning” over dissonances whose long appoggiaturas replace the real note of the harmony. he says he has read the “strange page” again and again, listened with full attention, and still cannot tell what the composer means. wagner, who had sent him the tristan score early in 1860, answered with an open letter in the same paper on 22 february. wagner, tristan und isolde, act i prelude (concert at the salle ventadour, february 1860) berlioz, review of wagner’s concerts, journal des debats, 9 february 1860 tristan-chord

title: Brahms builds twenty-five variations on a Handel aria
sub: George Frideric Handel → Johannes Brahms · documented
k: brahms builds twenty-five variations on a handel aria george frideric handel → johannes brahms · documented brahms took the theme of op. 24 from an aria in the third movement of handel’s suite no. 1 in b♭, hwv 434, and owned a copy of the 1733 first edition. he wrote the work in a single stretch in september 1861, twenty-five variations and a fugue, and gave it to schumann on her forty-second birthday, 13 september. she first played it in hamburg on 7 december 1861 and repeated it soon afterwards in leipzig. handel, harpsichord suite no. 1 in b♭, hwv 434: aria in the third movement (walsh, 1733) brahms, variations and fugue on a theme by handel, op. 24 (september 1861)

title: Saint-Saëns brings Schumann, Liszt and Wagner to Fauré’s school
k: saint-saens brings schumann, liszt and wagner to faure’s school camille saint-saens → gabriel faure · documented gabriel faure boarded at the ecole niedermeyer in paris from the age of nine, trained as church organist and choirmaster; louis niedermeyer himself taught piano, plainsong and composition. when niedermeyer died in march 1861, saint-saens took charge of piano studies and introduced the pupils to contemporary music, including that of schumann, liszt and wagner. faure recalled this in old age, and saint-saens remained a lifelong friend; in 1877 he took faure to weimar to meet liszt. saint-saens’s piano classes at the ecole niedermeyer, paris, from 1861 faure’s early melodies and piano works

title: Rimsky-Korsakov learns orchestration from Berlioz’s Treatise
k: rimsky-korsakov learns orchestration from berlioz’s treatise hector berlioz → nikolai rimsky-korsakov · documented inexperienced in orchestration when he began his first symphony in 1861, rimsky-korsakov turned to hector berlioz’s treatise as well as to the advice of balakirev. thirty years later, in the 1891 preface to his own principles of orchestration, he named berlioz first among the colourists, with glinka, liszt and wagner, who had brought orchestral colour to its zenith. he told students that weber, mendelssohn, berlioz, glinka, wagner, liszt and modern french and russian composers would be their best guides. berlioz, grand traite d’instrumentation et d’orchestration modernes (1844) rimsky-korsakov, symphony no. 1 (1861–65); principles of orchestration (preface 1891)

title: Wagner’s Beckmesser began as “Veit Hanslich”
k: wagner’s beckmesser began as “veit hanslich” eduard hanslick → richard wagner · inferred when wagner turned the meistersinger prose draft into a libretto in vienna in 1861, he named the pedantic town clerk who marks the singers’ faults “veit hanslich”, an open allusion to the vienna critic eduard hanslick. by the time wagner first read the text aloud in vienna on 23 november 1862, with hanslick among the listeners, the name had become sixtus beckmesser. hanslick, who championed schumann and brahms against wagner and liszt, knew he was the target. eduard hanslick, vienna’s leading critic (on the musically beautiful, 1854) wagner, die meistersinger von nurnberg: the merker, then beckmesser (prose draft 1861; reading in vienna, 23 november 1862)

title: Tchaikovsky attends all six Wagner concerts in St Petersburg
sub: Richard Wagner → Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky · documented
k: tchaikovsky attends all six wagner concerts in st petersburg richard wagner → pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · documented in 1863, in his first year at the conservatory, tchaikovsky attended all six concerts that wagner gave in st petersburg. they included the prelude and “liebestod” from tristan und isolde and beethoven’s third and fifth to eighth symphonies; tchaikovsky counted the experience among the most memorable of his life. in 1875 he heard klindworth play through the whole ring in piano transcription, and in august 1876 he reached bayreuth for the first rheingold as correspondent for a moscow newspaper. wagner conducting in st petersburg, 1863: tristan prelude and liebestod, beethoven symphonies and others tchaikovsky’s bayreuth reports of 1876 and his later verdict on wagner tristan-chord

title: Balakirev guides and premieres Rimsky-Korsakov’s First Symphony
k: balakirev guides and premieres rimsky-korsakov’s first symphony mily balakirev → nikolai rimsky-korsakov · documented rimsky-korsakov wrote his symphony no. 1 between 1861 and 1865 under the guidance of balakirev, who conducted its first performance at a free music school concert in december 1865. the composer acknowledged schumann’s manfred overture and third symphony, glinka’s prince kholmsky and balakirev’s king lear overture as models. he later wrote that he felt his own ignorance but was convinced that balakirev knew everything, and that balakirev cleverly concealed from him and the others of “the five” the insufficiency of his own training. balakirev’s guidance of the young naval cadet, 1861–65 rimsky-korsakov, symphony no. 1, op. 1 (premiered by balakirev, december 1865)

title: Mussorgsky sets Gogol’s Marriage as Dargomyzhsky set Pushkin
k: mussorgsky sets gogol’s marriage as dargomyzhsky set pushkin alexander dargomyzhsky → modest mussorgsky · documented mussorgsky’s idea of setting gogol’s comedy marriage came from the advice and example of alexander dargomyzhsky, who in 1866 began the stone guest, declaring that pushkin’s text would be set “just as it stands, so that the inner truth of the text should not be distorted”. it replaced the division between aria and recitative with a continuous, syllabic but lyrically heightened declamation. in 1868 mussorgsky quickly set the first eleven scenes of gogol’s prose, catching the natural accents of its humdrum dialogue; he left the work unfinished. dargomyzhsky, the stone guest, pushkin’s text set “just as it stands” (begun 1866) mussorgsky, zhenitba (marriage), after gogol’s comedy (begun 1868; unfinished)

title: Mussorgsky turns Pushkin’s Boris Godunov into an opera
k: mussorgsky turns pushkin’s boris godunov into an opera alexander pushkin → modest mussorgsky · documented in the autumn of 1868 the historian vladimir nikolsky suggested to mussorgsky an opera on pushkin’s “dramatic chronicle” boris godunov, and lyudmila shestakova gave him a volume of pushkin’s plays interleaved with blank pages; he began his own libretto in october. he finished the score in december 1869, and the imperial theatres rejected it on 10 february 1871 by six votes to one, ostensibly for lack of a major female role. the revised version of 1872 was first performed at the mariinsky theatre on 27 january 1874. pushkin, boris godunov (written 1825, published 1831); karamzin, history of the russian state mussorgsky, boris godunov (original version 1869; revised 1872; premiere 27 january 1874)

title: Balakirev sets Tchaikovsky’s Romeo and Juliet in order
sub: Mily Balakirev → Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky · documented
k: balakirev sets tchaikovsky’s romeo and juliet in order mily balakirev → pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · documented balakirev suggested the subject of romeo and juliet to tchaikovsky when they met in moscow in the summer of 1869, after criticising tchaikovsky’s fatum frankly. he sent a plan describing the type of music for each section, with advice on keys, and held up his own king lear overture as a model. tchaikovsky wrote on 14 october 1869 that he was “played out completely”; “abusive letters” from balakirev followed, and on 24 october he reported he was writing the overture. the work is dedicated to balakirev, though the inscription was left off the first printed scores. balakirev’s letters and his overture king lear (as formal model), 1869 tchaikovsky, romeo and juliet, fantasy overture (first version 1869; dedicated to balakirev)

title: Verdi annotates Lohengrin at Bologna, November 1871
k: verdi annotates lohengrin at bologna, november 1871 richard wagner → giuseppe verdi · documented angelo mariani conducted the first performance of a wagner opera in italy, lohengrin at the teatro comunale of bologna, on 1 november 1871. on 9 november verdi attended and annotated a copy of the vocal score with his impressions and opinions; it was almost certainly his first exposure to wagner’s music. in 1887 a german visitor recorded him as saying there was much to admire in tannhauser and lohengrin, but that in his later operas wagner seemed to overstep the limits of what music can express. wagner, lohengrin, italian premiere at the teatro comunale, bologna, 1 november 1871 verdi’s pencilled notes in a vocal score, 9 november 1871

title: Bruckner dedicates his Third Symphony to Wagner
k: bruckner dedicates his third symphony to wagner richard wagner → anton bruckner · documented in september 1873, before the third symphony was finished, bruckner visited wagner, whom he had first met at the munich premiere of tristan und isolde in 1865. he showed wagner his second and third symphonies and asked him to choose; wagner chose the third, and bruckner dedicated it to him. the 1873 score quoted wagner’s die walkure and tristan in the first movement and lohengrin and walkure in the adagio; after the vienna premiere of 1877 failed, bruckner’s revisions removed most of these quotations. wagner, die walkure, tristan und isolde, lohengrin, tannhauser bruckner, symphony no. 3 in d minor, wab 103 (1873 version) tristan-chord

title: Mussorgsky walks through Hartmann’s memorial exhibition
k: mussorgsky walks through hartmann’s memorial exhibition viktor hartmann → modest mussorgsky · documented viktor hartmann, an architect and designer, died suddenly on 4 august 1873, aged thirty-nine. the critic vladimir stasov helped organise a memorial exhibition of over 400 of his works at the imperial academy of arts in february and march 1874; mussorgsky lent the two pictures hartmann had given him in 1868 and viewed the show. he composed pictures at an exhibition between 2 and 22 june 1874 and dedicated it to stasov. “ballet of the unhatched chicks” answers hartmann’s costume sketch of canary chicks for the ballet trilby (1871). viktor hartmann’s drawings and designs, memorial exhibition, st petersburg, february–march 1874 mussorgsky, pictures at an exhibition, piano suite (composed 2–22 june 1874)

title: Brahms’s finale tune answers Beethoven’s Ode to Joy
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven → Johannes Brahms · documented
k: brahms’s finale tune answers beethoven’s ode to joy ludwig van beethoven → johannes brahms · documented the broad tune that brahms gives the strings in the c-major allegro of his first symphony finale resembles the “ode to joy” theme of beethoven’s ninth. when this was pointed out to him he is reported to have answered “any ass can see that”. in 1877 the conductor hans von bulow called the symphony “beethoven’s tenth”; it was first played at karlsruhe on 4 november 1876 under felix otto dessoff. beethoven, symphony no. 9, finale: “ode to joy” theme (1824) brahms, symphony no. 1, finale: main allegro theme (first performed 4 november 1876) ode-to-joy

title: Tchaikovsky sets Pushkin’s own verses in Eugene Onegin
sub: Alexander Pushkin → Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky · documented
k: tchaikovsky sets pushkin’s own verses in eugene onegin alexander pushkin → pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · documented in may 1877 the singer yelizaveta lavrovskaya proposed to tchaikovsky an opera on pushkin’s verse novel. he doubted the plot was strong enough, but after a sleepless night embraced the idea and drafted the scenario in a single night. with konstantin shilovsky’s minor help he used original verses from pushkin and chose scenes from the characters’ emotional lives, calling the work “lyrical scenes”. it was first performed at the maly theatre in moscow on 29 march 1879. pushkin, eugene onegin, verse novel (1825–32) tchaikovsky, eugene onegin, “lyrical scenes”, op. 24 (premiere 29 march 1879)

title: Brahms recommends Dvořák to Simrock; Slavonic Dances follow
k: brahms recommends dvorak to simrock; slavonic dances follow johannes brahms → antonin dvorak · documented dvorak won the austrian state prize in 1874, 1876 and 1877. brahms, on the committee, referred him to his own publisher, fritz simrock, who first issued the moravian duets and then asked for something dance-like. unsure how to begin, dvorak took brahms’s hungarian dances as a model, but only as a model: brahms used real hungarian folk melodies, whereas dvorak mostly used the characteristic rhythms of bohemian folk dances with melodies of his own. the op. 46 set, written for piano four hands, was orchestrated soon after at simrock’s request. brahms, hungarian dances (piano four hands) and his referral to simrock dvorak, slavonic dances, op. 46 (1878; orchestrated for simrock)

title: Brahms’s Fourth ends on Bach’s Cantata 150 bass
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Johannes Brahms · documented
k: brahms’s fourth ends on bach’s cantata 150 bass johann sebastian bach → johannes brahms · documented the finale of brahms’s fourth symphony is a passacaglia on an eight-bar theme adapted from the closing chaconne of bach’s cantata 150, which was then unpublished. brahms added a leading tone to bach’s bass and regularised its rhythm into eight dotted half notes that rise from the tonic e to the dominant b, drop an octave and return. the theme is stated thirty times, always eight bars long, before the coda begins at bar 253. bach, cantata nach dir, herr, verlanget mich, bwv 150, closing chaconne brahms, symphony no. 4 in e minor, op. 98, finale: passacaglia

title: Rimsky-Korsakov rebuilds Mussorgsky’s Bald Mountain in 1886
k: rimsky-korsakov rebuilds mussorgsky’s bald mountain in 1886 modest mussorgsky → nikolai rimsky-korsakov · documented mussorgsky finished st john’s eve on bald mountain on 23 june 1867, but balakirev refused to perform it, so he reused the music in the collaborative opera-ballet mlada (1872) and in the fair at sorochyntsi (1880). after mussorgsky’s death in 1881 rimsky-korsakov made his own version, completed and published in 1886, and wrote that its form, modulations and orchestration had resisted him for two years. he conducted the first performance at the russian symphony concerts in st petersburg on 15 october 1886 and made substantial “corrections” to melody, harmony, rhythm and dynamics. mussorgsky, st john’s eve on bald mountain (1867); mlada (1872); the fair at sorochyntsi (1880) rimsky-korsakov, night on bald mountain (completed and published 1886)

title: Tchaikovsky orchestrates Mozart piano pieces as Mozartiana
sub: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart → Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky · documented
k: tchaikovsky orchestrates mozart piano pieces as mozartiana wolfgang amadeus mozart → pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · documented tchaikovsky told his diary in 1886 that he loved beethoven as one fears god but loved mozart “as a musical christ”. at sixteen or seventeen he had heard don giovanni almost by chance and called it a revelation; on 17 may 1884 he wrote “played mozart and was in raptures. thought about a suite from mozart.” in june and july 1887 he orchestrated four pieces, among them the gigue, k. 574, and the minuet, k. 355, as the suite no. 4, which he described to his publisher as “the old given a contemporary treatment”. mozart: gigue, k. 574; minuet, k. 355; liszt’s transcription of ave verum corpus; variations on a theme of gluck tchaikovsky, suite no. 4 “mozartiana”, op. 61 (june–july 1887)

title: Rimsky-Korsakov takes Scheherazade from the Thousand and One Nights
sub: The Thousand and One Nights → Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov · documented
k: rimsky-korsakov takes scheherazade from the thousand and one nights the thousand and one nights → nikolai rimsky-korsakov · documented rimsky-korsakov composed scheherazade in 1888 on themes from the thousand and one nights. after weighing the opinions of anatoly lyadov and others, and his own dislike of a too-definite programme, he settled on thematic headings such as “the young prince and the young princess”, deliberately vague, though the finale’s epigraph does refer to the adventure of prince ajib. in a later edition he dropped the titles altogether, wanting listeners to hear oriental-flavoured symphonic music that suggests fairy-tale adventure. the thousand and one nights; the story of prince ajib rimsky-korsakov, scheherazade, op. 35 (1888; premiere 28 october 1888)

title: Fauré’s Requiem leaves out the Dies irae
k: faure’s requiem leaves out the dies irae gregorian chant → gabriel faure · documented faure’s requiem sets seven movements and omits the full sequence dies irae, keeping only its closing section, the pie jesu; he followed a french baroque tradition in this, did not set the benedictus, and added two texts from the burial service, libera me and in paradisum. he wrote that everything he could muster of religious illusion went into the work, which is “dominated from beginning to end by a very human feeling of faith in eternal rest”. the first version was sung at a funeral at the madeleine in 1888. the requiem sequence dies irae (gregorian chant; setting tradition) faure, requiem, op. 48 (1887–90; first version 1888)

title: Fauré and Messager turn the Ring into a quadrille
k: faure and messager turn the ring into a quadrille richard wagner → gabriel faure · documented from 1878 faure and his former pupil andre messager travelled to hear wagner: das rheingold and die walkure at cologne, the whole ring at munich and london, and die meistersinger and parsifal at bayreuth. their joint souvenirs de bayreuth, a “fantasy in the form of a quadrille on favourite themes from the ring”, was composed probably in 1888 and published in 1930. it grew from improvisations at marguerite de saint-marceaux’s salon, which colette recalled; faure admired wagner yet is described as one of the few of his generation to escape his musical influence. wagner, der ring des nibelungen, as heard by faure and messager at cologne, munich, london and bayreuth faure and messager, souvenirs de bayreuth, quadrille for piano four hands (c. 1888; published 1930)

title: Hoffmann’s Nutcracker reaches Tchaikovsky through Dumas
sub: E. T. A. Hoffmann → Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky · documented
k: hoffmann’s nutcracker reaches tchaikovsky through dumas e. t. a. hoffmann → pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky · documented the libretto of tchaikovsky’s last ballet was compiled by ivan vsevolozhsky and marius petipa from alexandre dumas’s histoire d’un casse-noisette (1845), which dumas adapted from e. t. a. hoffmann’s der nußknacker und mausekonig (1816). tchaikovsky wrote and orchestrated the score between february 1891 and april 1892, and drew a concert suite of eight numbers from it. the christmas eve setting is in eighteenth-century germany, in the home of president silberhaus. e. t. a. hoffmann, nussknacker und mausekonig (1816), in dumas’s histoire d’un casse-noisette (1845) tchaikovsky, the nutcracker, op. 71 (february 1891–april 1892)

title: Burleigh sings spirituals to Dvořák in New York
sub: Harry T. Burleigh → Antonín Dvořák · inferred
k: burleigh sings spirituals to dvorak in new york harry t. burleigh → antonin dvorak · inferred while dvorak directed the national conservatory in new york, the african-american student harry t. burleigh sang traditional spirituals to him; burleigh said dvorak absorbed their “spirit” before writing his own melodies. dvorak is said to have given the largo’s main theme to the cor anglais rather than the clarinet because it reminded him of burleigh’s voice. in the new york herald of 1893 he said the future music of america must be founded on what are called negro melodies. the first movement’s closing theme resembles “swing low, sweet chariot”, but dvorak wrote his own themes. spirituals sung by harry t. burleigh at the national conservatory, new york dvorak, symphony no. 9 “from the new world”, largo (premiere 16 december 1893)

title: Dvořák calls the Largo a Hiawatha study
sub: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow → Antonín Dvořák · documented
k: dvorak calls the largo a hiawatha study henry wadsworth longfellow → antonin dvorak · documented in the new york herald of 15 december 1893, the day before the premiere at carnegie hall, dvorak said that he regarded the second movement as a “sketch or study” for a later cantata or opera on longfellow’s hiawatha, and that the scherzo was suggested by the scene of the feast where the indians dance. no such cantata or opera was written. the symphony was commissioned by the new york philharmonic and first played on 16 december 1893 under anton seidl. longfellow, the song of hiawatha (1855) dvorak, symphony no. 9, largo and scherzo

title: The judgement chant joins a witches’ sabbath
k: the judgement chant joins a witches’ sabbath gregorian chant → hector berlioz · documented berlioz’s own programme names a burlesque parody of the dies irae in the finale of symphonie fantastique. the funeral chant and the witches’ round are first recognisable as separate ideas, then combined: the sacred melody becomes a participant in the nightmare. dies irae, the requiem plainchant symphonie fantastique, v, dream of a witches’ sabbath (1830) dies-irae

title: Liszt turns judgement into piano variations
k: liszt turns judgement into piano variations gregorian chant → franz liszt · documented liszt’s totentanz is a set of six variations on the dies irae, turning the chant into sharply etched writing for piano and orchestra. its plainchant source is secure even though accounts differ over whether a pisa fresco or holbein’s woodcuts supplied the decisive visual stimulus. dies irae, the requiem plainchant totentanz, s. 126, for piano and orchestra dies-irae

title: Saint-Saëns makes the death chant dance
k: saint-saens makes the death chant dance gregorian chant → camille saint-saens · documented in danse macabre, saint-saens recasts the dies irae in a major key inside his orchestral dance of the dead. the altered mode is part of the joke: recognition survives even when the solemn chant acquires a jaunty character. dies irae, the requiem plainchant danse macabre, op. 40 (1874) dies-irae

title: Bach’s name fills the Merseburg organ
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Franz Liszt · documented
k: bach’s name fills the merseburg organ johann sebastian bach → franz liszt · documented liszt planned his b–a–c–h organ work for the refurbished merseburg cathedral instrument, but missed the september 1855 inauguration. alexander winterberger premiered it there on 13 may 1856; liszt later revised the organ version, while also making a distinct virtuoso version for piano. the b–a–c–h musical signature prelude and fugue on b-a-c-h, organ version, s. 260 bach-motif

title: Bach’s name enters a Russian variation cycle
sub: Johann Sebastian Bach → Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov · documented
k: bach’s name enters a russian variation cycle johann sebastian bach → nikolai rimsky-korsakov · documented rimsky-korsakov’s six piano variations on b–a–c–h move through a waltz, intermezzo, scherzo, nocturne and prelude before reaching a fugue. the sequence makes bach’s name material for contrasting character pieces, not just an invitation to imitate an organ fugue. the b–a–c–h musical signature six variations on the theme b-a-c-h, op. 10 (1878) bach-motif

title: The Folia meets Liszt’s Spanish reminiscences
sub: La Folia tradition → Franz Liszt · documented
k: the folia meets liszt’s spanish reminiscences la folia tradition → franz liszt · documented liszt’s rhapsodie espagnole brings the folia together with material from the jota aragonesa. letters asking bulow how to describe its two themes make the inherited sources explicit, while the surviving fair copy fixes july 1864 more securely than liszt’s later recollection of composing it around 1863. folies d’espagne / la folia rhapsodie espagnole, s. 254, fair copy dated july 1864 la-folia

title: Dies irae
sub: The Dies irae is a medieval chant for the Day of Judgement whose opening notes became a musical sign of death. Its recognisable outline lets composers summon terror, turn a dance sinister, or pit mortal fear against consolation.
k: dies irae the dies irae is a medieval chant for the day of judgement whose opening notes became a musical sign of death. its recognisable outline lets composers summon terror, turn a dance sinister, or pit mortal fear against consolation.

title: B–A–C–H
sub: B♭–A–C–B♮ spells Bach in German note names, turning a surname into a four-note musical signature. Later composers used its tightly packed semitones both to salute Bach and to test what their own counterpoint could make of his name.
k: b–a–c–h b♭–a–c–b♮ spells bach in german note names, turning a surname into a four-note musical signature. later composers used its tightly packed semitones both to salute bach and to test what their own counterpoint could make of his name.

title: The Tristan chord
sub: The Tristan chord is the four-note sonority near the opening of Wagner’s prelude whose continuation keeps a firm arrival out of reach. It became a shorthand for unresolved longing that later composers could embrace, remember or mischievously puncture.

title: The lament bass
sub: A lament bass falls step by step through a fourth, sometimes filling the descent with chromatic notes. Returning beneath changing voices, it can make grief feel inescapable without requiring every lament to quote the same melody.

title: La Folia
sub: La Folia is an inherited dance framework whose familiar minor-key melody and harmonic circuit invite successive variations. Its fixed outline lets composers display wildly different rhythms, textures and virtuosity while listeners keep their bearings.

title: Ode to Joy
sub: Beethoven’s Ode to Joy melody carries Schiller’s appeal to human fellowship into the finale of the Ninth Symphony. Its plain, singable shape made it available for virtuoso transcription, symphonic argument and public ceremonies far beyond the concert hall.

title: Frère Jacques
sub: Frère Jacques is a round whose repeated phrases make its tune immediately recognisable even when the surrounding music changes. Mahler’s First Symphony turns that familiarity into estrangement by placing a minor-mode version inside a funeral procession.
